goddard-the-vacuum-and-the-correction-th.context_blurb:
In 1920 the New York Times mocked Robert Goddard, a physics professor at Clark College in Massachusetts, for proposing that rockets might one day fly to the Moon. Forty-nine years later, as Apollo 11 headed there, the paper took it back. Between those dates lies a simple puzzle: in empty space, what does a rocket push against?

The trouble began with a sober 1919 Smithsonian paper on reaching extreme altitudes. Near its end Goddard suggested how to prove a rocket had really got to the Moon: send a tiny load of flash powder to the Moon's dark face, where it would flare on impact brightly enough for a powerful telescope to see. Those few lines set the newspapers off. An unsigned Times editorial in January 1920 sneered that Goddard seemed to lack even the knowledge served up every day in any high school.

He kept building. In March 1926, in the snow of his aunt's farm at Auburn, he launched the first rocket ever to burn liquid fuel. It had no ignition switch, so an assistant lit it with a blowtorch fixed to a long pole and ran for cover. In 1929 another Auburn rocket rose some ninety feet before nosing into the ground and setting the field alight, and the fire marshal forbade any more launches there. Yet that flight was a first, because it carried a barometer, a thermometer and a camera, the first scientific instruments any rocket had lifted.

The editorial claimed a rocket in empty space would have nothing to react against. Goddard had already tested that in 1915. At Clark he sealed a loaded pistol inside a chamber pumped empty of air and fired it, and the escaping gas kicked the gun backward exactly as it would in open air. The chamber tests showed something stranger too: with the air gone, the push grew stronger, because the surrounding air had been cutting the thrust all along. Air is not a rocket's partner; it is in the way.

The editorial writer was not simply foolish. He applied to rockets a fact that is true of a jet engine, which dies in a vacuum because it scoops the oxygen it burns out of the air it flies through. A rocket carries its own oxygen supply along with its fuel.

So what does a rocket push against? Its own exhaust. The engine hurls hot gas backward out of its nozzle, and by Newton's third law the gas pushes the rocket forward just as hard. Don't equal and opposite pushes cancel out? No, because the two forces act on two different bodies: one shoves the gas, the other shoves the rocket, and each body speeds up on its own. The same bookkeeping makes a rifle kick against your shoulder.

Goddard had put the proof inside the very paper the Times was mocking. Its early pages give a formula for a rocket's top speed, which depends on only two things: how much of the rocket's mass is fuel, and the speed at which the exhaust gas shoots out of the nozzle. The air appears nowhere in it. A deaf Russian schoolteacher, Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, had worked out the same equation in 1903.

Goddard did not live to see the apology. The paper's correction came on 17 July 1969, the day after Apollo 11 launched. Experiment had confirmed Isaac Newton, it said, and it was now settled that a rocket works in a vacuum just as it does in an atmosphere. The Times, it added, regretted the error.

golden-rice-twenty-one-years-in-a-greenh.context_blurb:
Children who live mostly on white rice can go blind, and many then die, for lack of vitamin A. In the 1990s two scientists set out to make rice carry the missing nutrient inside the grain itself. They succeeded in 1999, and the rice came out golden. More than twenty years later, the poor rice-eating countries were still waiting to grow it.

The rice plant already makes beta-carotene, an orange pigment that our bodies convert into vitamin A, though only in its green leaves. In the starchy core of the grain, the endosperm, the chain of steps that builds the pigment is switched off. So white rice, the staple of half the world, carries almost none.

Two European plant scientists, Ingo Potrykus of ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer of Freiburg, spent about eight years turning that pathway back on, and announced their success in Science at the start of 2000. They borrowed just two genes from outside rice. The first came from a bacterium living in soil, and the other came from the daffodil, the yellow spring flower, which supplied an enzyme called phytoene synthase. Together the two genes woke the pathway inside the grain.

That July, Time magazine put Potrykus on its cover, standing among the rice plants, under a promise that the grain could save a million children a year. The World Health Organization estimated that between a quarter and half a million children went blind from the deficiency every year, and that about half of them died within twelve months.

Critics made one fair point: the first rice held too little beta-carotene for a child to meet the daily need from rice alone. In 2005 a team at Syngenta answered it by replacing the daffodil's phytoene synthase gene with the matching gene from maize, which raised the carotenoid level about twenty-three times. The dose objection was settled nearly two decades before anyone was allowed to grow the plant.

Opponents fought the crop in fields as well as courts. In August 2013 a government trial plot at Pili in the Philippines stood a few weeks from harvest when roughly four hundred protesters walked in and tore the plants out by hand. In June 2016 the biologist Sir Richard Roberts organised an open letter, signed at launch by about 107 Nobel laureates, urging Greenpeace to drop its campaign against Golden Rice. Greenpeace opposed every patented engineered crop and argued that Golden Rice would open the door to far wider use of them. It replied that the rice had failed after twenty years; the laureates' point was that twenty years of blocking had caused the delay.

In 2021 the Philippines became the first country to approve Golden Rice for commercial growing. In April 2024 the Court of Appeals revoked that permit under the Writ of Kalikasan, a special order the Philippine Supreme Court created in 2010 for large environmental cases; kalikasan is Filipino for "nature". The judges pointed to the constitution's precautionary principle and to conflicting scientific views on long-term safety.

goodyears-stove.context_blurb:
Raw rubber is a miserable material: sticky and foul-smelling in summer heat, brittle and cracked in winter cold. Through the 1830s Charles Goodyear, a bankrupt New England hardware merchant who had never studied chemistry, spent year after year trying to tame it. The cure he found in 1839, heating rubber with sulphur, is called vulcanization.

The search ruined him. He sold what the family owned, his wife and children lodged with neighbours, and two of his little boys died. In the worst winter the Goodyears lived on half-frozen potatoes dug from the ground and frogs caught by hand.

He thought he had won once already. A quicklime bath seemed to tan the gum and end its stickiness, and the finish was admired even in Europe. Then Goodyear himself found that a drop of weak acid made the rubber go soft again, and the process was dead. He had broken his own triumph, which is the first virtue of an honest experimenter.

Even the sulphur came from someone else. Nathaniel Hayward, the foreman of the rubber works at Woburn, had been adding sulphur and drying his goods in the sun, and Goodyear bought Hayward's claim in February 1839. Others had tried sulphur before, including a Mr. Chaffee at Roxbury. The trouble with sulphured goods was simple: the goods stank of sulphur, and nobody would buy them.

Later that year Goodyear was at the Woburn works to shut it down when a piece of his sulphured rubber touched a hot stove. Rubber always melted in heat; this one charred and stiffened like leather instead. His own account has no rage and no flung sample; popular retellings added those. Sure that this mattered, he showed it to the rubber men around him, his own brother among them. They shrugged it off as one more of his endless experiments. Qualified witnesses watched the turning point of the rubber trade and judged it worthless.

Yet a burnt scrap can look like a failure. To check, he scorched another strip of rubber-coated fabric before a fire, and it blackened again. But along the edge of the burn ran a narrow border that had not charred at all: it was perfectly cured, firm and springy. That thin band proved heat had a right amount, so the question became how hot, and for how long. Months of work alone gave him the answer.

Goodyear admitted he had no chemical training but refused the word accident. He compared the stove to Isaac Newton's falling apple: a small event that speaks only to a mind already prepared to read it. Newton's apple, fittingly, is itself a story Newton told late in life.

His 1844 patent gives the recipe: five parts of sulphur for every twenty-five of rubber, with some white lead, heated close to 270 degrees Fahrenheit. He could not explain why so little sulphur worked. Raw rubber's molecules are long chains, tangled together but each one free, so in warmth they slide past one another and flow. The sulphur builds short bridges from one chain across to its neighbour, called cross-links, so the chains still stretch and spring back but can no longer slide apart.

In England, Thomas Hancock was shown a few scraps of the American rubber in the autumn of 1842 and caught a faint whiff of sulphur on one. He decided someone had dusted sulphur on to mislead him. The real clue was under his nose, yet he still reached his own method of curing rubber with sulphur and heat. Hancock filed his English patent on 21 November 1843, about ten weeks ahead of Goodyear's American filing, though Goodyear's working discovery came years before both.

Goodyear earned a fortune from his patent but owed far more, and he died in debt in 1860. In 1898 Frank Seiberling named a new rubber company in Akron, Ohio, after him, though the family had no part in it. Cars barely existed yet, so the young firm made bicycle and carriage tyres, rubber horseshoe pads and poker chips.

gravitational-waves-predicted-1916-doubt.context_blurb:
In 1916 Albert Einstein's new theory of gravity predicted that massive bodies whirling around each other should send ripples through spacetime itself. Physicists argued for decades over whether the waves were real. In 2015 a pair of giant American detectors finally felt one pass.

LIGO, a laser observatory built to catch the waves, has twin machines at Livingston, Louisiana, and Hanford, Washington. The first wave arrived on 14 September 2015, four days before the official science run was due to start, while the upgraded machines were still in their engineering shakedown. In Hannover, a young Italian physicist named Marco Drago saw the matching traces pop up in an email. About an hour later he wrote to the whole collaboration, asking whether anyone knew of anything that could have faked the signal.

He had reason to be wary. In 2010 LIGO had caught a strong signal from the direction of Canis Major, nicknamed the Big Dog. The team analysed it for half a year and drafted a paper before opening a sealed envelope in March 2011: the signal was a test, planted by physically shaking the detectors' mirrors and known in advance to just four people.

The 2015 wave was real. It reached Livingston 6.9 thousandths of a second before Hanford, 3,002 kilometres away. Light needs about ten thousandths of a second for that trip, so the lag fit a ripple sweeping in from the sky at light speed, which no local truck or quake can imitate.

In each machine, mirrors bounce a laser along the arms until its light has covered about 1,120 kilometres, and the passing wave changed that whole path by roughly one thousandth of a proton's width. The source was two black holes, about 36 and 29 times the Sun's mass, merging 1.3 billion light-years away into one of about 62. The missing three Suns of mass were turned into the energy of the ripples themselves, which spread out through space. For an instant the merger poured out more power than all the stars in the observable universe shining together, and none of it was light.

LIGO began as homework. In 1967 Rainer Weiss was teaching relativity at MIT when his students asked how Joseph Weber's detectors were supposed to work. Weber's bar was a big aluminium cylinder covered in sensors, and he claimed it was catching waves, but Weiss could not explain it. So he turned it into an assignment: design the simplest gravitational-wave detector you can. His own answer, an L-shaped laser instrument with hanging mirrors, grew into LIGO.

Weber announced detections in 1969 and became famous, but no one could repeat them; Richard Garwin's copy saw almost nothing in half a year. David Douglass then combed through Weber's software and found that it allowed for noise whose amplitude was random, but not for noise whose phase was random.

Einstein himself had wavered. In 1936 he and his colleague Nathan Rosen submitted a paper to Physical Review asking whether gravitational waves exist, and answered that they are not physically real. Their mathematics blew up at one point. The referee, the cosmologist Howard Percy Robertson, showed that the blow-up came from their choice of coordinates, a quirk of their own bookkeeping that they had mistaken for a feature of spacetime. Einstein angrily withdrew it. That autumn his assistant Leopold Infeld worked through the problem with Robertson and found the mistake. When Infeld brought it to him, Einstein said he had found an error himself the night before, then rewrote the paper to the opposite conclusion.

Rosen kept doubting, insisting the waves carried no energy. At a 1957 meeting in Chapel Hill, Richard Feynman answered with two beads threaded loosely on a stiff rod: a passing wave would rub the beads along the rod and warm it by friction, and heat means the wave delivers real energy.

The first solid evidence came from the sky. In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a pulsar locked in orbit with a second neutron star. Years of timing its pulses showed the orbit shrinking, the two stars drawing closer year after year at exactly the rate Einstein's formula predicts for energy carried off by the waves. Then, in August 2017, a wave from two colliding neutron stars 140 million light-years away was followed 1.74 seconds later by a burst of gamma rays from the same spot. After so long a journey, that tiny gap proved that gravitational waves and light move at one and the same speed.

gravity-is-not-a-pull-the-falling-man-th.context_blurb:
In 1907 a patent clerk in Bern named Albert Einstein had what he later called the happiest thought of his life: a man falling freely from a roof would not feel his own weight. From that idea grew general relativity, in which gravity is not a pull at all.

Galileo's old claim that all things fall alike got a television test in August 1971. On the Moon, Apollo 15 commander David Scott let go of a hammer and a falcon feather together, and with no air to slow it, the feather hit the dust at the same instant as the hammer. Scott had meant to rehearse it in private, worried that static charge might make the feather cling to his glove, but time ran short, so he simply winged it.

Galileo himself never described dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Every account of that scene traces back to a single source: a biography of Galileo by his student Vincenzo Viviani, written twelve years after Galileo died. Most historians think the drop was only a thought experiment.

Einstein's next step was a sealed, windowless box drifting far out in space. Suppose a giant hauls it upward on a rope, speeding it up by the same amount each second as a falling stone gains on Earth. The man inside feels exactly as if his room stood at rest in a gravitational field: his feet press the floor and dropped things fall. No experiment inside can tell the difference: this is the equivalence principle.

In 1911 he calculated that starlight grazing the Sun should bend by about 0.83 arcseconds. When he completed general relativity in November 1915 and worked it again, the prediction doubled, to about 1.75 arcseconds, because the full theory added the curving of space. The box also predicted something about time. Fix one clock to the floor and another to the ceiling. Light sent up from the floor reaches a ceiling that has been speeding away from it, so fewer waves arrive each second, and Einstein concluded that the floor clock must run slow compared with the ceiling clock. So a clock lower in a gravitational field runs slow too.

Glen Rebka and Robert Pound tested it in 1959 by firing gamma rays up and down a 22.5-metre tower at Harvard. The effect was hundreds of times narrower than the gamma-ray line itself, so they fixed the source of the rays to the coil of a vibrating loudspeaker, rocking it gently back and forth until the absorption dipped. A GPS satellite's atomic clock gains about thirty-eight millionths of a second a day, because weaker gravity aloft speeds it up more than its orbital speed slows it down. Left uncorrected, that would throw your position off by about ten kilometres a day.

Some 250 miles above us, where the space station circles, gravity is still about 90 per cent as strong as at the ground. The crew float because they are falling, moving sideways so fast that the Earth curves away beneath them as quickly as they drop.

The classroom picture of relativity, a bowling ball denting a rubber sheet, has a flaw that Kelly Foyle and Philip Freeman point out: Earth's gravity is what makes the sheet sag, so the model explains gravity with gravity. Their repair is to drape the fabric over the top of a laboratory flask, so it bulges upward and keeps its curve without Earth's pull doing the work.

General relativity bends both space and time, and Foyle and Freeman stress that everyday gravity, a thrown ball or your weight on the ground, comes almost entirely from the bending of time, while bent space contributes only a little. In this picture a diver who has just left the board feels no force at all: she is following the straightest path through curved spacetime. You, in a poolside chair, are different: the chair keeps shoving you off that straightest path, and that shove is what you feel as your weight.

Newton disliked the idea of a force acting instantly at a distance. Two thinkers, Fatio de Duillier in 1690 and Le Sage in 1748, each offered a replacement: unseen particles stream in from every direction, and two bodies shade each other from the rain, so each is pushed toward the other. James Clerk Maxwell killed the idea by showing that the collisions would heat the Earth impossibly.

guatemala-1946-the-study-in-the-archive.context_blurb:
Between 1946 and 1948, doctors of the US Public Health Service ran a secret experiment in Guatemala on some 1,300 people, among them inmates of prisons and asylums, soldiers and sex workers, to learn whether the new drug penicillin could prevent syphilis and gonorrhea. The study's director, John Cutler, later worked on the Tuskegee study as well.

The infamous Tuskegee study in Alabama watched black men who already had syphilis go untreated for decades. Guatemala went further. Cutler's team deliberately gave healthy people the disease, by arranging contact with infected sex workers, scratching the skin and injecting the germs directly. Some of the researchers admitted at the time that they could not have done this in their own country.

In those same years, judges at Nuremberg were trying twenty-three Nazi doctors for experiments in the camps. Their verdict of August 1947 set down a code of ten points, and the first demands that every human subject give voluntary, informed consent before any experiment begins. The captive people in Guatemala could give no such thing.

Cutler died in 2003, leaving his own papers to the University of Pittsburgh, where he had taught. Susan Reverby, a medical historian at Wellesley College, was researching Tuskegee when she opened his files there and found the Guatemala records, which she made public in 2010. That October, President Obama and Secretary of State Clinton apologised to Guatemala.

halleys-comet-keeps-its-appointment.context_blurb:
Comets once seemed to blaze across the sky at random, as omens. Edmond Halley, an English astronomer, used Isaac Newton's new law of gravity in 1705 to do something bolder: he named the year one particular comet would come back. The comet that now carries his name turned that forecast into one of science's great tests.

Halley set side by side the orbits of the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 and found them nearly identical. He argued that they were a single comet returning about every seventy-six years, and predicted it would reappear in 1758. He knew he would not see it: he died in 1742, sixteen years before the comet came back.

Gravity made the timing harder. Jupiter and Saturn tug on the comet as it passes them, so in November 1758 three French calculators, Clairaut, Lalande and the astronomer Nicole-Reine Lepaute, told the Paris Academy that the comet would be late and would round the Sun in mid-April 1759, with an uncertainty of about a month either way. It arrived on 13 March, a month early and inside the margin they had admitted.

The first person to see it return was no professional. On Christmas night 1758, Johann Georg Palitzsch, a farmer near Dresden, picked it up with a homemade telescope, ahead of every observatory in Europe.

In March 1986 the European probe Giotto flew close enough to photograph the comet's heart: a peanut-shaped core of ice and rock some fifteen kilometres long. It reflects only about 4 per cent of the light that falls on it, which makes it darker than coal. The glowing comet we see is gas and dust that the Sun's warmth boils off that dark core.

The 1986 visit was a poor show, because the comet rounded the Sun on the far side from Earth. On 28 July 2061 Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet when it swings closest to the Sun, so the sunlit comet will be near us and far brighter. Mark the date.

hararis-documented-sentences.context_blurb:
Yuval Noah Harari is an Israeli historian whose books Sapiens and Homo Deus have sold in the tens of millions and made him a star of the global conference circuit, where he forecasts what artificial intelligence will do to humanity. His exact words have become a battleground, so they are worth reading closely.

His training is in the past, not the future. His Oxford doctorate was on Renaissance soldiers' memoirs, and at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem he teaches medieval and military history.

In Homo Deus (2016) he writes that as machines outdo people at nearly every job, the most important question in twenty-first-century economics may be what to do with all the people whose work is no longer needed. In a 2017 essay drawn from the book, he gave such people a name: the useless class, people not merely out of work but with no chance of ever finding a job again. He defines them as lacking any economic or political worth, or even artistic worth, and as adding nothing to society's prosperity, power or glory.

In a Guardian essay of September 2018 he called free will no scientific reality but a myth inherited from Christian theology. Believing in it, he argued, had suddenly become dangerous, because the people easiest to manipulate are those who believe they choose freely.

Harari insists he is describing a danger as a historian, not recommending a policy. Critics reply that the real tell is his vocabulary: terms like superfluous and useless come from the language a warehouse uses for unsold surplus inventory, and they shape how readers learn to see the people so labelled, whatever the author intends. Both readings are on the record, and the sentences are there for anyone to judge.

harrisons-sea-clocks-and-the-longitude-p.context_blurb:
One dark October night in 1707, Sir Cloudesley Shovell's fleet ran onto the rocks of the Isles of Scilly, and well over a thousand sailors drowned. The navigators had their longitude wrong: they had no way to tell how far west they really were. The disaster pushed Parliament to act.

Latitude was easy to read from the Sun. Longitude needed time. The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, so each hour of difference between local noon and the time back at your home port means 15 degrees of longitude. A captain needed a clock that would keep home time for months at sea.

In 1714 Parliament offered £20,000, a huge fortune, for a method accurate to within half a degree, proven on a voyage to the West Indies. The finest clocks on land were pendulum clocks, and every one taken to sea failed, because a rolling, pitching deck upset the pendulum's swing with each wave.

The man who solved it was John Harrison, a self-taught joiner from a Yorkshire village with no clockmaking tradition. His early clocks ran on gears cut from lignum vitae, an oily tropical wood that lubricates itself, so they needed none of the clock oils of the day, which thickened in cold and thinned in heat.

His fourth machine, H4, looked like a large silver pocket watch. In 1761 HMS Deptford carried it to Jamaica, and after 81 days at sea it had lost only about five seconds, roughly one nautical mile of longitude, more than sixty times better than the prize demanded.

The Board of Longitude would not pay. It called the result lucky and demanded a second trial at sea. In 1764 H4 did as well or better on a voyage to Barbados, and still the Board balked, arguing that one handmade watch was not yet a method others could copy.

No one ever officially received the £20,000 prize. In 1773, when Harrison was eighty, his son's appeal reached King George III, who had tested Harrison's fifth clock himself, and Parliament granted Harrison £8,750 by a separate act.

harvey-does-the-arithmetic-on-blood.context_blurb:
For fourteen centuries Europe's physicians took their teaching from Galen of Pergamon, who held that blood is used once and never returns. In 1628 the English physician William Harvey published a short Latin book arguing the opposite: the same blood goes round and round, driven by the heart. His strongest weapon was not a scalpel but arithmetic.

In Galen's picture the liver was the factory. It turned digested food into fresh blood all day long, the veins carried that blood outward one way, and the body's tissues absorbed it and used it up. Galen's scheme also hit a snag inside the heart itself. Blood entering the right chamber somehow had to reach the left, though a thick wall of muscle lies between, so anatomists taught that it oozed through invisible pores in that wall, holes too small for any eye. No one ever saw them, because the wall is solid.

Harvey's book came out in Frankfurt on cheap paper, so riddled with misprints that the printer added a page listing 126 corrections, and much of the blame lay with Harvey's cramped, atrocious handwriting. Inside, he invited readers to test him on their own bodies. Bind your upper arm with a band and let it dangle, and the forearm veins rise like ropes, dotted with small firm knots. Each knot is a valve inside the vein. Press a finger below one and stroke the blood toward the hand, and that stretch of vein stays empty until you lift your finger.

His best teachers were cold-blooded animals such as snakes, frogs and fish, whose hearts beat slowly enough to follow one stroke at a time. He saw that the heart grows paler at the instant it squeezes and turns red again as it rests. In a living snake he pinched shut the great vein that feeds the heart, and the heart and the aorta, the main artery leaving it, both emptied and went pale. Pinching the aorta instead made the heart swell. Blood comes in by one door and leaves by the other.

He bound a volunteer's arm so tightly that the man could barely bear it, and the wrist lost its pulse while the hand turned pale and cold. Loosened to a middling tightness, the band made the forearm and hand swell and grow warm. The deep arteries, pushing hard, could again force blood in, but the shallow veins stayed squeezed shut, so blood piled up below the band: it arrives by artery and leaves by vein.

Then came the sum. The left chamber of a dead man's heart held two or three ounces. Harvey allowed that only a small part leaves with each beat, and counted the pulse at over a thousand in thirty minutes. Multiplied out, the heart throws more blood in half an hour than the whole body contains. No liver could make that much, so the same blood must keep coming back. He chose his own lowest guesses, an eighth of the chamber per beat and a stingy chamber size, because a total that is impossible even on the smallest figures cannot be argued down by haggling over the measurement.

The valves were not Harvey's find. Hieronymus Fabricius, who had taught him at Padua, printed pictures of them in 1603, but thought they held the blood back so that every part of the body received an even share. Harvey saw that a one-way gate only makes sense if the traffic runs one way, toward the heart.

One link was missing: blood had to get from the tiniest arteries to the tiniest veins, and Harvey could not see how. He covered the gap with a single phrase, saying the blood passes through hidden porosities, as fluid seeps through a kidney. Four years after his death in 1657, Marcello Malpighi studied a living frog's lung under a microscope and saw blood moving in vessels too fine to follow. So he let the lung dry out and followed the web of vessels through the dead tissue. These were the capillaries.

Publishing had cost Harvey dearly. His friend John Aubrey heard him say that his medical practice fell away and that ordinary people took him for crack-brained. Yet within about twenty years his circulation was generally accepted.

he-jiankui-and-the-line-that-was-crossed.context_blurb:
He Jiankui, a biologist in Shenzhen, China, posted a video in November 2018 claiming he had rewritten the DNA of human embryos with the gene-editing tool CRISPR, and that the resulting twins were already born. They were the first gene-edited babies in history. Scientists everywhere condemned him, and the reasons they gave matter as much as the verdict.

To shield the girls, he called them by the pseudonyms Lulu and Nana; a third edited child, called Amy, followed the next year.

His target was a gene called CCR5. It makes a protein on the outside of certain immune cells that most HIV strains use as an entry door. People who inherit a broken copy shrug off most HIV, and He claimed to be copying that natural variant because the twins' father had HIV. But fertility doctors already had a simple answer: sperm washing, which separates the virus from the sperm before IVF, had protected the children of such couples for decades.

Outside labs that later read the twins' genes found something else entirely. The girls carried brand-new mutations never studied in any human, with unknown effects, and each can pass hers on to her own children. Three days after his video, He defended the work before some seven hundred colleagues at a Hong Kong summit on genome editing. The summit's own organisers called what he had done unexpected and deeply disturbing.

The consent form was a warning sign in itself. It described the work as an AIDS vaccine project and threatened any couple who pulled out after implantation with repaying all the project's costs, plus fines for late payment. The twins themselves could consent to nothing. In December 2019 a Shenzhen court sentenced He to three years in prison, convicting him under a charge that already existed: the illegal practice of medicine.

The field did not simply call gene editing wicked. Its case against He was specific: he had edited embryos with untested methods, for no medical need, without real consent, and in a way the children will pass on to their descendants. Treatments such as Casgevy for sickle-cell disease, given to consenting patients for real illness and never inherited, pass every one of those tests, which is why the same decade could praise them and condemn him.

heard-once-never-again-the-wow-signal-an.context_blurb:
Astronomers listening for alien radio have one famous signal they still cannot explain, and a string of others that turned out to come from much closer to home. Telling the two apart is the whole craft: a real discovery has to survive every check of your own equipment first.

On 15 August 1977 Ohio State's Big Ear radio telescope logged a burst far stronger than the background hiss. When Jerry Ehman went through the printout several days afterward, he circled it in red and wrote Wow! beside it, and the name stuck. The circled characters, 6EQUJ5, are often called a coded message, but they are only a loudness record: the telescope printed one character every twelve seconds as the signal rose and fell, with letters standing for the strongest readings.

The burst sat almost exactly at 1420 megahertz. That is the natural radio note of neutral hydrogen, the most common atom in the universe, and for years SETI astronomers had argued that any intelligent broadcaster would choose it, since every radio astronomer in the galaxy would know it.

It has never repeated; repeated searches of the same stretch of sky have found nothing. In 2017 Antonio Paris claimed that two comets had produced it. Ohio State's observatory staff rejected the claim: on 15 August 1977 neither comet was anywhere near the spot where the telescope was pointing. The honest verdict is that the signal is unexplained, neither proof of aliens nor debunked.

Australia's Parkes telescope taught a lesson in self-deception. In 2007 Duncan Lorimer and a student, combing old Parkes recordings, found a radio blast lasting five thousandths of a second. Parkes then caught more short bursts, nicknamed perytons. In 2015 Emily Petroff's team caught three in the act: they came from the observatory's own microwave ovens, which leaked a burst whenever someone yanked a door open before the timer finished.

Lorimer's original burst survived the check. On its journey the lower frequencies had lagged behind the higher ones, a delay caused by loose electrons in space, and the lag showed far more electrons than our whole galaxy could supply. So the team argued it came from outside the Milky Way, across cosmological distances. Richard Feynman had put the discipline in one line in his essay Cargo Cult Science: the first principle is never to fool yourself, because you are the easiest person to fool.

Fast radio bursts remain partly a mystery. On 28 April 2020 one flashed from inside our own galaxy and was traced to SGR 1935+2154, a magnetar: a neutron star whose magnetic field is extreme. That proved magnetars can make such bursts, though not that they make all of them.

heat-you-can-hold-endothermic-and-exothe.context_blurb:
Squeeze an instant cold pack and it chills in seconds; open a hand warmer and it stays warm for hours. Both run on the same bookkeeping. Breaking chemical bonds costs energy and forming them releases it, and whether your hand warms or chills depends on which side of that account wins.

The cold pack holds no ice. Inside is a pouch of water and crystals of ammonium nitrate; squeeze, the pouch bursts, and the dissolving crystals soak up energy fast enough to bring the pack close to freezing. The pack does not make cold, because cold is not a substance. What you feel is heat leaving your hand and pouring into the pack, where the dissolving crystals swallow it up.

A disposable hand warmer works the other way. Tearing its wrapper lets air reach the powder inside, and the iron powder in it slowly rusts, giving off heat for hours.

A reusable heat pad holds a clear liquid that is overdue to crystallise: it has cooled far below the point where it should have turned solid, but it has had no seed to start on. Click the little metal disc, a wave of crystals races through the pouch, and the liquid, turning solid, gives off the energy it was storing. Boil the pad until every crystal dissolves and it is ready again.

The fiercest everyday example is thermite. In 1895 Hans Goldschmidt patented a mix of aluminium powder and iron oxide that, once lit, burns hotter than 2,500 degrees as the aluminium grabs the oxygen from the iron, leaving molten iron behind. Since about 1899 railway crews have used it on remote track, needing no electricity, to weld one steel rail to the next.

heisenbergs-uncertainty-is-not-clumsy-in.context_blurb:
In 1927 Werner Heisenberg published the uncertainty principle, and students have been told ever since that measuring a particle disturbs it, as if the problem were clumsy instruments. The deeper truth is stranger: a particle simply does not have a sharp position and a sharp momentum together. Ordinary waves behaved this way long before quantum physics.

Ask a sound engineer for a pure 440-hertz note, the A that orchestras tune to, lasting only a thousandth of a second, and he will tell you it cannot exist. A sound that starts and stops that quickly is not one pure tone; it spreads across a band of frequencies. A better speaker cannot fix it, because it is a rule of waves. Pluck a guitar string and let it ring, and a phone tuner finds the note; clamp it dead at once, and the tuner finds nothing. In 1946 the engineer Dennis Gabor hit the same wall trying to describe a siren whose pitch climbs. Fourier analysis builds every sound out of pure tones that run forever, so it cannot say when a pitch happened. Gabor's fix, analysing short chunks of sound, is the ancestor of every spectrogram.

Heisenberg nearly failed to become a physicist at all. At his doctoral oral in Munich in 1923 he fumbled Wilhelm Wien's questions on optical instruments, the microscope among them, and then even a non-optical one: how a storage battery does its job. He scraped through with a poor grade.

Four years later his famous argument rested on an imaginary microscope that finds an electron by bouncing a gamma ray off it. A short wavelength pins down the position, but the photon kicks the electron, knocking its momentum to an unknown value. Niels Bohr, back from a skiing holiday in Norway, judged the microscope story misleading. Partly it was plain optics: as Ernst Abbe had shown in the 1870s, a microscope's resolution depends on how wide the lens opens, since that fixes the spread of angles it can collect, and Heisenberg had left that out. The two men argued hard. The paper was already submitted, so Heisenberg added a note in proof crediting Bohr's point but left the argument standing. That is one reason the clumsy-measurement picture survived.

The strict inequality that textbooks print was proved first by Earle Kennard in 1927, and it says nothing about instruments. It describes which quantum states can exist at all: no state of any particle holds both a sharp position and a sharp momentum, however gently anyone handles it.

That floor has visible effects. Helium is the only substance that will not freeze at ordinary pressure, however cold it gets: its atoms can never come fully to rest, and that leftover jiggle beats the feeble pull between them. The same rule holds atoms together. Squeeze an electron into the small space near a nucleus and its momentum must spread, which forces on it a kinetic energy that keeps it from falling in.

In 2012 a Vienna team led by Yuji Hasegawa broke a limit that had carried Heisenberg's name since 1927, and Scientific American explained that nothing had died, because two statements had shared one name. What fell was Heisenberg's claim that observing something must inevitably disturb it; Kennard's limit on the states themselves was never touched.

The same trade-off links energy and time. The rho meson, made in particle colliders, has no single mass but a broad bump about 150 million electron-volts wide. That width tells physicists how short the particle's life is before it breaks apart: the briefer the life, the wider the bump.

hela-the-cells-that-outlived-henrietta-l.context_blurb:
In 1951 Henrietta Lacks, a young mother of five from a family of Virginia tobacco farmers, was treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore and died within months. Cells taken from her tumour became the first human cells to keep multiplying in a lab, and they are still dividing today. Science gained enormously; her family was told nothing for decades.

On 8 February 1951, while she lay unconscious and before radium went in to treat her, Dr Lawrence Wharton Jr cut two dime-sized pieces from her cervix, one healthy and one tumour. Her treatment did not need them, and nobody asked her.

The tissue went to the laboratory of George Gey, where every human sample had died within weeks. Margaret Gey, his wife, and Mary Kubicek, his assistant, chopped it fine and fed it a home-brewed broth of umbilical cord serum, calf embryo extract and chicken plasma, spinning the tubes in Gey's own roller drum. The healthy tissue withered as usual, but the tumour cells doubled about once a day and never stopped. Kubicek labelled the tubes HeLa, from the first two letters of each of Henrietta's names, and HeLa cells is still what labs everywhere call them. For a quarter of a century the public knew the donor only by a false name.

Gey never patented the cells or earned a penny from them. He gave them away by post to any lab that wrote, cushioned in sawdust, and they travelled in airline pilots' pockets and once, for part of the way, in a mule's saddlebag. Gey, working with William Scherer and Jerome Syverton, showed in 1953 why the cells mattered: poliovirus infects HeLa and visibly kills it, so a tube of the cells made a simple yes-or-no test for live virus. When Jonas Salk's vaccine needed testing on a vast scale, the polio charity set up a HeLa factory at the Tuskegee Institute, a black college in Alabama, which shipped twenty thousand tubes a week. It had nothing to do with the notorious Tuskegee syphilis study in the same town.

Henrietta died on 4 October 1951. Mary Kubicek, sent to the autopsy, kept her eyes off the dead woman's face, then saw the red polish, chipped, on her toenails and nearly fainted: this was a real person. Gey himself died of pancreatic cancer in 1970. Before the operation he had asked the surgeons to cut a piece of his tumour to start a new cell line; they judged that cutting would kill him and took nothing, and he woke up furious.

Why won't HeLa die? A normal human cell divides only about fifty times, because each division wears down the protective caps on its chromosomes, the telomeres. In Henrietta's tumour, DNA from a papillomavirus keeps an enzyme called telomerase switched on, so fresh caps are built after every division. The cells were so vigorous that they invaded other cultures. In the mid-1960s the geneticist Stanley Gartler told a meeting that eighteen supposedly different human cell lines were all HeLa: every one carried G6PD-A, an uncommon form of an enzyme found almost only in black Americans, which was Henrietta's own marker.

Her family learned of the cells only because of that mess. In 1973 Victor McKusick needed their genetic markers to sort HeLa from the cultures it had invaded, so he sent Susan Hsu to take blood from her husband and children. Given almost no explanation, the family believed they were being tested for the cancer that had killed her. Was taking her tissue a crime? In 1951 no American law and no Hopkins rule required a hospital to ask a patient before keeping leftover surgical tissue. Both things are true at once: no law was broken, and the family was kept out of every choice about the cells, and out of every profit, for decades.

In 2013 a European lab published HeLa's full genome, which carried the inheritance of Henrietta's descendants, without asking them. After the family objected, the National Institutes of Health agreed to put the data behind controlled access and give the family two seats on the board that reviews every request to use it. The cells also closed a circle. Harald zur Hausen, who isolated two of the dangerous papillomavirus types in the early 1980s, proved that such viruses cause cervical cancer. The Gardasil vaccine blocks both types, and one of them, HPV-18, was the very virus in Henrietta's tumour.

helium-found-in-the-sun-before-it-was-fo.context_blurb:
Helium is the only element discovered in space before anyone found it on Earth. Astronomers first met it as a single unexplained line of yellow light in the Sun's glow, and for almost thirty years it was nothing more than that line on a chart.

On 18 August 1868, during a total eclipse over southern India, the French astronomer Pierre Janssen pointed a spectroscope at a glowing arch of gas standing off the Sun's edge. He recorded a yellow line close beside the familiar lines of sodium but not on them, matching nothing known on Earth: the signature of helium. The lines were so bright that Janssen realised he could pick them out of the ordinary daytime sky, with no eclipse needed. In London Norman Lockyer found the same daylight method within weeks, and the French Academy later struck one medal bearing both their faces.

Lockyer proposed a name built from the Greek helios, meaning the Sun, and the profession accepted helium. Naming an element nobody had ever held struck many chemists as reckless, until William Ramsay found the gas in a uranium mineral in 1895.

Other mystery lines ended differently. Astronomers had blamed strange green lines in glowing nebulae on a new element, nebulium. In 1927 Ira Bowen showed that they came from oxygen stripped of two electrons, making "forbidden" jumps that happen only in gas far thinner than any laboratory on Earth can produce. A familiar element was simply living under exotic conditions.

Helium was also the final everyday gas to resist being turned into a liquid. In 1908 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in Leiden at last liquefied it at 4.2 kelvin. Three years later, cooling a thread of mercury in his helium bath, he watched its electrical resistance drop to zero: superconductivity.

hennig-brand-boils-urine-and-finds-cold-.context_blurb:
In 1669, in the German city of Hamburg, an alchemist named Hennig Brand went looking for riches in an unlikely place: human urine. He found something nobody expected, and became the first person known by name to discover a chemical element.

Brand reasoned from colour alone. Urine is yellow, so by the old belief that like reveals like, it must hide gold, the metal he hoped to make. He was chasing the philosopher's stone, the legendary substance said to turn base metal into gold, which Isaac Newton and Robert Boyle also hunted for years.

He gathered some fifty buckets from Hamburg's beer drinkers, let them rot for weeks, boiled the lot down to a paste and roasted the residue. What condensed was a white, waxy solid that glowed pale green in the dark without any heat. He called it cold fire; its Greek name, phosphorus, means light-bearer.

Brand kept his recipe secret and sold it to a Dresden merchant, and another alchemist, Johann Kunckel, worked out his own method by about 1678. In 1680 the Englishman Robert Boyle worked out his own preparation, left an account of it with the Royal Society and, unlike Brand, published it in full. Publication turned a fairground wonder into an experiment anyone could repeat.

henrietta-leavitts-ruler-for-the-univers.context_blurb:
Around 1900 Harvard College Observatory employed a room of women to measure the stars on glass photographic plates. One of them, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, found a pattern in certain blinking stars that gave astronomers their first ruler for distances far beyond our own neighbourhood, and with it the true size of the universe.

The observatory's director, Edward Pickering, called these women computers, in the days when a computer was a person who computed; Leavitt earned about thirty cents an hour. She never used a telescope herself. The plates of the southern sky that she studied were exposed at Harvard's station in Arequipa, Peru, in South America, and shipped north to Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Her hunting ground was the Magellanic Clouds, two small galaxies seen only from the southern hemisphere. Laying a print of one night's plate over another, she picked out stars that had changed brightness, and her 1908 catalogue listed 1,777 variable stars in the two clouds.

Some were Cepheids, stars that brighten and fade on a steady schedule. Their prototype, Delta Cephei, can be seen with the naked eye and completes one cycle in about 5.4 days, so anyone with a notebook can time it against the stars nearby.

In 1912 Leavitt plotted 25 Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, brightness against cycle length. All the stars in the cloud lie at roughly the same distance, so a brighter-looking star really is brighter, and the pattern was simple: the slower a star's cycle, the more light it truly gives out. Time a Cepheid and you know its true brightness; compare that with how bright it looks and you know how far away it is.

She was honest about one limit. With no measured distance to any single Cepheid, her law gave only relative distances, not distances in miles or light-years, and she said so in her own paper. Ejnar Hertzsprung supplied the first calibration the next year.

In October 1923 Edwin Hubble, studying a plate of the great Andromeda Nebula, marked a dot with N for nova. Older plates showed that star brightening and dimming on a schedule, so he struck out the N in red and wrote VAR! across the plate. Timed against Leavitt's law, that one Cepheid put Andromeda far outside the Milky Way: it was a galaxy of its own.

Leavitt never knew. When Gösta Mittag-Leffler, a Swedish mathematician, wrote to Harvard in 1925 planning to nominate her for the Nobel Prize in Physics, he learned that she had died of stomach cancer about three years before. The Nobel is never given after death.

herd-immunity-honestly.context_blurb:
Herd immunity is the idea that a disease stops spreading once enough people are immune, so that even those who are not immune are sheltered. It began as a farmer's observation, became an experiment and then an equation, and like every model it rests on assumptions that have to be checked against the real world.

Daniel Elmer Salmon, a government veterinary scientist, wrote in 1894 that well-fed hogs resisted disease as a herd. Topley and Wilson, working in Britain, put the idea to the test in 1923 by letting infections sweep through cages of mice; the outbreaks faded before every mouse was immune. Hedrich's study of Baltimore's measles records from 1900 to 1931 then found the same protection in people. Once enough children had already had measles, epidemics faded and spared even those never infected, the effect now called herd immunity.

William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick, in Edinburgh, proved in 1927 that when the share of people still susceptible falls below a certain level, a big epidemic cannot get going. That theorem underlies every herd-immunity figure since.

The key number is R-nought: how many others, on average, a single infected person passes the disease to when everyone around is susceptible. In the simplest textbook version, which assumes everyone mixes evenly, the share that must be immune is one minus one divided by R-nought, written 1 - 1/R-nought. Measles is the hard case, with an R-nought thought to lie between about 12 and 18, which puts its classic threshold at 92 to 95 per cent. Flu, with an R-nought near 1.3, needs only about 23 per cent.

Real people do not mix evenly; they cluster by age, school, work and neighbourhood. In 2020 Britton and his colleagues took a disease with an R-nought of 2.5, whose textbook threshold is 60 per cent, and rebuilt it in a population where people mostly meet their own age group. The threshold reached through infection fell to about 43 per cent. The same maths warns the other way, since a high national average can hide a poorly protected local pocket.

The threshold also marks an outbreak's turning point, not its end. People already sick keep infecting others after the peak, an extra tail called overshoot, and in 2023 Kreck and Brauner calculated that in the standard model it can reach at most about 30 per cent of the population.

herschels-accidental-planet.context_blurb:
On 13 March 1781, in the back garden of his house in Bath, William Herschel, a professional musician who built his own telescopes, found the first new planet in recorded history. Every other planet had been known since ancient times.

That night one point of light looked faintly green and not quite starlike. To check, Herschel turned up the magnification, and the object swelled into a disc, which a star never does. Stars stay points however hard you magnify; compare Jupiter and a bright star through a telescope tonight and you will see the difference.

Herschel reported a comet. Then the astronomer Anders Johan Lexell calculated its path around the Sun and found an almost circular orbit lying far outside Saturn's, the mark of a planet rather than a comet. The new world, now called Uranus, orbits about twice as far out as Saturn, so it nearly doubled the size of the known solar system.

Others had seen it without noticing. It turned up in at least twenty earlier records, always mistaken for a fixed star; John Flamsteed had listed it in 1690 as 34 Tauri, a star in Taurus. What people expected to see had filtered out what was in plain sight.

Uranus seemed to confirm a number rule devised by Titius and Bode, which had predicted a planet 19.6 times as far from the Sun as the Earth; Uranus sits at 19.2. Trusting the rule, astronomers searched another of its slots, the empty gap between Mars and Jupiter, and on 1 January 1801 Giuseppe Piazzi found a body there that he named Ceres. It and the many like it found later are now called asteroids.

But the rule had no mechanism behind it. The rule placed the next planet out near 39 of those Earth-Sun distances, or astronomical units; Neptune, found later, orbits at about 30. A recipe that merely fits the data you already have is a curve fit, not a law of nature.

herschels-thermometer-past-the-red.context_blurb:
William Herschel, an astronomer living in Slough near London, found in 1800 a kind of light that no human eye can see. He did it with a prism and a few thermometers, and anyone can repeat the experiment on a sunny afternoon.

He was solving a practical problem. Herschel wanted to watch and sketch sunspots through his telescope eyepiece, and for that he needed a tinted glass that would dim both the blaze and the burning heat. Some tinted glasses let through far more heat than others, so he set out to measure the heat carried by each colour.

A glass prism fanned the sunlight out into a band of colours. He set out three soot-blackened thermometers but kept just one in the rainbow at any moment. The other two were controls, there to catch the room itself growing warmer, so that a rise in the beam could be trusted.

Then he moved the thermometer beyond the red, into darkness where nothing could be seen. It read hotter than any visible colour. He had found infrared, light lying below the red; he called it calorific rays, and the word infrared came decades later.

The classic home version needs only three blackened-bulb thermometers, a prism and a sunny window. Catch the rainbow on a table, move a bulb from violet to just past red, and the space beyond the red reads warmest.

Herschel's discovery explains why engineers keep the James Webb Space Telescope so cold, with detectors near 40 kelvin. Every warm object glows in the infrared, the telescope included, so a warm instrument's own glow would drown the faint light of distant galaxies.

hertz-makes-the-waves-and-calls-them-use.context_blurb:
In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell worked out from his equations that electricity and magnetism together should ripple across space as waves travelling at the speed of light. In a darkened laboratory in Karlsruhe, Germany, a young physicist named Heinrich Hertz set out to make those waves and catch them.

In November 1886 he charged an induction coil hard enough to make a spark leap between two brass balls. Some yards away, a simple ring of copper wire, broken by a tiny gap and attached to nothing, flashed in reply. He had built the first working radio: a transmitter and a receiver linked only by an invisible wave. Maxwell had died seven years earlier without seeing it.

Hertz then showed that the waves behaved exactly like light. He bounced them off metal mirrors, filtered them through rows of parallel wire, and bent them through a prism about 1.5 metres tall made of pitch, a black tar that blocks visible light but lets these waves through.

In 1887 he noticed that his receiver's spark jumped more easily whenever ultraviolet light fell on the gap. He reported it and moved on. In 1905 Albert Einstein explained it as the photoelectric effect: light knocking electrons out of metal.

When a student asked what use the new waves might have, Hertz, as his students later remembered it, said they had none; his only aim, he said, had been to show that Maxwell was correct. Within seven years the young Guglielmo Marconi, experimenting in an attic near Bologna, proved him spectacularly wrong.

Marconi was not alone. The English physicist Oliver Lodge, a year ahead of Marconi, in June 1894 demonstrated wireless signalling at the Royal Institution in London, but he never pursued the commercial side. Marconi became the famous name because he turned the discovery into a business.

hms-challenger-sounds-the-abyss.context_blurb:
In December 1872 a Royal Navy warship, HMS Challenger, left Portsmouth on a voyage of three and a half years around the world. She went not to fight but to study the deep sea, and on that one voyage the science of oceanography was born.

To make room, the navy cut down her spars and took out 15 of her 17 guns, and the gun deck was filled with laboratories for chemistry, biology and sounding the depths. Depth was measured the hard way. The crew paid out a weighted line until it went slack, hauled it back, and logged its length in fathoms, the six-foot reach of a sailor's outstretched arms. One deep sounding could take most of a day.

Before the voyage, many naturalists followed Edward Forbes, who had dredged the Aegean in 1843 and concluded that no animals could survive below about 300 fathoms. Challenger's dredges kept hauling up living creatures from thousands of fathoms down and finished that idea off.

Off the Marianas in the western Pacific, on 23 March 1875, the line ran out and out. The crew sounded twice in the same place to be sure: 4,475 fathoms, about 8,184 metres, the deepest sounding anyone had ever made. The spot is still called the Challenger Deep.

The voyage also killed a famous mistake. In 1868 Thomas Huxley had found a veined slime in a stored jar of mud dredged from the Atlantic and announced it as Bathybius haeckelii, a primordial protoplasm, the bridge between non-living matter and life. Aboard Challenger the chemist John Young Buchanan tested fresh mud and showed it was nothing alive at all. The alcohol used to preserve the samples had reacted with salts in the seawater and thrown down a jelly-like chemical precipitate in the bottle. Huxley publicly took back his own celebrated discovery; Ernst Haeckel refused to.

John Murray mapped the seabed by what the dredges brought up. In the deepest, most barren stretches, where shells dissolve before they reach the bottom, the floor was red clay formed from volcanic dust, scattered with black lumps of manganese.

The voyage's sleeper success was the thermometer. Lowered to the seabed in every ocean, it read cold everywhere, from the tropics to the poles, the first hint that cold polar water sinks and creeps along the ocean floor around the world.

Writing it all up took nineteen years. Charles Wyville Thomson died before it was done, and John Murray saw the Report through to 1895: 50 volumes and more than 29,500 pages, still the largest publication from any single expedition.

A rope drifts, snags and stretches, so no deep reading could be double-checked, and each one ran too shallow. In the 1920s the rope gave way to new physics: timing the echo of a sound pulse bounced off the seabed. Modern sonar puts the Challenger Deep at about 10,935 metres.

hooke-names-the-cell.context_blurb:
In 1665 Robert Hooke, who ran the experiments at London's Royal Society, published Micrographia, a big, lavishly illustrated book of what he had seen through a microscope. It became one of the first science bestsellers, and one small drawing in it gave biology its most important word.

With a razor-keen penknife Hooke shaved a slice of cork so thin that light passed through it. Under the lens the cork turned out to be full of tiny empty boxes, and he named them cells. Live subjects were harder. An ant kept twisting and would not hold still, so Hooke soaked it in brandy till it collapsed, dead drunk; it lay motionless for about an hour while he drew it, then suddenly revived and ran away.

The diarist Samuel Pepys sat up in his room reading the book until two in the morning, and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read. Readers loved the giant fold-out plates best: the louse and the flea were printed so large that each unfolded to roughly ten inches by seventeen.

Hooke also counted. He found about sixty boxes in an eighteenth of an inch and multiplied outward: one cubic inch of cork, a lump the size of a sugar cube, held some 1,259,712,000 cells. You can do the same with anything that repeats: count a short measured row, then multiply.

The boxes solved an old puzzle. Everyone knew cork floats and rides high in water, but nobody knew why; Hooke saw that it is almost all air sealed in tiny boxes, hardly any solid matter spread over a large volume.

The book also holds the earliest printed picture of a microorganism: blue mould growing on the leather covers, made of sheepskin, of a little book in Hooke's house, drawn as slender stalks each bent by a round white knob. Hooke concluded that such mould needs no seed at all, but arises from rotting matter kept moist and warm. That was spontaneous generation, the idea Louis Pasteur's flasks would later demolish.

Hooke's microscope, built by the London maker Christopher Cock, was no great instrument, and he conceded that one simple lens showed things more sharply. His real ingenuity went into the light: a lamp whose beam he focused through a glass globe filled with clear brine, so he could study a specimen in any light, at any hour. Try it with any magnifier: better light often beats more magnification.

Comparing petrified wood with ordinary wood through one lens, Hooke found the same structure and argued that fossils are the remains of living things. Learned opinion held that such stones had never lived, and owed their lifelike shapes to a shaping power hidden in the Earth itself.

The common claim that Hooke saw only dead, empty walls is wrong. He went on to cut elder pith, fennel, carrots, ferns and reeds, and reported cells full of juices, sweating them out little by little. He had no idea he had named the unit every living thing is built from; that took until 1838 and 1839, when Schleiden and Schwann founded cell theory.

Textbooks often add that he chose the word because the boxes reminded him of monks' bare little rooms. When Winfried Peters, a plant biologist, combed through Hooke's text in 2024, he found no monks at all. What Hooke actually wrote was that cork is porous like a honeycomb, except that its pores are irregular.

horror-autotoxicus-the-self-or-other-che.context_blurb:
Your immune system has to tell self from other: attack the germs, spare your own tissues. Around 1900 the German immunologist Paul Ehrlich declared that the body has built-in protections against attacking itself, and his authority held the field back for half a century. Then twin calves, mice and rabbits showed that the line between self and other is learned, and that it sometimes fails.

The stakes are real. In type 1 diabetes, which is not caused by weight or eating habits, a child's immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas. Genes load the dice but do not decide: about 80 to 90 per cent of those who develop it have no relative who ever had it.

Ehrlich's Latin name for the danger was horror autotoxicus: the dread of poisoning oneself. Textbooks flatten his idea into a claim that the body cannot make antibodies against itself at all, but that is not what he wrote. He allowed that the body can make them, and held that built-in safeguards stop them from doing harm. Even so, doctors who saw the body attacking itself kept looking for some other explanation. Hakaru Hashimoto, a Japanese surgeon, published an account in 1912 of four thyroids he had taken out: swollen and scarring, with no infection or cancer, and packed with crowds of the patient's own white blood cells. The disease still carries his name.

The first crack in the doctrine came from cattle. In 1945 Ray Owen found that fraternal twin calves in Wisconsin each carried two kinds of red blood cell. The second kind came from its twin, through blood vessels that had fused across a shared placenta in the womb, and neither calf ever attacked the borrowed cells. Tolerance, it seemed, is learned, and learned before birth.

In 1948 the cattle researcher Hugh Donald asked the zoologist Peter Medawar how to sort identical twin calves from fraternal pairs. Medawar suggested swapping skin grafts, but the test failed: fraternal twins kept each other's grafts just as readily as identical twins did. Whatever is present while the immune system is being built gets filed as self. Medawar, Rupert Billingham and Leslie Brent turned that failure into an experiment in 1953. They gave unborn and newborn mice of one strain an injection of another strain's cells, and the grown mice kept the donor strain's skin grafts for good. A critic might say the injections had simply wrecked the mice's defences, but the same mice still rejected skin from a third, unrelated strain on schedule.

In 1961 Jacques Miller removed the thymus, a soft lump behind the breastbone long dismissed as a leftover, from newborn mice. Grown up, they would accept grafted skin even from a different species. The thymus was the immune system's training school. Each young T cell must pass a test there, and cells that react too strongly to pieces of the body's own proteins are destroyed. But the thymus never meets the pancreas or the eye. Thymus cells switch on thousands of genes that belong to other organs, under the control of a gene called AIRE, so trainees can be shown insulin and eye proteins too. When AIRE breaks, autoimmunity strikes several organs at once.

Sometimes a germ provokes the attack. Weeks after a strep throat has cleared, a child's heart valve may begin to scar, with no bacteria left anywhere. The damage comes from antibodies the body raised against the bacterium that also stick to heart tissue, because parts of the germ resemble heart proteins. No single shared target has yet been formally identified.

Ehrlich's heirs fought hard. When Noel Rose found that rabbits given purified thyroid protein attacked their own thyroids, his teacher Ernest Witebsky, trained in Ehrlich's scientific line, made him repeat it twice. Then Witebsky named the one test he would accept: remove the protein from a rabbit's own body and return it to that very rabbit. The rabbit still destroyed its own thyroid.

A little self-recognition is normal. Healthy bodies make self-binding IgM antibodies that stick to damaged and dying cells and mark them for clean-up. Why autoimmune disease strikes women far more often than men is still unknown. In 2024 Howard Chang's team tested one clue, Xist, an RNA that only females make. They engineered male mice to make a form of Xist that silences nothing, and the males began making autoantibodies. It is the best clue so far, not the answer.

how-a-dark-chapter-gets-found.context_blurb:
How does a hidden wrong in science ever come to light? Rarely because an institution confesses. More often an insider objects, the victims' own bodies hold evidence nobody can edit, or a perpetrator's own files outlive him. Behind each is the scientific habit: ask what would prove a claim wrong, then go and look.

In 1966 Peter Buxtun, a young investigator for the US Public Health Service, objected in writing to the Tuskegee syphilis study, in which black men with syphilis were left untreated. He was overruled, and overruled again. In 1972 he gave the documents to the press, the Associated Press reporter Jean Heller broke the story in more than a hundred newspapers, and the study ended within months.

In the 1920s women who painted watch dials with radium paint, shaping their brushes between their lips, were dying, and the companies insisted the paint was harmless. Harrison Martland, a New Jersey medical examiner, proved the radium was inside the living women from a single breath: he captured traces of radon gas, which radium gives off as it decays. He also set the bones of dead dial-painters on fresh photographic film. The film developed a ghostly picture, because the radium lodged in the bones had exposed it.

The Guatemala experiments of the late 1940s, in which American doctors deliberately gave syphilis and gonorrhoea to hundreds of people, came out only in 2010. The evidence lay in the personal papers of a dead Public Health Service doctor, John Cutler, who had donated them to the University of Pittsburgh, where the historian Susan Reverby found them. Perpetrators keep files, and files outlive them.

Sometimes a wrong is prevented by someone who simply refuses to sign. In 1961 Frances Kelsey, a reviewer at the US Food and Drug Administration, kept asking the maker of thalidomide for proper safety data from animal tests, and would not approve the drug until she got it. She never got it. Thousands of babies in Europe were born with severe birth defects; her demand for evidence spared America.

how-a-wing-really-lifts-and-why-the-text.context_blurb:
Nearly every schoolbook explains a wing's lift the same way: the air over the curved top has farther to go, must hurry to meet the air underneath at the back edge, and faster air has lower pressure. Much of that story is a myth. The real physics is better, and some of it you can test at a kitchen table.

Bernoulli's principle itself is real. Pump water through a glass pipe that narrows to a throat, and liquid in side tubes set into the wall stands lowest at the throat, where the flow runs fastest. The same physics gives a pilot his airspeed through a pitot tube. Henri Pitot built the first one in 1732 and pushed it into the current of the Seine, to measure how fast the river ran. The tube must stay clear. In 1996 a Boeing 757 that had stood uncovered for days in the Dominican Republic took off with a mud dauber wasp's nest of mud and grit inside its captain's tube; the false airspeed fooled the autopilot, and all 189 aboard died.

Many classroom demonstrations misuse Bernoulli, though. Blow across the top of a paper strip held to your lip and it rises; blow beneath it instead, and it rises again, just as before. What lifts it is your breath curving along the paper, not low pressure above. A ping-pong ball floating in a hair-dryer's jet is held there because if it drifts off-centre it meets lopsided flow that shoves it back inward; the jet's pressure is the same as the room's.

The Cambridge aerodynamicist Holger Babinsky asks audiences whether they were taught the wing story, and nearly all raise a hand. Only one step is invented: the claim that the two streams of air must meet again at the trailing edge. Nothing forces them to, and the faster-air, lower-pressure part is sound. Babinsky filmed pulses of smoke splitting at a wing's nose in a wind tunnel and published the frames in 2003. In a single frame, the half that went over the top has already passed the trailing edge, while the half underneath has not yet reached it.

The shape story fails another test: stunt planes fly upside down. A pilot flying inverted simply holds the nose up, and the wing's tilt against the oncoming air, its angle of attack, makes all the lift. Even a flat plate lifts once it is tilted, as any balsa glider shows.

What a wing really does is turn air. A famous photograph by Paul Bowen shows a hole punched through a flat fog bank just after a plane flew low over it: the wing had flung a whole column of air downward as it passed. By Newton's third law, air pushed down pushes the wing up. Tilt a wing too far, past about fifteen degrees, and lift collapses in a stall: the air over the top tears away from the surface instead of following it round, and drag surges.

The ideal-flow equations alone allow endless solutions around a wing, each with a different amount of swirl, or circulation. One physical requirement picks the real one, the Kutta condition: the air must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly instead of whipping round it. That is why wings are built with sharp back edges, and the circulation it fixes sets the lift.

So which comes first, the pressure difference or the turned air? The equations of fluid flow say neither: curving streams create pressure differences, and pressure differences curve the streams, each producing the other together.

how-far-is-the-sun-the-transits-of-venus.context_blurb:
By 1700 astronomers had a perfect map of the solar system with no scale bar: they knew Mars sits about one and a half times as far from the Sun as Earth does, but not how many miles that was. Measure one real distance and all the rest follow. For nearly three centuries the best way to get it was to watch Venus cross the face of the Sun.

Around 280 BC Aristarchus of Samos tried to work out the ratio of the Sun's distance to the Moon's by pure geometry. He waited for the moment the Moon was exactly half lit, when the angle at the Moon between Earth and Sun must be a right angle, and measured the angle between Moon and Sun. His geometry was sound, but no eye could measure that angle finely enough, so he put the Sun only about twenty times farther away than the Moon instead of nearly four hundred.

By Kepler's tables, Venus would not cross the Sun again until 1761. In 1639 Jeremiah Horrocks, a young Lancashire astronomer, reworked Kepler's own numbers and found that a near miss that year was really a hit. With under four weeks' warning he became the first person to predict and watch Venus cross the Sun. He kept his sight by never looking through the telescope: he cast the Sun's image out of it onto a sheet of paper with a circle drawn on it. Never look at the Sun through a lens.

In 1716 Edmond Halley laid out how a transit could measure the Sun's distance. Observers far apart on Earth see Venus cut slightly different lines across the Sun and time slightly different crossings, and the difference gives the distance. He insisted on Venus rather than Mercury because Venus passes far nearer the Earth, so the shift between observers is far bigger. Knowing he would not live to see the 1761 or 1769 transits, Halley closed his paper by urging astronomers not yet born to make the observation.

The French astronomer Guillaume Le Gentil sailed for India in 1760 to time the 1761 transit, but war kept him at sea on the day, and a timing from a rolling deck is worthless. Instead of sailing home, he waited eight years for the next transit, and meanwhile charted the east coast of Madagascar. On the 1769 transit morning, Pondicherry's sky clouded over just as Venus crossed. When he reached France after more than eleven years away, French law had declared him dead, and his heirs had divided his estate. Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche dragged his telescopes overland to Tobolsk, Siberia, for 1761. He timed the whole transit from a hilltop guarded by armed Cossacks, because local peasants blamed that spring's terrible floods on his meddling with the Sun.

In 1769 James Cook sailed the Endeavour to Tahiti, and under a perfectly clear sky he, Charles Green and Daniel Solander timed the contacts. Their times disagreed far more than expected, and Cook blamed what he described as a dim, dusky haze surrounding the planet. Astronomers came to call it the black drop: as Venus touches the Sun's inner edge, a dark thread seems to cling to the rim, smearing timings by around ten seconds when Halley's method needed two. Many blamed the air of Venus, but the same dark thread appears when airless Mercury crosses the Sun. The true culprits are the dim edge of the Sun itself, telescope blur and our own shimmering air.

In St Petersburg, Mikhail Lomonosov watched the 1761 transit and saw a glowing arc around the part of Venus still off the Sun's disc. He read it correctly as sunlight bent through the planet's own air: the first atmosphere ever detected on another planet.

One accusation needed checking too. Carl Littrow, going through Maximilian Hell's sheets from the 1769 transit at Vardo in the Arctic, saw corrections that looked to him like a second, darker ink, and charged Hell with faking his results. Simon Newcomb looked at the same pages in 1883 and found that Littrow was colour-blind and that the two inks were one ink.

The transits did their job: Johann Encke's 1824 reanalysis put the Sun about 153 million kilometres away, within a few per cent of the truth. In 1961 American, Soviet and British teams each measured the distance independently, without any transit. They bounced radio pulses off Venus and timed the echoes, fixing the distance to within a few hundred kilometres.
