schrodingers-cat-was-a-rebuke.context_blurb:
Schrödinger's cat, alive and dead at once, is usually quoted as a celebration of quantum weirdness. Its author meant the opposite. Erwin Schrödinger, an Austrian physicist, built the thought experiment in 1935 to show how absurd one reading of quantum theory becomes when applied to everyday objects.

The imagined box held a cat, a Geiger counter, a speck of radioactive material with an even chance of one atom decaying within the hour, a relay, a hammer and a glass vial of hydrocyanic acid, a cyanide poison, which the hammer would smash if the atom decayed. Read literally, the Copenhagen interpretation's rules for measurement put the cat in a blend of alive and dead until someone looks; Schrödinger called the case ridiculous and aimed it squarely at that interpretation. Albert Einstein had egged him on: in a letter earlier that year he described a keg of gunpowder that quantum mechanics would treat as a mixture of exploded and unexploded.

The same year Schrödinger named what he considered the defining feature of quantum theory: entanglement, the linking of particles so that measuring one fixes the other. For decades little work on entanglement followed; today it is the raw material of quantum computers.

A real cat could never stay in such a blend. Every moment it trades light and air molecules with everything around it, and that contact drains the superposition out into its surroundings in well under a billionth of a second, a process called decoherence. Serge Haroche's group in Paris watched it happen on a tiny scale, trapping a few microwave photons bouncing between superconducting mirrors in a superposition and watching it fall apart step by step; Haroche shared the 2012 Nobel Prize for it. Why one particular outcome appears in the end, the measurement problem, is still debated.

screening-embryos-from-disease-to-specif.context_blurb:
Couples using IVF can now have their embryos tested before one is chosen for transfer. The technique began in 1989 at Hammersmith Hospital in London, to help families avoid passing on serious inherited disease, and it has since spread toward ranking embryos on predicted traits, where the science is far weaker.

Embryo tests come in three kinds. The first, PGT-M, hunts for one particular faulty gene that runs in the family, such as the cystic fibrosis gene; for families carrying a disease like Huntington's, choosing an embryo free of it is a genuine mercy. Another, PGT-A, counts chromosomes, checking whether the embryo has the right number, since a missing or extra one usually means miscarriage. The third gives each embryo a polygenic score from thousands of common DNA variants to predict a trait. Such scores are built from differences among unrelated people, but brothers and sisters share on average about half of their variable DNA, so embryos from one couple differ much less, and Shai Carmi's team showed in 2019 that picking the top-ranked embryo gains very little. That has not stopped the market. In 2024 an undercover Guardian investigation found the US start-up Heliospect Genomics offering to rank a couple's embryos by predicted IQ, for about $50,000. Selecting embryos on predicted IQ is illegal in Britain.

seeing-one-atom-and-then-picking-it-up.context_blurb:
For most of history atoms were an idea no one could see. In 1955 a physicist at Penn State finally saw them, and within forty years scientists could not only image single atoms but push them around and photograph the waves of electrons between them.

In 1955 Erwin Müller and his student Kanwar Bahadur chilled a needle-sharp tungsten tip, let in helium gas, and watched bright dots appear on a screen in neat rings: they were the first people to see individual atoms directly. Müller is said to have shouted at the screen in delight.

A different instrument rests on a quantum effect. In classical physics a particle lacking the energy to get over a barrier simply bounces back, but in quantum mechanics it has a small chance of slipping straight through, which is called tunnelling. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in Zurich held a needle just above a surface so that electrons tunnelled across the gap. Their scanning tunnelling microscope kept that current constant as the needle swept across, so the needle's rise and fall traced the bumps of individual atoms. Strictly these are not photographs: each image is assembled from measurements of tunnelling current, with no light or lens involved.

The same needle could move atoms. In 1989 Don Eigler and Erhard Schweizer dragged 35 xenon atoms across cold nickel to spell the company's three letters, IBM. In 1993 Eigler's group set out a ring of 48 iron atoms on copper, a quantum corral, and the image showed circular ripples inside it: the waves of electrons trapped by the ring, a wavefunction made visible. Leo Gross's team at IBM Zurich went further in 2009, fixing one molecule of carbon monoxide to the tip of an atomic-force microscope and imaging every bond in a pentacene molecule.

semmelweis-and-the-two-wards.context_blurb:
In the 1840s, at the Vienna General Hospital, childbed fever was killing new mothers in terrible numbers, but far more in one maternity clinic than in the one next door. The doctor Ignaz Semmelweis counted, compared and found the cause, years before anyone knew germs existed, and his profession punished him for it.

The two clinics were next-door neighbours that admitted women on alternating days, so the calendar alone decided where a woman gave birth. In the First Clinic, run by physicians and medical students, mothers died at several times the rate of the Second Clinic, run by midwives. Women knew it. Some begged on their knees not to be admitted to the First Clinic, and some gave birth in the street and then arrived claiming it had happened on the way.

Semmelweis, an assistant in the First Clinic from 1846, tested the explanations on offer. Crowding could not be the cause, because the hospital's records showed the safer midwives' clinic was always the more crowded. He had his own wrong ideas too: for a time he blamed the priest who walked through the ward to give the last rites, frightening the women. Then he compared the two staffs' days, and one difference stood out: the doctors and students spent their mornings dissecting corpses in the pathology room and went straight from there to the delivery beds, while the midwives never touched the dead.

The clue came in March 1847, when his friend Jakob Kolletschka died after a student accidentally cut his finger with a scalpel during an autopsy. Kolletschka's body showed the same findings as the dead mothers. Semmelweis concluded that the doctors carried what he called cadaverous particles, decaying matter from the dead, on their hands; he knew nothing of bacteria. In May 1847 he ordered every hand scrubbed with chlorinated lime before examinations, because chlorine, unlike soap, got rid of the stench of the corpses, and that smell was his only way to tell whether a hand was clean. The First Clinic's death rate fell from 18.3 percent in April to about 2 percent in June.

He was not the first. In 1843 Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr had argued in Boston that physicians spread childbed fever from one mother to the next. The Philadelphia obstetrician Charles Meigs answered with no evidence at all: doctors are gentlemen, he wrote, and a gentleman's hands are clean. Vienna dismissed Semmelweis in 1849. In the maternity ward of St Rókus in Pest he imposed the same rule, and over four years his ward delivered 933 babies and lost only eight mothers to childbed fever, a replication in a new hospital with new staff.

When his 1861 book on childbed fever was shrugged off, he published open letters attacking named opponents as murderers, which turned colleagues against him. In 1865 he was taken to an asylum, where guards beat him, and he died two weeks later from blood poisoning that spread from a gangrenous wound on his right hand, the same kind of infection that had killed his patients. His name now labels the Semmelweis reflex: the knee-jerk dismissal of fresh evidence simply because it clashes with what everyone already believes.

shechtman-counts-ten-points.context_blurb:
On 8 April 1982, at the US National Bureau of Standards, Dan Shechtman, an Israeli materials scientist, saw a pattern that every textbook said was impossible. It took him years to be believed, and in 2011 it won him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

He fired electrons through a rapidly cooled alloy of aluminium and manganese, and around the centre of the pattern he counted ten bright points; in his notebook he wrote "10 fold" followed by three question marks. Ten points meant fivefold symmetry, which crystals were not supposed to have. A crystal was defined as a pattern that repeats, and you can see the rule on a tiled floor: simple shapes such as squares tile it with no gaps, but regular pentagons always leave gaps, however you arrange them.

When Shechtman showed his result to the head of his research group, the man gave him a crystallography textbook and suggested he read it, and later asked him to leave the group. The chemist Linus Pauling, winner of two Nobel Prizes, mocked him for years, saying there were no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists.

Mathematics had already shown how such order can exist. In 1974 Roger Penrose found a way to tile a floor forever, with fivefold symmetry and no repeating pattern, using just two shapes: a thin rhombus and a thick one. A quasicrystal is the three-dimensional version, ordered but never repeating. Nature had got there first. Luca Bindi and Paul Steinhardt showed in 2009 that a speck of a meteorite found in Russia held a natural quasicrystal, and its rock was about 4.5 billion years old, from the birth of the solar system.

six-out-of-fifty-three-when-industry-che.context_blurb:
In the early 2010s two drug companies tried to build new medicines on famous published cancer research and found that most of it would not hold up. Their audits, and a public project that followed, showed how much of the scientific record cannot be repeated, and why.

Bayer in Germany checked first, reviewing 67 of its own projects in cancer, cardiology and women's health: only about a quarter agreed fully with the published work behind them. Then the biotech firm Amgen had its scientists redo 53 landmark cancer studies, and C. Glenn Begley and Lee Ellis reported in Nature that only six could be confirmed. The audits were hard to dismiss for a simple reason: the companies had poured money into hoping those papers were right, so nobody could call the checkers hostile.

In 2013 the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology set out to repeat 193 key experiments from 53 high-profile papers. Its most damaging finding came before any lab work: none of the 193 was written up fully enough for anyone to redo it from the published paper alone, and most required writing to the original authors. Money and time ran short, and only about 50 experiments were finished. Among those, the effects came out about 85 percent smaller than the originals on average.

The cost is large. In 2015 Leonard Freedman and two colleagues estimated that the United States spends roughly $28 billion every year on preclinical research that cannot be reproduced. The National Institutes of Health changed its grant rules in response: from 2015, Francis Collins, the director, and Lawrence Tabak, his deputy, made every applicant address scientific rigour, the authentication of key resources, and the strength of the prior evidence.

smallpox-eradication-honestly-told.context_blurb:
Smallpox was a virus that covered its victims in blisters, scarred or blinded many who lived, and killed hundreds of millions over the centuries. Between 1967 and 1980 a worldwide campaign hunted it down case by case. The honest telling has a surprise in its method, a hero from a hospital kitchen and a death in a laboratory.

The last person on Earth infected by smallpox in nature was Ali Maow Maalin, the cook at the hospital in Merca, Somalia. In October 1977 he rode briefly in a vehicle with two sick children and caught the milder form, variola minor. He lived, and nobody anywhere has caught smallpox naturally since. Once recovered, he joined the campaign to wipe out polio, going from village to village as a vaccinator and often telling his own smallpox story to win over wary parents. Malaria killed him in 2013, while he was still at that work.

The deadlier form, variola major, made its last natural stand in Bangladesh in 1975, in a little girl named Rahima Banu. An eight-year-old named Bilkisunnessa reported the sick child and earned the reward of 250 taka, the price of ending variola major forever. The two forms look alike on the skin and are near-identical in their DNA, yet variola major killed roughly one victim in three and variola minor about one in a hundred. The World Health Organization ran the global campaign from 1967 and, once its teams were sure no wild case remained, certified the disease gone.

The campaign did not win by vaccinating everybody. In December 1966, in eastern Nigeria, William Foege, an American doctor serving with a mission there, found his vaccine running low. So he tracked every case by radio and vaccinated only the people in contact with each sick person, a circle drawn around each outbreak. That method, ring vaccination, later called surveillance and containment, is what finished the disease. Planners had reckoned that some four people in five across a whole region needed the vaccine. In Foege's districts, vaccinating just the rings, about 7 to 8 percent of the local people, was enough to stop the spread. It worked because of the virus itself. Smallpox hid in no animal, every infected person showed the rash, and nobody carried it silently, so every case could be found and fenced in.

The final death was not natural at all. In 1978 Janet Parker, a medical photographer, worked in a darkroom one floor above Professor Henry Bedson's smallpox lab at the University of Birmingham. The virus drifted up to her through an unsealed air duct that linked the lab to her office rooms. She died on 11 September 1978. A germ had escaped from a laboratory and killed someone, a warning worth keeping beside the triumph.

The World Health Assembly, the WHO's governing body, declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980. Only one other disease has ever been wiped out worldwide: rinderpest, a cattle disease whose German name means cattle plague, declared gone in 2011 as the first animal disease ever eradicated.

soap-bubbles-oil-slicks-and-newtons-ring.context_blurb:
A soap bubble, an oil slick on a wet road and the purple sheen on a camera lens all glow with colours that no dye put there. The colour comes from the thickness of a film far thinner than a hair. Working that out took Hooke, Newton and Thomas Young over a century.

Light striking a bubble reflects twice, off the film's outer surface and off its inner one. The two reflected waves come back slightly out of step, so for some colours the crests line up and that colour shines, while for others a crest meets a trough and that colour cancels. Which colours survive depends on the film's thickness at that spot, so as the water drains downward, the bands slide down too.

The top thins first. Once the film there is under about a hundred nanometres, far thinner than any wavelength of visible light, the two reflections cancel for every colour at once and the crown goes dark. That black patch means the bubble will burst within seconds.

Newton laid a curved lens on flat glass, trapping a thin wedge of air, and measured the coloured rings so carefully that his numbers still work. What he saw was interference, light bouncing off the glass face above the air wedge meeting light bouncing off the glass face below it. But Newton believed light was made of particles, so he explained the rings with "fits of easy reflection" instead.

He was not first. Robert Hooke had pictured the colours of thin mica and soap films in Micrographia in 1665, nearly forty years before Newton's Opticks of 1704, and guessed they were wave-like. The quarrel over who saw it first soured the two men for life.

Around 1802 Young read the rings as interfering waves and found the clinching detail. Where lens touches plate, the gap shrinks to nothing, so the reflections should add into a bright bullseye; yet the centre is dark. Light reflecting off a denser material, here the flat glass below the air, flips by half a wavelength, while light reflecting off thinner air does not, so at the contact point the two waves cancel. Particles could never explain that dark spot.

Lens makers use the trick on purpose. A camera lens coating is made just one quarter of a wavelength deep, so light reflected from its top and from the glass beneath returns exactly half a wavelength out of step and cancels, letting more light pass into the camera. Tuned for green, it leaves a faint purple glow of red and blue.

Not every shimmer is a thin film. A DVD flashes rainbows because its data tracks sit side by side at an even spacing, and like the ruled lines of a grating they diffract sunlight, sending each colour off at its own angle.

sputniks-beep-and-the-accidental-inventi.context_blurb:
In October 1957 Soviet engineers sent up the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, a polished metal ball that did little but beep. Within days two American physicists, listening out of curiosity, read its whole orbit from the beep's changing pitch. Their boss then turned the trick around, and that turn became satellite navigation, the ancestor of GPS.

The pitch trick was a century old. In 1842 Christian Doppler argued that a moving source changes the pitch it gives off. In 1845 the Dutch scientist Buys Ballot tested him with horn players riding a railway car past listeners, but his first try that February failed because hail and snow pelted the musicians too hard for them to blow a note. In milder June weather the note sounded a half-tone high coming and a half-tone low going. You can hear the same thing beside any road.

Sputnik was a sealed aluminium sphere 58 centimetres wide, trailing four antennas. Inside sat only a radio transmitter, a thermistor to sense the temperature and a gauge for the pressure, with no scientific instrument at all. The launch was secret but the signal was not: in June 1957 a Soviet magazine called Radio told amateurs the satellite would broadcast near 20 and 40 megahertz, and Radio Moscow repeated the frequencies just before launch, so radio hams everywhere could listen from the first beep. Anyone could check the claim without taking Moscow's word for it.

Crowds who watched a light cross the dusk sky were almost certainly fooled: the ball was barely visible, and the bright light was the R-7 rocket's spent core stage, 26 metres long, tumbling along the same orbit.

Even so, the ball did science. A sphere shows the air the same face however it tumbles, so its drag stays steady, and the speed its orbit sank gave a clean measure of how thin the air is a few hundred kilometres up. With no data channel, the two sensors reported by changing the length of each beep.

On the Monday after launch, two young physicists at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, realised over lunch that nobody at the lab had tried to catch the signal. Nobody asked them to. They rigged a receiver and Guier's new home tape deck, and to time each beep they mixed in the broadcast of WWV, the national time station, which stood twelve miles away.

The tone rose as Sputnik approached and fell as it left. On the lab's new Univac computer the pair showed that one pass could fix the whole orbit, nine unknowns at once, including a model of the charged upper air that fell out as a bonus. The catch was that the solve needed nearly the whole curve of the pass, from horizon to horizon.

On 17 March 1958 their director, Frank McClure, called them in, closed the door and asked whether they could run it backwards: given an orbit already known, could they solve for the position of the listener? They had solved for the satellite; he asked for the observer, and that question, his and not theirs, gave birth to satellite navigation. McClure expected the reversed problem to be more accurate, and it was, because only five unknowns had to come out of the same data instead of nine.

The Navy needed exactly that. Its Polaris missiles would launch from submerged submarines, and each boat had to know its spot to a few hundred feet. The Naval Observatory offered to track satellites by direction with a big dish on a steadied mount, and the laboratory rejected it because such a dish would make an easy target for enemy radar. A Doppler fix needed only a simple antenna, so the boat could listen and give nothing away.

The result was Transit. Each Transit satellite sent two signals, at 150 and 400 megahertz, because the charged upper air bends radio waves by an amount that depends on frequency, and comparing the two let navigators cancel that bending instead of guessing it. Transit retired at the end of 1996, handing over to GPS, which times how long signals take to arrive. Three satellites would fix a point if the receiver kept perfect time, but the satellites carry atomic clocks and a phone does not, so a fourth signal lets the receiver work out how far off its own clock is and fix that.

static-electricity-one-phenomenon-at-thr.context_blurb:
Rub a balloon on your hair and it grabs scraps of paper; shuffle over a carpet and a doorknob bites your finger; a storm cloud lets go and a tree splits. All three are static electricity at three sizes, studied for some 2,600 years, and both the smallest and the biggest still hide unsolved puzzles.

The science is named after a lump of tree resin. Thales of Miletus noticed some 2,600 years ago that amber, the hardened resin of ancient trees, pulled straw toward it once rubbed; the Greek for amber is elektron, and William Gilbert, an English doctor, coined the Latin electricus from it. Pull a plastic comb through dry hair in winter and the comb comes away negative, leaving every strand positive. Each strand now carries the same charge, and like charges push each other away, so the hairs fan out.

A thin stream from a tap bends toward a charged balloon, and toward a charged glass rod too, though the two carry opposite charges. Each water molecule is lopsided, positive at one end and negative at the other, and free to turn, so it swings its attracting end toward whatever charge comes near without gaining any charge itself.

Storing charge came next. In October 1745 Ewald Georg von Kleist, a Pomeranian amateur, filled a small medicine bottle with alcohol, pushed a nail through its cork and charged it; touching the nail numbed his arm and shoulder. Pieter van Musschenbroek, a Dutch professor, built one at Leiden early in 1746 and took its full jolt. In a letter to Reaumur in Paris he called the experiment terrible and swore that, having survived it by God's grace, he would not repeat it even for the entire kingdom of France. The device took his city's name: the Leyden jar.

That year the Abbé Jean-Antoine Nollet wired about two hundred Carthusian monks into a ring roughly a mile around and discharged his jars into them. Every monk leapt at once, all the way round, so whatever electricity was, it crossed a mile faster than any eye could time.

In 1747 Benjamin Franklin, watching men on wax stands pass sparks, drew the rule physics has kept: rubbing does not create electric fire but gathers what matter already holds, moving it from one body to another. He called a surplus of his single electric fluid plus and a shortage minus, and guessed the flow's direction backwards: electrons carry the negative charge and drift from minus to plus. Physics kept his labels anyway, so circuit diagrams still draw current running from plus to minus, opposite to the electrons.

Air insulates well until the electric push across it reaches some three million volts for every metre, or three thousand per millimetre, and then it gives way at once. So when a spark leaps a full millimetre from your finger to a doorknob, you were carrying roughly three thousand volts. Lightning breaks air down at that same threshold. What separates a sting from a killer is the charge standing behind the spark: a whole charged person stores about a hundredth of a joule, while a bolt carries tens of coulombs at currents near thirty thousand amperes.

A flash reaches you almost at once, but its thunder travels at the speed of sound, taking about five seconds to cover a mile, so counting the gap tells you how far off the strike was. The cloud charges itself in its cold middle, at roughly fifteen to twenty degrees below freezing, where rising air lifts small ice crystals past heavier pellets of soft hail called graupel. Each brief touch leaves the heavy graupel negative and sinking and the light crystals positive and rising, stacking the cloud into a battery kilometres tall.

Balloons, rockets and armoured planes flown through storms have never measured a field strong enough to break air down: ordinary storms sit near a tenth of the threshold, and the strongest field ever found reaches only about a third of it. What sets lightning off is still an open question.

Even the balloon is unsolved. In 2025 Scott Waitukaitis and Juan Carlos Sobarzo in Austria touched identical silicone blocks together thousands of times. At first the charging went either way, but after about two hundred contacts the blocks sorted into a fixed order, and a block with more contacts behind it reliably charged negative against one with fewer. Nobody yet knows why.

stem-cells-one-cell-that-can-become-any.context_blurb:
A stem cell can do two things at once: copy itself, and give rise to many specialised kinds of cell. The marrow inside your bones uses a rare stock of them to make hundreds of billions of blood cells a day. Their story runs from Toronto to Oxford to Kyoto, with one famous fraud on the way.

Blood stem cells are scarce: roughly one in every ten thousand marrow cells, and stricter modern tests find them rarer still. The field began in Toronto in 1961. James Till, a physicist, and Ernest McCulloch, a blood doctor, destroyed the marrow of mice with radiation, injected fresh marrow, and days later found small lumps on the spleens. What mattered was that the lumps rose in step with the dose, more injected cells giving more lumps, which meant each lump grew from a single cell and they could count something nobody could see.

A marrow transplant moves blood stem cells from one body to another, and of all stem-cell therapies it has the real record of saving lives. Yet the first six patients of the American doctor Donnall Thomas, reported in 1957, were all dead within weeks, and of some two hundred transplants tried worldwide through the 1950s and 1960s, not one patient survived long-term. Thomas kept going, and won a Nobel Prize.

At Eton in 1949, John Gurdon came last of 250 boys in biology. His school report called his hope of becoming a scientist quite ridiculous, and he kept that report framed in his office until he died, as a reminder on days when experiments failed.

Each spleen lump counted only if it came from one cell. In 1963 the graduate student Andy Becker proved it: radiation had snapped the donor cells' chromosomes in a random pattern, different in every cell, and every cell inside a single lump carried the identical pattern of breaks. Then, with Lou Siminovitch, Till and McCulloch broke up one colony and put the pieces into another mouse whose marrow had been wiped out, and the pieces seeded new colonies of their own, just as in the first. That self-renewal, plus many kinds of blood cell from one ancestor, became biology's definition of a stem cell.

Meanwhile, in 1962 at Oxford, Gurdon killed the nucleus of a frog egg with ultraviolet light and replaced it with a nucleus from the gut lining of a tadpole that was already feeding, and got a healthy swimming tadpole. A committed gut cell still carried the full instructions for a whole animal. Critics had a fair objection: a sample of gut lining could include a stray cell that had never specialised. The doubt ended in 1975, when a team at the Basel Institute for Immunology used the nucleus of a white blood cell busy making one particular antibody, a cell whose finished identity nobody could dispute, and still got living tadpoles.

In 1957 Conrad Waddington pictured how a cell settles on its fate: a ball rolling downhill through a landscape of branching valleys, each groove leading to a stable end, and nothing rolling back uphill on its own. Gurdon had pushed a cell back up that hill.

In January 2014 Haruko Obokata, a young researcher at RIKEN in Japan, claimed in two Nature papers that soaking ordinary mouse cells for half an hour in a mildly acidic bath turned them back into embryo-like cells without adding a single gene. Labs everywhere failed to repeat it. RIKEN found misconduct, Nature retracted both papers, and when investigators sequenced the famous cells, they proved to be ordinary embryonic stem cells already growing in the same lab. Top journals had rejected it two years before, and they were right.

The real reset came from Kyoto. In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi put 24 genes active in embryonic cells into adult mouse skin cells, and a few cells reset. To find the ones that mattered, they took the genes out one at a time and tested again each time, watching for the reset to fail when an essential gene went missing. Twenty-four came down to four. One of them, c-Myc, is a known cancer gene, and about a quarter of the mice grown from the reset cells died of tumours. In 2007 Yamanaka's team simply left c-Myc out, accepting a reset that was far slower and rarer in exchange for safety. Gurdon and Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize.

steno-and-the-tongue-stones.context_blurb:
Nicolas Steno was a young Danish anatomist working for the Medici court in Florence in the 1660s. A shark's head on his dissecting table solved an old riddle about stones, and the short book he wrote next gave geologists the rules they still use to read time in a cliff. Then he left science for the Church.

Across Europe people prized small triangular tongue stones dug from hillside rock. Nobles and royals wore them as pendants or kept them in a pocket, trusting them to guard against poison and snakebite. On Malta, where the stones were everywhere, a story from the 1100s tied them to the Apostle Paul, who was shipwrecked there: the stones were serpents Paul had turned to stone, which is why they were thought to beat venom. The Maltese still call them Saint Paul's tongue.

In October 1666 fishermen hauled a huge shark ashore near Livorno, and Tuscany's Grand Duke had its head sent to Steno. Dissecting it, Steno saw that its teeth matched the tongue stones: the stones were the teeth of sharks, buried in mud that later hardened around them. Some Maltese ones are megalodon teeth longer than your hand.

Walking the hills around Florence, he studied cliffs of flat layers, or strata, stacked like the leaves of a book, the lowest laid down first. He noticed that the lowest layers carried no fossils whatever, while those above were rich in them: the first geological evidence that Earth had passed through distinct ages.

Steno was not the first to call the stones teeth. Fabio Colonna, an Italian botanist, had argued in 1616 that they came from living creatures. What Steno added was a set of rules for reading the order in which layers of rock were laid down, which turned a tooth in a rock into a record of time. He set them out in 1669 in a book he called the Prodromus, Greek for a forerunner, meant as a short preview of a full treatise. He never wrote that treatise at all.

The book asked how one solid can come to sit inside another. In a fossil tooth set in stone, the stone has moulded itself around each ridge and saw-edge of the tooth, yet the tooth bears no print of the stone. Steno reasoned that the body which stamps its shape on the other hardened first, so the tooth had already hardened before the rock did. It was buried, and only later did the mud set into stone.

His rules read a cliff like a page. Layers settle flat under gravity, so a band of rock standing almost on end must have been tilted after it hardened. Sand can rest on a gentle slope, but nothing settles standing upright. A layer also spreads sideways until something stops it, so when one bright band appears at matching heights on both walls of a canyon, it was once a single sheet, and the canyon was cut through it later.

Last, anything that cuts across a layer is younger than that layer. Suppose a fault breaks the lower beds but ends against an old eroded surface, an unconformity, with fresh layers laid on top, and then a dike, a wall of rock that rose molten, slices through everything. The order is fault first, then the eroded surface, then the dike, with no date needed.

Then Steno's interest in nature faded. He became a Catholic in 1667, a priest and then a bishop sent to the Protestant north, and he lived poor: he sold his bishop's ring and cross and gave the money to the needy. He died at Schwerin in 1686, aged forty-eight, and was beatified in 1988.

stern-gerlach-and-the-cheap-cigar.context_blurb:
In Frankfurt in 1922 Walther Gerlach and Otto Stern ran one of the first experiments to show the quantum world directly. They sent a beam of silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field onto a glass plate. Classical physics said the atoms, tiny magnets pointing in every direction, should pile up in a single smeared patch.

Instead they landed as two separate spots with a clean gap between, as if nature allowed only two values and nothing in between.

Seeing it took luck. The silver film was too thin to see, and Gerlach was ready to give up until Stern, on a junior salary and smoking cheap cigars, leaned over the plate. The sulfur on his breath turned the silver into jet-black silver sulfide, and the pattern appeared. In 2003 Bretislav Friedrich and Dudley Herschbach tried it again and found that clean breath does nothing; it takes cigar breath.

The two men believed they had confirmed the leading theory of the day, Bohr and Sommerfeld's space quantization of the electron's orbital motion. They were right about the split and wrong about the cause: silver in that state has no orbital angular momentum at all.

The real cause came in 1925, from two graduate students at Leiden, Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck. They proposed that every electron spins on its own, with only two directions allowed, and that silver's single outer electron is what the magnet sorts. Wolfgang Pauli at first thought the idea was nonsense.

Spin makes a puzzle you can follow on paper. Block the lower beam and pass only the upper one through a second magnet turned ninety degrees, so that it asks about left and right instead of up and down. The beam splits again into two spots, one left and one right. Those atoms were definite about up and down but undecided about sideways, so the new question gets a fresh coin toss.

strachans-siblings-and-the-amish-barn.context_blurb:
Why do some children get hay fever and asthma while others never do? In 1989 the London epidemiologist David Strachan found a clue in family size. His idea, later nicknamed the hygiene hypothesis, holds that early contact with the microbial world trains the immune system not to overreact. Two American farming peoples later turned his clue into a natural experiment.

Strachan worked through records on more than 17,000 British children, all born during a single week in 1958. Of sixteen background factors, the one that stood out was how many older brothers and sisters a child had: hay fever at age 23 fell from about one in five among those with none to about one in fifteen among those with four or more. He suggested that infection in early childhood, carried home by older siblings and passed from child to child, might be what protects. He hedged the idea carefully and never wrote the words hygiene hypothesis; others pinned that label on him.

His data even held its own control. Infant eczema fell as the number of older children rose, but showed no link at all to younger brothers and sisters, who had not been born when the rash appeared and so could not have caused it. If big families simply reported illness differently, that column would have sloped too.

Just after German reunification, the paediatrician Erika von Mutius expected children in polluted, coal-burning East Germany to suffer more allergy than those in the wealthy West. She found the reverse and reported it against her own hypothesis: West German children were about twice as often allergically sensitised.

The cleanest test came from the American Midwest. Amish and Hutterite children eat similar food, live in tidy homes and grow up much alike, yet Hutterite children are about four times as likely to have asthma, 21.3 percent against 5.2. The geneticist Carole Ober and her colleagues found the difference on the farms: the Amish barn stands right beside the house, and Amish children run in and out of it all day, while Hutterites farm on an industrial scale with barns well away from their homes.

Genes could not explain it. Both peoples descend from small sixteenth-century Anabaptist communities, the Amish from Switzerland and the Hutterites from the South Tyrol, and when the team compared their whole genomes with other Europeans, the two landed side by side, set apart from the rest. Measuring the house dust, they found that Amish homes held nearly seven times as much endotoxin, a piece of the outer wall of bacteria. The Amish house is not dirtier; it is busier with microbes, because the barn is next door.

Then they tested cause. They collected ordinary indoor dust from the houses themselves, not the barns, and dripped extracts of it into the noses of mice. The mice were also being sensitised to egg white, the standard laboratory model of asthma. After fourteen doses, the mice given Amish dust had calmer airways and less of the antibody aimed at egg, while Hutterite dust protected nothing. To learn what in the mouse sensed the dust, the team repeated the test in mice each bred without a single signalling protein. Without MyD88, the relay that carries signals from the Toll-like receptors of the fast, inborn half of immunity, the protection largely vanished.

Not every germ helps. Nils Sigurs followed Swedish babies hospitalised with severe RSV infection of the small airways for eighteen years, and they ended up with roughly seven times the risk of asthma.

One chemical link is known. Yukihiro Furusawa's Japanese team showed in 2013 that butyrate, a fatty acid that gut bacteria make from fibre, loosens the packaging around a gene called Foxp3 in young T cells of the colon wall, turning them into regulatory T cells, immune cells whose job is to call off an attack.

Strachan also tested his own idea in public. A popular version cast allergy as a see-saw between two arms of immunity, Th1 and Th2. In 2004 he and his co-author Sheikh judged that picture somewhat simplistic, because allergic and autoimmune diseases often strike the very same person, which a simple see-saw cannot allow. Nor are children simply too clean. Hygiene researchers led by Sally Bloomfield found that bleach use varies about thirtyfold across Europe with no matching pattern in allergy, and warned against relaxing hygiene. Which microbes protect, and exactly how, is still unsettled.

surgisphere-2020-the-database-that-was-n.context_blurb:
In May 2020, early in the COVID-19 pandemic, The Lancet and America's New England Journal of Medicine both published studies built on what looked like a vast hospital database spanning six continents. The Lancet paper said that hydroxychloroquine, a malaria drug, raised patients' risk of dying, and the World Health Organization paused that arm of its big trial within days. The database could not have existed.

The data came from Surgisphere, a small Illinois firm run by the vascular surgeon Sapan Desai. Its whole staff numbered about eleven people, not enough to field a football side, yet it supposedly ran a live records network linking hundreds of hospitals.

Outside readers began with arithmetic. They set the paper's count of in-hospital COVID deaths in Australia beside the national total anyone could check, and the paper's deaths came out higher than every COVID death Australia had recorded so far. That was only the way in. Across six continents the patients' ages, illnesses and drug doses were implausibly uniform, when real hospital records differ wildly from country to country.

Days later James Watson, an Oxford statistician working in tropical medicine, sent an open letter with over 140 fellow signers, asking, in effect, to see the workings: the data hospital by hospital, an independent check of it, and the reviewers' comments. A few of the authors themselves then asked for an independent audit, and when the auditors requested the raw dataset, Surgisphere refused to hand it over, citing confidentiality agreements with its clients. With nothing to check, three of the four Lancet authors retracted, saying they could no longer vouch for the data; Desai did not sign. Both papers were withdrawn in early June.

How did two elite journals miss it? Journal reviewers read the write-up an author sends in; they do not see the raw records behind it, and they cannot audit a private company's servers. The correction came from strangers with a calculator.

One more lesson is easy to miss. Exposing the Lancet paper as worthless proved nothing about the drug either way, because a bad study being wrong is not evidence that the drug works. That question needed proper randomised trials, and Britain's RECOVERY trial and the WHO's own trial both found no benefit in patients sick enough for hospital.

survivorship-bias-walds-bombers-and-the-.context_blurb:
In 1943 the mathematician Abraham Wald, working in New York for the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, was handed a wartime question: where should American bombers carry more armour? His answer exposed a trap now called survivorship bias, which hides wherever the failures quietly drop out of the data.

Bombers returning from Europe came back with bullet holes clustered on the wings and fuselage. Wald saw that the sample held only planes that survived; planes hit in other places had not come home. So he advised reinforcing the parts that came back unmarked. The famous scene of Wald jabbing at a drawing of a plane covered in red dots is a modern retelling. What he actually produced in 1943 was a series of eight technical memoranda, one giving a way to estimate how vulnerable each part was from the damage on planes that returned.

The same trap hides in science. Journals print striking results and turn away studies that find nothing, so the published record looks stronger than the evidence. In 1979 the psychologist Robert Rosenthal named this the file drawer problem, after the drawers where dull results end up.

In the 1930s the parapsychologist Rhine, at Duke University, reported card-guessers with astonishing streaks of extrasensory perception. Test enough people and chance alone produces streaks. The magician and sceptic Martin Gardner charged that Rhine repeated his tests and left the failures unreported, so the streaks proved nothing.

Everyday advice falls into it too. Saying that dropping out of college makes people rich because a few famous billionaires dropped out ignores the many dropouts who stayed poor: the failures never make it into the sample at all.

The modern fix is preregistration. Before seeing any data, researchers commit in public to their plan of analysis, so they cannot later hunt through subgroups until one, say left-handed women over sixty, happens to work, and a null result cannot vanish into the drawer. It is Wald's lesson made into a rule: decide what counts before you see who survived.

sv40-the-virus-nobody-was-looking-for.context_blurb:
Polio vaccines of the late 1950s were grown in kidney cells from rhesus monkeys. In 1960 scientists found that those cells carried a monkey virus that no safety test had been looking for, and it had already gone into millions of doses. The story of that virus, SV40, shows how a product can pass every test on the books and still carry something nobody had yet learned to see.

In its natural host, the rhesus macaque, SV40 settles into the kidneys for life and causes no disease, which is why nobody went looking for it. Late in 1960 Maurice Hilleman and Ben Sweet of the drug company Merck described the new virus, named for the bubbles it raised in cultured cells, and reported it already present in all three types of Sabin's live polio vaccine.

The Salk vaccine was a killed vaccine, made safe by soaking the poliovirus in formaldehyde for a time measured against poliovirus. SV40 is tougher: by the virologist Leonard Norkin's estimate, about one in 10,000 SV40 particles came through the soak alive. About 98 million Americans, most of them children, got the Salk shot in the eight years from 1955. Looking back in 1976, Shah and Nathanson estimated that 10 to 30 percent of that vaccine carried live SV40, which would mean some 10 to 30 million people exposed.

Bernice Eddy, a virologist at America's National Institutes of Health, injected plain extracts of the monkey kidney cells into 154 newborn hamsters, and 109 of them grew tumours. In October 1960 she described the result at a New York cancer meeting. Joseph Smadel, her superior, had dismissed her finding, and afterwards he forbade her to speak about it in public unless she cleared her words with him first. Hilleman argued that her experiments were poorly controlled, so the dispute cut both ways. In 1962 Eddy supplied the control herself. Virus recovered from the tumours raised new tumours in fresh hamsters, but when she first mixed a batch with rabbit antiserum against SV40, no tumours grew at all.

In hamsters, SV40 needs one protein, large T antigen, to turn a cell cancerous. One brake in a cell, p53, tells a damaged cell to halt or kill itself; the other, Rb, keeps the cell from starting to divide. Large T clamps onto both at once and holds each out of action, with no mutation of the cell's own genes needed.

American rules from 1961 required every lot to test free of SV40, though lots already approved were not recalled. A 2005 study by Cutrone's team checked old stored vaccines from 13 countries and found that one eastern European manufacturer's oral vaccine still held live SV40 as late as about 1978, because its heating step had not killed the virus.

Did it cause human cancer? Reports kept finding SV40 DNA in mesothelioma tumours. In 2004 Lopez-Rios and colleagues retested 71 of them and at first matched those reports, until they examined their primers, the short probes that pick out a DNA sequence. The primers were reading a stretch of SV40 that is also built into ordinary laboratory plasmids, tools made from the virus; with primers that avoided it, only four faint positives remained.

Of 1,073 people given contaminated vaccine as newborns and followed for 35 years, total cancer deaths matched expectations, but one cancer broke the pattern: testicular cancer, with two deaths where 0.05 were expected. Larger registry studies found no clear excess. In 2002 the Institute of Medicine judged the evidence inadequate to accept or reject a link. The exposure is not in dispute; the consequence is not settled.

szilards-traffic-light-the-chain-reactio.context_blurb:
On 11 September 1933 Ernest Rutherford, who had discovered the atomic nucleus, told a scientific meeting that anyone expecting power from transforming atoms was talking moonshine. Next morning in London, Leo Szilard, an out-of-work Hungarian physicist, read the report in The Times and went for a walk.

By his own account, told decades later, the idea struck while he waited for the lights to change where Southampton Row meets Russell Square: if some element, struck by one neutron, threw off two, the reaction would feed itself. A great expert's sensible verdict was overturned within a day by an idea the expert never had.

Szilard patented the chain reaction in 1934, but he had nothing to run it on. In 1934 and 1935, at St Bartholomew's Hospital and Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory, he tested beryllium and indium himself, and neither gave out more neutrons than it swallowed. The idea waited until uranium fission was found in 1939.

On 2 December 1942, beneath the stands of the University of Chicago's football field, Enrico Fermi's team slowly drew the final control rod, made of cadmium, from a pile of uranium and graphite. Cadmium soaks up neutrons, so as the rod slid out, the neutron count stopped falling and began to climb on its own: the first self-sustaining chain reaction, running just as Szilard had imagined at the kerb.

teisserenc-de-bort-and-the-layered-sky.context_blurb:
Does the air just keep getting colder the higher you go? For centuries everyone assumed so. Around 1900 Léon Teisserenc de Bort, a French weather scientist, sent instruments where people could not safely go and found that the sky is built in layers: a churning lower deck where the weather lives, and a calm deck above it.

The cost of sending people was paid on 15 April 1875. Gaston Tissandier and two companions, Sivel and Crocé-Spinelli, took the hydrogen balloon Zenith past 8,000 metres to study the thin upper air. Their oxygen bags were not enough: Sivel and Crocé-Spinelli suffocated up there, and only Tissandier came down alive, partly deaf.

French upper-air science drew the lesson: send the instrument, not the man. Unmanned balloons, small and cheap, now took self-recording thermometers aloft by themselves, and from his private observatory at Trappes, near Versailles, Teisserenc de Bort launched more than two hundred of them. He ran many launches at night. In daylight a warm reading high up could be blamed on sunshine heating the thermometer, but with no sun in the sky, no critic could make that argument.

Above about 11 kilometres over France his thermometers stopped dropping: the temperature held nearly steady while the balloons climbed on. Most scientists would have suspected faulty thermometers. What won scientists over was independent confirmation: Richard Assmann, working in Berlin with balloons of his own, found the same layer and announced it just three days after Teisserenc de Bort did, in the spring of 1902.

Teisserenc de Bort named the churning lower deck the troposphere and the calm one the stratosphere. The boundary between them, the tropopause, is no flat shelf: pushed up by vigorous tropical updrafts it stands about 17 kilometres high over the equator, and it sags to only about 8 over the cold poles.

Where, then, does space begin? Nobody discovered the answer; committees chose it. The FAI, the body that certifies flight records, uses 100 kilometres, called the Kármán line, while the United States gives astronaut wings for passing 50 miles, roughly 80 kilometres. Von Kármán's own aerodynamic estimate was nearer 84 kilometres, and the FAI rounded it up to a tidy 100.

The stratosphere is upside down, warm on top and cold below, because ozone there absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet light and heats the air around it. Warm air lying over cold air will not overturn, so the layer barely mixes, which is why airliners cruising in it ride so smoothly. It is also why volcanic ash and pollution injected there linger for years.

thalidomide-one-molecule-two-hands.context_blurb:
In 1957 the West German company Grünenthal began selling a sedative named Contergan; elsewhere it went by the name thalidomide. Grünenthal claimed nobody could take an overdose. Within four years the drug had caused one of medicine's worst disasters, and the reasons reach all the way down to the shape of a single molecule.

Doctors prescribed it for anxiety and sleeplessness, and the company pushed it to expectant mothers for morning sickness, though its rodent tests had never checked what it did to an unborn baby.

In late 1961 two doctors working independently, the German paediatrician Widukind Lenz and the Australian obstetrician William McBride, tied the drug to a sudden rise in babies born with missing or shortened limbs, sometimes with hands or feet set close to the body. The injury gave everyday language a word: phocomelia, from the Greek for seal and limb, because such limbs can look like a seal's flippers. Between ten and twelve thousand children were harmed worldwide, and the damage fell above all on the arms and legs. The United States was largely spared because of Frances Kelsey, a new medical officer at the Food and Drug Administration, who kept sending the application back for missing safety data, month after month.

The harm struck only babies exposed between roughly the 20th and 36th days after conception, the two weeks or so when the limb buds form and pattern themselves; exposure near day 24 hurt the arms, near day 28 the legs.

Thalidomide comes in two mirror-image forms, like a left and a right hand. The S form fits a human protein called cereblon, part of the cell's machinery for tagging proteins to be destroyed, and turns that tagging against proteins the growing limb needs; Handa's group in Japan identified the target in 2010.

A popular moral says nothing would have happened if the company had sold only the harmless R hand. That is wrong. The molecule's central carbon carries an acidic hydrogen that drops off and re-attaches from either side, so inside the body the R form spontaneously turns into S anyway.

In 1962 President Kennedy honoured Kelsey, and the Kefauver-Harris Amendment became law. Besides safety, American drug makers now had to show, for the first time, that a drug actually works for the use it claims, and hundreds of useless old remedies came off the shelves.

The molecule has since come back under strict rules against pregnancy: for a painful complication of leprosy, and since 2006, with dexamethasone, for the blood cancer multiple myeloma, whose cells rely on proteins that the same cereblon trick destroys.

the-alvarez-iridium-layer.context_blurb:
Sixty-six million years ago the dinosaurs died out, along with much of the life in the sea. In the late 1970s a father and son, the geologist Walter Alvarez and the Nobel-winning physicist Luis Alvarez, found the killer's fingerprint in a thin layer of clay in Italy. Their answer, an asteroid, made a bold prediction, and the hunt for its crater took ten years.

In the pink limestone above Gubbio, in central Italy, Walter found a clay band about a centimetre thick: below it the rock teems with tiny plankton shells, above it they are almost gone. He wanted to know how long the clay took to settle. Luis offered a physicist's clock: measure iridium, a metal that space dust sprinkles down onto Earth at a slow, steady rate, so the amount in the clay would reveal how long it took to form.

Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, chemists at Berkeley, measured the samples. Slow settling should have made the clay a little richer in iridium, fast settling a little poorer; instead it held about thirty times as much iridium as the limestone around it, and no settling rate could explain that. Iridium makes a sharp clue because Earth's crust has almost none. When the young planet was molten, its iron sank to form the core, and the iridium, which dissolves readily in iron, went down with it; asteroids never separated that way, so meteorites keep plenty.

In Colorado and Utah, just above the boundary clay, the fossil pollen suddenly turns almost all fern, up to ninety percent in places. Ferns are pioneers, the first plants onto scorched and emptied ground, so the spike shows bare land being recolonised from scratch.

In 1980 the Alvarez team published its bold step. Added up across boundary clays worldwide, the iridium totalled some fifty thousand tonnes, and from that mass they worked out the size of the body that fell: about ten kilometres across. Such an impact must have left a crater 150 to 200 kilometres wide. The rival idea, proposed in 1971 by Dale Russell and Wallace Tucker, was a nearby exploding star, which would have left isotopes such as plutonium-244 and iron-60 in the clay. The search found none of them at any boundary site, and the supernova idea died on its own test.

Harder evidence followed. The boundary clay holds quartz grains crossed by dead-straight glassy lines that only a shock far beyond any volcano can make. Geologists compared them with reference grains dug from beneath a buried nuclear test, the 1962 Sedan blast in Nevada, and the boundary grains matched.

The crater was already on oil-company maps. Antonio Camargo and Glen Penfield, flying magnetic surveys for Mexico's state oil company in 1978, had found a buried arc 180 kilometres across beneath the Yucatán. Penfield's 1981 conference talk drew little notice. In 1990 Carlos Byars, a reporter for the Houston Chronicle, told the geologist Alan Hildebrand about it, and the buried crater finally reached the impact hunters. Its name is Chicxulub.

The asteroid also struck unlucky ground. Beneath the Yucatán lay kilometres of limestone over a thick bed of gypsum, sulfur-rich rock left by dried-up seas. When drillers cored the crater's central ring of hills in 2016, the gypsum was almost entirely missing: it had been vaporised and flung into the high atmosphere as sulfate haze, which blocks sunlight far better than dust. Those cores were granite that normally lies some ten kilometres down, heaved up in a matter of minutes. The violent shaking briefly cancelled the friction inside the broken rock, so for a few minutes it flowed like a liquid, rose and slumped into a ring.

The asteroid also has a rival suspect. In India the Deccan Traps poured out vast floods of lava over the same span, and the geologist Gerta Keller has long blamed the volcanoes for most of the killing. Paul Renne and Mark Richards of Berkeley, with Walter Alvarez on their team, argue a third view: the impact's shaking set off the biggest Deccan eruptions. The argument has narrowed, but it has not closed.

the-antimatter-ledger-why-is-there-anyth.context_blurb:
Every atom you have ever touched is a leftover from a contest the universe should have drawn. Physicists predicted antimatter on paper, then photographed it, and have since tested it every way they can. The more perfectly it mirrors ordinary matter, the stranger it is that anything exists at all.

In 1928 Paul Dirac, a British physicist of 25, found that his equation describing the electron had a second solution he could not get rid of. It called for a twin of the electron with the opposite charge, which nobody had ever seen. Four years later Carl Anderson at Caltech photographed a cloud-chamber track that bent the opposite way to an electron's in a magnet's field: a positive electron, made by cosmic rays striking the atmosphere. He named it the positron.

Bring an electron together with a positron and both vanish completely, with no ash or fragments: all their mass turns into energy, carried off as gamma rays. It is the only reaction in nature that uses up matter entirely.

The hot early universe ought to have produced matter and antimatter in equal measure, and the two should have annihilated each other into pure light. Instead about one particle in a billion survived, and that tiny excess built every star, planet and person. The light from all that annihilation still fills space as the cosmic microwave background.

Could the missing antimatter be hiding in far-off galaxies? If it were, the borders where matter and antimatter met would glow with gamma rays, and stray antihelium would drift our way. Telescopes, and detectors such as the space station's Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, have found no evidence of antimatter regions anywhere.

Does antimatter fall up? In 2023 CERN's ALPHA-g team released antihydrogen atoms inside a tall magnetic bottle for the first time, and they dropped just as ordinary atoms do. The light antihydrogen gives off and the antiproton's mass match ordinary matter too. Each matched result makes the puzzle harder to explain, not easier, because the smaller the difference between matter and antimatter, the harder it is to leave even a one-in-a-billion excess. Nobody yet knows the answer.

the-bell-that-fell-silent-in-the-jar.context_blurb:
Can sound cross empty space? Robert Boyle, an Anglo-Irish chemist, put the question to a test in 1660 with his new air pump. The textbook version says he proved it at once. The true story is better: it took some 45 years, honest doubt and better equipment to settle.

Boyle suspended a ticking watch on a thread within the glass vessel of the pump, which he had built with the young Robert Hooke, and drew the air out. As the vessel emptied, the ticking faded to nothing, and it came back the moment he let air in. The reason is how sound travels: a shout crosses a room as patches of air squeezing together and springing apart, each patch pushing on the next, so with no air there is nothing to pass the push along.

Boyle himself would not call it settled. His pump still leaked, and the thread holding the watch might itself be carrying the ticking out to his ear.

Others had reported the opposite. In 1650 the Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher described a bell set in the empty top of a tall barometer tube, its clapper worked by a magnet from outside; it could still be heard, and he took that as proof that air remained. His supposed vacuum was not truly empty. He was a serious man defeated by his equipment, not a fool.

Around 1705 Francis Hauksbee settled the matter at the Royal Society, not with a better argument but with a far tighter pump that reached a much better vacuum. Even a hanging bell went nearly silent, and squeezed air made it louder.

Space really is silent, except where it holds a medium. In 2003 Andrew Fabian's team, studying 53 hours of Chandra X-ray images of the hot gas in the Perseus galaxy cluster, found pressure waves driven by the black hole at its centre. Their pitch is a B-flat some fifty-seven octaves under middle C, far below any piano key or human ear.

the-bill-for-the-closed-classroom.context_blurb:
In 2020 and 2021 governments around the world shut schools to slow COVID-19. Researchers have since measured what that cost children, in learning and in mental health. One country that kept its primary schools open supplied the closest thing to a controlled comparison.

The story starts with who was at risk. Blood surveys that found every past infection, even mild ones, showed the death rate climbing steeply with age, from near zero in children to several percent in the very old, and it was lowest of all among children aged five to nine. Schools were closed for the age group least at risk from the disease.

America's longest-running check on learning, the NAEP long-term trend test, has followed nine-year-olds for about fifty years. In 2022 their maths score fell seven points, the first drop in mathematics the test had ever recorded, while reading fell five.

Bastian Betthäuser's team, early in 2023, pooled 42 studies from 15 countries into a single estimate, and the loss was larger in mathematics than in reading. The headline figure was a loss of 0.14 standard deviations. A typical pupil gains about 0.4 standard deviations in a normal school year, so the loss came to roughly a third of a year's learning, about 35 percent. It was not shared evenly. The widest gap opened by family background: children from low-income homes fell furthest behind, so the closures widened the very gap they were said to protect. The deficit also appeared early in the pandemic and then held steady; children took one step down and went on learning at the normal pace from the lower level, neither sliding further nor catching up by themselves.

The Netherlands looked like a best case, with good internet, equal schools and a closure of just eight weeks. Yet when Per Engzell and colleagues compared national exams taken before and after it by about 350,000 primary pupils, the loss roughly equalled the time out of school, about a fifth of a year, and was up to 55 percent larger for children from less-educated homes.

Sweden kept its primary schools open throughout. Researchers who tracked the reading of 97,073 Swedish children in the first three grades found no measurable fall compared with the years before the pandemic. That makes Sweden's open primary schools, set beside its neighbours' closed ones, the cleanest comparison the pandemic produced: similar rich countries facing the same virus, with school policy the big difference. Comparisons between American states are muddied by shifting dates and local politics.

The cost was not only academic. In March 2022 the World Health Organization estimated that anxiety and depression worldwide rose by a quarter in the pandemic's first year and named young people and women as the hardest hit, though such a global estimate carries wide uncertainty.

the-blacklists-and-the-courtroom-twitter.context_blurb:
Can a government lean on social-media companies to bury posts it dislikes? Between 2022 and 2024 two sets of records put that question before the public: the companies' own internal files, and emails pried loose by a lawsuit. The facts in those records were never disproved; whether what happened was lawful is still open.

Soon after buying Twitter in 2022, Elon Musk let a handful of journalists, among them Matt Taibbi and Bari Weiss, read the company's private messages and publish what they found on the site itself. The releases became known as the Twitter Files.

The files showed tools that could quietly shrink an account's reach without telling its owner, keeping it out of search suggestions and trends while leaving the follower count untouched. One account Weiss named, put on a Trends Blacklist, belonged to the Stanford professor Jay Bhattacharya, who had argued that lockdowns would harm children. Making a user quietly harder to find, without banning him, is called shadow-banning. Weiss also quoted a Twitter engineer who wrote that the company controlled visibility and amplification quite a bit, and admitted that ordinary users had no idea how much of that the company did.

The government's side came out in court. In May 2022 Missouri and Louisiana, through their attorneys general, sued the federal government, and pre-trial discovery produced emails showing White House staff, among them the digital-strategy director Rob Flaherty, pressing Facebook and Twitter to take posts down.

The legal test reaches back to 1963. That year, in Bantam Books v. Sullivan, the Supreme Court struck down a Rhode Island commission's warning letters to booksellers, though nobody was arrested and no law was passed: official pressure alone can be censorship. Lawyers call that kind of unlegislated pressure on a private party jawboning.

On 4 July 2023 Judge Terry Doughty issued a sweeping injunction against much of the administration, and his ruling said the case arguably involved the most massive attack against free speech in American history.

When Murthy v. Missouri reached the Supreme Court in June 2024, six justices declined to decide whether anyone had been censored. They held that the challengers lacked standing, the threshold requirement to sue: they could not tie particular takedowns to particular government demands closely enough to show an injury a court could remedy. The line between a government persuading and a government pressuring remains the open question.

the-bright-spot-that-was-meant-to-kill-t.context_blurb:
Is light a stream of particles or a wave? Isaac Newton's great authority stood behind particles. In the early 1800s a London doctor and a French road engineer argued for waves, and the clinching test came from an enemy of the idea: a bright spot predicted as an absurdity, then found exactly where it was said to be.

The puzzle was old. In 1665 Francesco Maria Grimaldi noticed that light passing a narrow opening fans out more widely than straight rays could, leaving coloured fringes along shadow edges, and he named the effect diffraction. He took light to be a very fine fluid that undulates like ripples on water.

Thomas Young, a London doctor, darkened a room at the Royal Institution in 1803, let in a thin sunbeam and split it with a slip of card held edge-on. On the far wall he saw stripes, bright alternating with dark. Two beams of light adding up to darkness is something particles cannot do, but waves do it easily, crest cancelling trough. Young told his audience anyone could repeat his experiments whenever the sun shone. You can: hold two fingers almost touching close to one eye and look through the narrow gap at a lamp or bright window, never the sun, and dark lines appear in the gap, light cancelling light.

From January 1803 Henry Brougham, a founder of the Edinburgh Review, attacked Young's work anonymously as worthless. The smear worked: the publisher of Young's lectures backed out, and Young turned to medicine, and later to the Rosetta Stone, leaving the wave theory ignored for more than a decade.

The revival came from France. Augustin-Jean Fresnel was a government road engineer. When Napoleon escaped from Elba in March 1815, Fresnel walked off the job to side with the royalists, was suspended, and spent the forced holiday doing experiments on light at his mother's home.

In 1818 the Paris Academy set a prize on diffraction, and Fresnel entered a wave theory. One judge, Siméon Poisson, believed in particles and combed Fresnel's own mathematics for an absurd consequence. He found one: a small round disc lit from in front should show a bright spot at the very centre of its shadow. The committee's chair, François Arago, went and looked. The spot was there, Fresnel won, and it has carried Poisson's name ever since.

Roundness is what makes it work. Every point on the disc's rim lies the same distance from the centre of the shadow, so light grazing the edge all the way round arrives there in step, crest on crest, and adds up instead of cancelling. Aim a laser pointer at a small ball bearing and you can see the dot yourself.

The spot had been seen before. Delisle described it in 1715 and Maraldi in 1723, yet their reports started no argument for a century, because no theory of light then existed for the spot to confirm or refute. An observation becomes a test only when an idea could fail on it.

Fresnel also explained polarisation, but only if light shakes from side to side, across its path. Waves like that cannot run through an ordinary fluid, so the ether thought to carry light had to be as rigid as a solid, yet let the planets sail through it untouched.

His practical monument was a lighthouse lens made of concentric glass prisms. On 20 August 1822, to convince the commission paying for it, he set a rotating eight-panel lens on top of the Arc de Triomphe and had it judged by observers 32 kilometres outside Paris. In July 1823 the first stepped lens shone from the Cordouan lighthouse, replacing twelve polished reflectors. Fresnel's complaint against reflectors was blunt: their mirrors never sent even half of the lamp's light out of the tower, while his lens kept only the light-bending surfaces of glass and threw the dead bulk away.

The wave victory looked final for nearly a hundred years. Then, in 1905, Einstein took up the photoelectric effect: light striking a metal frees electrons from it. On the wave picture brighter light should kick each electron harder, but the energy of each electron tracked only the colour of the light, from red to violet, while brightness changed only how many came out. Einstein argued that light arrives in packets whose energy rises with frequency, and the old argument reopened.

the-clock-nothing-can-reset-how-radiomet.context_blurb:
How can anyone know a rock is four billion years old? Radioactive atoms decay at steady, measured rates, so each sample carries a clock. The art lies in knowing what starts each clock, how far it can read, and how to check it against ages already known.

Every living thing takes in carbon-14 from the air, by breathing or by eating. At death the intake stops and the carbon-14 inside starts a steady countdown, so a bowl, a shirt or a needle dates from the death of the tree, the flax or the deer it was made from. Carbon-14 would have vanished long ago, but the upper air keeps making more: a cosmic-ray neutron strikes a nitrogen-14 atom and knocks out a proton, turning it into carbon-14.

The clock has a limit. Carbon-14 halves every 5,730 years, and after about 50,000 years too little is left to measure. A mammoth tusk from Siberian ice falls well inside that window; a dinosaur bone 66 million years old does not, because its carbon-14 ran out long ago and there is none left to count.

Willard Libby, who built the method, burned each sample to pure carbon and counted its decays. A gram of modern carbon ticks only some fourteen times in a minute, so his counters wore a ring of extra detectors to reject stray signals from outside. Libby earned trust by retelling stories already known: he ran timber from an Egyptian pharaoh's tomb and rings from a felled giant sequoia through his counters and plotted the results against their known ages. His half-life of 5,568 years was a little short. Labs still compute raw ages with his number, so that a date published in 1955 means the same as one published today, and fix the error openly at the calibration step.

Calibration rests on tree rings. A run of fat and thin rings is a barcode that wet and dry years stamp on every tree in a region, so overlapping ring patterns chain dead logs onto younger logs and finally onto living trees, with no radiocarbon used at any step. Hohenheim's oak and pine record reaches back 12,460 years. In 1977 physicists at McMaster and Rochester found a better way to measure: machines that count individual carbon-14 atoms inside an accelerator, sorting them by mass, so a single seed or thread can now be dated.

Humans made one clock by accident. Open-air nuclear tests up to 1963 nearly doubled the carbon-14 in the air, which then drained away fast. Tooth enamel forms in childhood and is never replaced, so when a Karolinska team led by Spalding and Frisén measured its carbon-14 in 22 people, they recovered the calendar year each person was born, to within about a year and a half.

Rocks need slower clocks, such as uranium decaying into lead. The trouble is knowing how much lead a rock started with, so geologists use zircon, a tough crystal that takes uranium into its structure as it grows but shuts lead out. Every lead atom inside it was made there by decay. Earth's oldest dated fragment is a zircon crystal narrower than two hairs side by side, from Western Australia's Jack Hills, 4,404 million years old. Its oxygen isotopes show that the magma it grew in had already met liquid water near the surface, only about 150 million years after Earth formed.

Could heat and pressure over the ages have sped the clocks up? Labs have heated, frozen, squeezed and magnetised radioactive samples and found no change, because decay happens in the nucleus, while heat and chemistry act on the electrons far outside it. The one dramatic exception proves the point. Ordinary rhenium-187 has a half-life of 42 billion years, but when physicists at the GSI storage ring in Darmstadt stripped every electron away, opening a new route to decay, the half-life fell to about 33 years. Atoms in rocks keep their electrons.

Geologists also stopped assuming the starting amount. They take several minerals from one rock and graph rubidium against strontium for each: if the rock stayed sealed, the points fall on a straight line whose intercept gives the starting strontium and whose slope gives the age.

Some ages are bracketed instead. Lucy, the 3.18-million-year-old skeleton from Hadar in Ethiopia, carries no usable clock in her bones; her age comes from volcanic ash layers above and below her, dated by the argon that builds up as potassium decays.
