the-cloud-chamber-how-to-see-a-single-pa.context_blurb:
A cloud chamber is a box of damp, chilled air in which invisible particles leave white threads of fog. A Scottish weather scientist invented it by accident, and for forty years it was physics' best tool for finding new particles. You can build one at home.

In 1894 the Scottish physicist Charles Wilson worked a fortnight as a relief observer on the summit of Ben Nevis. Sunlight breaking through threw his shadow onto the mist beneath him, circled by coloured rings, and he went home wanting to recreate the effect in a jar in his laboratory. Physics then held that clouds need dust to form on. In 1895 Wilson filtered his air until no dust was left, yet a hard enough expansion still produced fog. The droplets were growing on ions, molecules that had lost or gained electrons and so carried an electric charge.

A fast charged particle rips electrons from the molecules along its path, leaving a line of ions, and the overloaded vapour condenses on them into droplets large enough to see. By the time the thread appears, roughly one tenth of a second has passed and the particle is long gone: you see its wake, not the particle. Wilson won a Nobel Prize in 1927, but he stayed a weather man to the end. His last paper, published in 1956 when he was 87, was a theory of the electricity inside thunderclouds.

The easiest particles to watch are muons, heavy cousins of the electron made about 15 kilometres up when cosmic rays hit the top of the atmosphere. At sea level about one crosses your palm every second. CERN publishes a manual for a home detector: a clear box roughly as big as a fish tank, felt soaked in isopropyl alcohol over 90 percent pure, a black metal floor plate, dry ice beneath it and a bright torch. Dry ice burns skin and must never be sealed airtight, and the alcohol is poisonous, so use gloves, goggles and a ventilated room.

The alcohol evaporates from the warm felt at the top and, being heavier than air, sinks toward the cold floor, where the dry ice chills it into a thin layer overloaded with vapour. Every track appears there, running along the floor like spider's thread. Most threads, thin and straight, are muons. A thread that suddenly turns a sharp corner is a muon decaying in flight into an electron and two neutrinos.

A muon lives only about 2.2 microseconds, and the trip down takes about 50, so almost none should survive it. They arrive in floods because, moving almost as fast as light, their internal clock runs slow compared with ours: each thin thread is evidence for Einstein's special relativity that you collected yourself.

Laboratories made discoveries with the chamber. In 1925 Patrick Blackett fired alpha particles into nitrogen and kept photographing for weeks to catch a rare head-on hit, and his photographs showed, for the first time, nitrogen turning into oxygen as a proton flew out, a change Ernest Rutherford had claimed.

A still photograph cannot show which way a particle moved, so Carl Anderson at Caltech laid a slab of lead across his chamber: a particle crossing it loses energy and curves more tightly afterwards, so the tighter half of a track must be the later half. On 2 August 1932 he developed a frame with a track too light to be a proton that bent the opposite way to any electron. His first thought was mundane: students must have reconnected the wires to his magnet, reversing it. Nobody had; he had found the positron.

In 1936 Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer took a chamber with a platinum slab up Pikes Peak and caught a particle about 207 times as heavy as an electron. For eleven years physicists mistook this mesotron for the particle Yukawa had predicted to glue nuclei together, though the plates already showed its tracks driving straight through a centimetre of the metal, barely deflected; a particle that hardly touches nuclei cannot be what holds them together. It was the muon.

At Manchester, Clifford Butler and George Rochester ran their chamber for 1,500 hours and found, in two of some 5,000 photographs, a pair of tracks splaying into a V from a point in empty gas, with nothing leading in. The parent was electrically neutral, so it left no ions and drew no trail until it decayed into charged pieces: the kaon, first of the strange particles.

the-contested-polio-elimination-story.context_blurb:
Polio once paralysed thousands of children a year, and its defeat is usually told as one simple story. The record holds several separate questions: what caused the disease, why it suddenly came in epidemics, whether paralysis really fell, whether the counting rules changed, and how much the vaccines did. Keeping them apart keeps the facts straight.

Before the 1880s cases came singly. Then epidemics began, in Sweden in 1887, Vermont in 1894 and Norway in 1905, and the places struck first shared something surprising: the cleanest water supplies and the best sewers. In 1979 Neal Nathanson and John Martin explained why. Cleanliness postponed the age at which a child first caught the virus, and infants carry antibodies handed on by their mothers that fade within months; a protected baby usually has a silent infection and lifelong immunity, while a child infected later risks paralysis.

Was it a germ at all? In Vienna in 1908 Erwin Popper and Karl Landsteiner took spinal cord from a boy who had died of polio, passed the ground tissue through a filter fine enough to hold back every bacterium, and injected what came through into two monkeys. Both were paralysed, with the same spinal damage. The cause was smaller than a bacterium and could be passed on: a virus. That experiment is what any rival theory must get past. In a 2018 book the author Forrest Maready argues that DDT and, before it, the pesticide lead arsenate shaped the curve of paralysis. His critics point to Landsteiner and Popper's monkeys: a transmissible agent produced polio's exact lesion decades before DDT existed, so a poison could at most change who the virus paralyses. That narrower question remains open.

Others suspected insects. In August 1945 Rockford, Illinois, declared an emergency and sent a B-25 bomber over the town to spray DDT, hoping to wipe out the houseflies that bred in its garbage and sewage. The epidemics came anyway. The virus is tough: alcohol gel kills flu and cold viruses by dissolving their fatty outer envelope, but poliovirus has no fatty envelope to dissolve, only a bare protein shell, so soap and running water are needed to wash it off.

When paralysis reached the chest it could kill. In 1928 Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw of Harvard built an airtight iron tank to do the breathing for such patients, its pumps taken from two vacuum cleaners, and on 12 October it revived a dying girl in Boston. Yet that ward of iron lungs misleads: most infections caused no symptoms at all, and only one infection in roughly two hundred ended in any paralysis.

Did paralysis fall after the Salk vaccine of 1955, or did the counting change? Before labs could type viruses, a summer fever with a stiff neck was often logged as polio on a doctor's judgement. Herman Kleinman, Minnesota's state epidemiologist, said much of his state's non-paralytic polio in 1956 was really Coxsackie B-5 virus, and a huge 1957 outbreak was ECHO 9. In 1960 the biostatistician Bernard Greenberg told Illinois doctors that in 1955 health offices had changed what counted as paralytic polio. The old rule wanted paralysis found on two exams; the new one demanded that the paralysis remain when the patient was checked again some sixty days after it began. Greenberg still credited the vaccine with reducing cases to some extent. Kleinman, who had measured two Salk doses as 83 percent protective, backed Greenberg's point: doctors now reported only cases of unmistakable paralysis. Herbert Ratner, Oak Park's health commissioner, added that a town's epidemic line had been twenty cases for every hundred thousand residents in a year, and that after the vaccine it was raised to 35. The counting change is agreed; how much of the fall it explains is still argued.

Some folk observations proved real. From 1910 doctors noticed that children whose tonsils were removed in a polio summer were more often paralysed, and the Harvard Infantile Paralysis Commission confirmed it in the 1940s. The mechanism came in 1998 from Eckard Wimmer and Matthias Gromeier: injured tissue gives the virus a route into the nerves, which it follows inward toward the spinal cord and brainstem.

Since 1988 the case definition has held steady, so the later fall is no bookkeeping trick. When the global eradication drive began, wild polio crippled some 350,000 children yearly across more than 125 countries; in 2024 it was confirmed in just 99 cases, in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

the-control-group-from-linds-six-pairs-t.context_blurb:
How do you know a treatment works? You compare people who get it with otherwise similar people who do not, so that the one thing you changed is the only thing that can explain the difference. That idea, the control group, took two centuries to sharpen, from a naval surgeon's twelve sailors to sealed envelopes in 1948.

In 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, James Lind kept twelve sailors with scurvy in the same quarters on the same diet and gave each pair a different remedy. The pair given a lemon and two oranges every day recovered fastest, one of them fit for duty within about six days, while the other remedies did little or nothing.

Lind did not draw the clean conclusion. He still blamed scurvy on blocked sweating, and to keep the cure aboard ship he had the juice boiled down into a syrup he called a rob, but the heat destroyed the vitamin C that had done the curing. The Navy took 48 more years to act. In 1795 Gilbert Blane persuaded the Admiralty to give every sailor a daily ration of lemon juice, and scurvy, which had killed more British seamen than enemy cannon, all but vanished from the fleet within two years.

In the 1830s the Paris doctor Pierre Louis tallied survivors and deaths. His numerical method, published in 1835, showed that bleeding pneumonia patients with lancets and leeches, a treatment handed down since Galen, did not help.

Matched groups can still mislead. A kind doctor may steer the sickest patients away from a new drug, making it look better than it is. The cure is to let chance alone decide which group each patient joins.

Ronald Fisher turned that into a method. At Rothamsted in the 1920s the biologist Muriel Bristol said she could taste whether milk had been poured before the tea or after it. Fisher set out eight cups, four with milk first and four with tea first, shuffled at random, and his test became the template for the randomized experiment, the opening example of his 1935 book The Design of Experiments. If she were only guessing, her chance of picking out every milk-first cup was 1 in 70, because there are exactly 70 ways to choose four cups from eight. A colleague of Fisher's later said she got every cup right.

The first properly randomized trial in medicine, published by Britain's Medical Research Council in 1948, tested streptomycin against bed rest for tuberculosis of the lungs. Its designer was the statistician Austin Bradford Hill. Each hospital received a set of sealed, numbered envelopes, one opened for each new patient. That safeguard, allocation concealment, stops the doctor doing the enrolling from choosing whom to take in next, since a doctor who could guess the next envelope might wait for a sicker or a healthier patient.

the-country-that-kept-the-schools-open.context_blurb:
In the spring of 2020, as COVID-19 swept Europe, most governments shut their schools. One country did not, and it became the closest thing to a natural experiment the pandemic produced, with honest results on both sides of its ledger.

Sweden kept classrooms open for children under sixteen through the whole first wave, with no closures, no masks and no distancing rules, while its Nordic neighbours closed theirs; only its upper-secondary schools, for older teenagers, went remote. The state epidemiologist, Anders Tegnell, built the national response on advice people were trusted to follow rather than orders enforced by police: stay home when ill, avoid crowds, keep away from the over-70s.

In January 2021 the paediatrician Jonas Ludvigsson and colleagues reported on nearly two million Swedish schoolchildren, aged one to sixteen, who had stayed in class. 15 were admitted to intensive care, and not one died of COVID-19. The loudest worry had been for teachers. Compared with other jobs, health workers left out, Swedish schoolteachers' risk of severe COVID-19 came out below average, at a relative risk of about 0.43. Nor did the children lose ground: standard primary-school reading assessments after the spring wave showed no measurable learning loss.

The other side of the ledger was grim. Sweden's excess deaths in 2020 were worse than its Nordic neighbours', and its own Corona Commission reported in December 2020 that the extra deaths were concentrated in nursing and care homes, after discharge policies without testing and failures to shield the elderly. Tegnell and the government admitted that failure. Across 2020 to 2022 taken together, most methods place Sweden, beside its Nordic neighbours, among the European countries with the lowest excess mortality. The school decision was borne out by measurement; the care-home decision was not.

the-curies-shed-tonnes-of-ore-for-a-tent.context_blurb:
In a leaky wooden shed in Paris, Marie and Pierre Curie laboured some four years, boiling down tonnes of ore, to win a pinch of a new element, radium, weighing a tenth of a gram. The work began with a number Marie refused to explain away, and it ended by changing what scientists thought an atom was.

In 1898 Marie Curie built a sensitive electric meter to chase the uranium rays Henri Becquerel had found. Pure uranium metal read 24, yet pitchblende ore, which is only partly uranium, read 67 and even 83. She did not blame her instrument; she printed the likely reason, that an unknown element, far more active than uranium, might be hiding in the ore. She tested the idea with a control. Natural chalcolite read 52, so she made chalcolite from pure laboratory chemicals, the same formula with nothing from the mine, and her copy read only 9: the extra activity was something hidden in the real rock.

The Curies had no budget for ore, but Austria's government gave them a hundred kilograms of Joachimsthal waste for nothing: residue left after the uranium, the valuable part, had been extracted and sold. The new elements had stayed behind in the discards. In July 1898 they announced the first, and Marie, born in Warsaw, named it polonium after Poland, her homeland, which Russia, Prussia and Austria had carved up until it vanished from the map of Europe. By December a barium-bearing fraction had grown sixty times stronger than uranium, but strength alone proves nothing. The chemist Eugène Demarçay examined its light and found a spectral line matching no known element, and the Curies announced radium.

Winning the pure element took four more years. Outdoors in the courtyard, because the shed had no fume hoods, Marie stirred boiling cauldrons of ore with a heavy iron rod almost her own height and ended each day broken with fatigue. The tale of her toiling alone is partly legend: a factory did the first rough processing, and André Debierne worked beside them. Radium sits under barium in the periodic table and behaves almost identically. The one difference she used was that radium chloride dissolves a little less readily than barium chloride, so the first crystals to form from a cooling solution are slightly richer in radium, and she repeated that step thousands of times. By 1902 she held one tenth of a gram of radium chloride, pure at last, and the point of it all was one number, the weight of a single radium atom, which tells a chemist where a new element belongs. She got 225, close to the modern 226.

The German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald came to see the famous laboratory and wrote that it looked half stable, half potato cellar; without the worktable of apparatus he would have taken it for a practical joke. Marie loved it anyway. At night she and Pierre would slip into the dark workroom to see the faintly glowing outlines of bottles and capsules of their products on the shelves.

Becquerel carried a radium tube in his waistcoat pocket and got a burn. Pierre Curie decided that an accident was not evidence, and in 1901 he strapped radium salt to his own arm for ten hours, then charted the wound as it reddened, blistered and scarred. Something that destroys healthy skin can be aimed at a tumour instead: radiotherapy began here. In 1903 Pierre and Albert Laborde found that radium salt gives off heat, roughly a hundred calories from each gram per hour, month after month, with nothing going in. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy explained it: radium atoms are breaking up, each changing into a different element.

That year the Paris Academy nominated Becquerel and Pierre for the physics Nobel, leaving Marie out. Told privately by the mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler, Pierre wrote asking to be considered jointly with her, and because a doctor, Charles Bouchard, had already nominated her, the committee could add her name. In 1911 she won the chemistry prize alone.

Neither of them knew what the glow was doing to them. Marie died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, and her notebooks, stored by France's national library in boxes lined with lead, are still so radioactive that a reader must wear protective clothing and sign away the library's liability. Radium has a half-life of about 1,600 years.

the-cutter-incident-1955.context_blurb:
In April 1955 America celebrated the news that Jonas Salk's polio vaccine worked. Within days, freshly vaccinated children began arriving at hospitals paralysed. The cause was a failure of manufacture and oversight at one company, and the fullest record of it was written by one of the vaccine's leading defenders.

Five drug firms were licensed to make the vaccine. One, Cutter Laboratories of Berkeley, was a small family firm known mostly for veterinary vaccines and medicines, with little experience of growing viruses in bulk. The warning came a year early. In 1954 the NIH scientist Bernice Eddy tested the makers' vaccines in monkeys, found three of Cutter's six batches paralysing them, and attached pictures of the stricken monkeys to her report. The NIH director rejected it, and she was moved off polio work.

In late April 1955 doctors in California saw five freshly vaccinated children struck by paralytic polio roughly seven days after being vaccinated. The clue that it was no coincidence was where the paralysis began: in each child, the arm that had received the vaccine. In Pocatello, Idaho, seven-year-old Susan Pierce developed fever and paralysis days after her injection and died, and local officials first said she must already have been carrying the infection when she was vaccinated. The vaccinated children then passed the virus on. Children given Cutter's vaccine shed live poliovirus, and in Idaho a mother who had never had the shot was paralysed after catching it from her two vaccinated children.

Nathanson and Langmuir later counted the two groups apart. Among vaccinated children about 40,000 fell ill without paralysis, 56 were paralysed and 5 died; among relatives and neighbours infected by them, 113 were paralysed and 5 died, so most of the paralysed had never been vaccinated.

Cutter's vaccine was halted at the end of April. Although only Cutter's lots were implicated, Surgeon General Leonard Scheele stopped every polio vaccination in the country on 8 May until the cause was found. Two NIH inspectors, William Tripp and Karl Habel, questioned Cutter's workers and read its records, and found nothing wrong with its production methods. The paperwork showed that the bad lots had passed every test the licence required; Cutter's tests were simply less sensitive than other makers' and missed small amounts of live virus.

The flaw was in the killing. Virus grown on monkey kidney cells was soaked in formaldehyde for roughly a fortnight, but after a change in filtration, clumps of cell debris shielded some particles from the chemical, and some Type 1 virus came through alive into the finished vaccine. Salk's safety rule assumed formaldehyde killed virus at a steady, straight-line rate, so a maker could calculate when none was left. At the later trial Salk said he could make safe vaccine every time, but the Nobel laureate Wendell Stanley testified that he had many times watched the killing curve stray from that straight line.

Congress, at hearings that June, faulted the NIH laboratory meant to watch Cutter. The NIH director and the Health Secretary resigned, and a new Division of Biologics Standards replaced the lab, with the power to test every batch itself and release it only once it was proven free of live virus. Vaccination resumed that autumn, and the killed vaccine proved itself: US polio cases fell from about 35,000 in 1953 to under 6,000 by 1957. Cutter showed a failure of manufacture and oversight, not that such a vaccine cannot work.

In January 1958 an Oakland jury heard the case of Anne Gottsdanker, paralysed after a Cutter shot. It found Cutter not negligent, since the vaccine had been made as the licence required, and then ordered the company to pay the families anyway, under an implied warranty that a product is fit for its purpose. Paul Offit calls this liability without fault. It seeded America's later vaccine-liability laws.

Offit wrote the fullest account, The Cutter Incident, in 2005, and he is no outsider: he is co-inventor of the RotaTeq rotavirus vaccine and a former adviser to the CDC. The record is not hidden; it is simply seldom told.

the-cylinder-that-wasnt-empty.context_blurb:
Teflon, the slipperiest solid ever measured, was found by accident in 1938 by a DuPont chemist who was hunting for something else entirely. What made the discovery was not luck but a scale, and the nerve to cut open a cylinder that might explode. The chemistry that makes the material untouchable also makes some of its chemical cousins very hard to get rid of.

Roy Plunkett, aged 27 and fresh from a doctorate, worked for DuPont in New Jersey. His assignment was a non-toxic replacement refrigerant, and the gas tetrafluoroethylene was only his starting material. With his assistant, Jack Rebok, he had stockpiled some hundred pounds of it in cylinders packed in dry ice, because warm tetrafluoroethylene could explode and burst its container.

On 6 April 1938 Rebok opened the valve on one cylinder and nothing came out, though the valve worked. Before writing it off, Plunkett put it on the scale, and it weighed exactly as much as a full cylinder. The gas had gone, but something was inside. Knowing the gas often exploded, the two men sawed the steel shell open anyway and found a waxy white powder caked on the floor and lower sides of the cylinder. The gas had joined itself into long chains, a polymer, with nobody adding anything. No photograph of that morning exists: the famous picture of three men cutting a cylinder open was set up in 1966, Plunkett and two colleagues posing for the camera.

What set the reaction off is still unproven. The prime suspect is the cylinder's own iron wall, acting as a catalyst under pressure.

The polymer, PTFE, is a backbone of carbon atoms, each one wrapped in fluorine, and the carbon-fluorine link is the strongest single bond carbon makes with anything. An attacker finds no weak point, so even aqua regia, the acid mixture that dissolves gold, does nothing to it, and its surface is so slick that almost nothing sticks. Inertness has a price. Heated PTFE barely flows, so factories press the powder in a mould and bake it until the grains fuse, the way a potter fires a ceramic.

Its first real job was secret war work. At the Oak Ridge uranium plant in Tennessee, uranium hexafluoride, the corrosive gas pushed through hundreds of miles of piping, was eating ordinary seals, and PTFE gaskets held. Teflon reached the shops only after the war.

The frying pan came from France. In the early 1950s the engineer Marc Grégoire was coating his aluminium fishing tackle with PTFE to stop his line tangling, and his wife Colette told him to coat her frying pan too; the Tefal company followed in 1956.

Cousin chemistry arrived by spill. At 3M in 1953 Patsy Sherman's experimental fluorochemical latex splashed onto an assistant's white canvas tennis shoes, and over the following days the spattered spot kept clean while the canvas around it turned grubby. Sherman and Samuel Smith turned the accident into Scotchgard.

Bob Gore's heated PTFE rods kept snapping when he pulled them gently. One night in 1969 he yanked a rod fast instead, and it stretched about eight hundred percent into a solid that is mostly air: expanded PTFE, the basis of Gore-Tex.

Read backwards, the same strong bond is a problem. PFOA, a processing chemical in PTFE factories from 1951, does not break down easily in rivers or in bodies; retired plant workers who took in no more of it needed about four years to shed half of what they carried. The finished coating is a large molecule the body does not absorb; the persistence problem lies with small processing chemicals like PFOA.

the-day-the-last-artifact-died.context_blurb:
Until 2019 the kilogram was a thing: one small metal cylinder in a vault outside Paris, against which every scale on Earth was ultimately checked. Physicists replaced it with a constant of nature, and doing so took two rival experiments that had to agree.

The cylinder, nicknamed Le Grand K, was about the size of a plum and made of a platinum-iridium alloy, nine parts platinum to one of iridium, chosen for its hardness and its resistance to tarnish. It sat in the vault of the BIPM at Sèvres under three nested glass bell jars, inside a safe that opened only with three keys, each in the keeping of a different official, all of whom had to be present.

About forty official copies went out to other nations, and every few decades they came back to be weighed against the master. Over a century the master and its copies wandered some 50 micrograms apart, roughly the mass of a fingerprint, yet no one could say which had changed, because the prototype could not itself be weighed: by definition it was exactly one kilogram.

Other units had already escaped from objects. In 1967 the second was redefined as a fixed number of oscillations of the microwave radiation given off by caesium-133 atoms, so every atomic clock traces its ticks to that atom. In 1983 the metre became the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That had a strange side effect: the speed of light in a vacuum, once a measured quantity, became fixed by rule and is now beyond measurement, even in principle, so better measurements now refine the metre instead.

The kilogram needed two independent routes. One, the International Avogadro Project, set out to tally every atom in a polished sphere about 94 millimetres across, said to be the roundest thing humans have ever shaped. It used almost pure silicon-28 so that nearly every atom had the same mass, and counting the atoms would then give the weight. The other route, the Kibble balance, weighs a mass against an electromagnetic force and yields a value for the Planck constant. Even when it worked, the international conference that governs the units waited until the silicon-sphere count independently confirmed that value to the required precision, because two methods with entirely different sources of error agreeing is far stronger than either alone.

On 20 May 2019 the change took effect. The Planck constant was fixed at exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, with zero uncertainty, and the kilogram now hangs on it.

The payoff is practical: with a Kibble balance, the fixed value of that constant and an atomic clock, a properly equipped lab anywhere, on Earth or on Mars, can make a kilogram from scratch, with no need to borrow a cylinder from France.

the-doctor-was-the-guinea-pig.context_blurb:
Some scientists have tested their ideas on the one patient who is always available: themselves. Their stories run from a weighing chair in seventeenth-century Padua to a tube in a young surgeon's heart, and they show both the courage of the method and why a sample of one can fool you.

Santorio Santorio, a physician of Padua in the early 1600s, lived, ate and worked for some three decades in a big hanging chair that weighed him. He weighed every meal and every waste, and the books never balanced: more went in than came out. He concluded that the missing weight had escaped unseen through his skin and his breath, a loss he called insensible perspiration. Step on a bathroom scale at bedtime and again in the morning and you can watch the same gap open.

In 1929 a young trainee surgeon in the German town of Eberswalde, Werner Forssmann, believed a fine tube could reach a living heart through a vein, though textbooks warned it would kill. His supervisor forbade it. Forssmann persuaded the surgical nurse Gerda Ditzen to bring him the instruments; she insisted that he use her as the subject instead of himself, and allowed her arm to be strapped down. Then, while she lay waiting, he fed the tube into a vein of his own arm. He pushed the thin rubber tube 65 centimetres along until its tip rested in the right-hand chambers of his heart. With the tube still in place, he went down the corridors to the X-ray department and had a picture taken of his chest, so that his feat could not be waved away. He was fired, and cardiology closed to him.

Twenty-seven years later André Cournand and Dickinson Richards of New York had turned his stunt into cardiac catheterisation, the standard way to measure pressures in a living heart, and in 1956 the Nobel Committee gave the prize jointly to all three: Forssmann, Cournand and Richards.

Self-experiment could cost everything. In Cuba in 1900 Jesse Lazear, a doctor on the army's yellow fever commission, let mosquitoes that had fed on sick patients bite him; the fever took hold, and he was dead within weeks, aged 34. His death led Walter Reed to draw up written consent contracts for volunteers, among the first in medical research.

It could also fool you. In 1892 in Munich the hygienist Max von Pettenkofer, who denied that a germ alone caused cholera, first swallowed baking soda so that his stomach acid could not kill the germs, then drank a flask of live cholera bacteria in front of witnesses. He got only diarrhoea and claimed victory, but a sample of one proves little, and the drinker is the person least able to judge his own result.

That is why the rules changed. A researcher today who wants to experiment on his own body must first win the written approval of an independent ethics board, because, as Richard Feynman put it, you are the easiest person to fool.

the-double-helix-and-the-sentence-at-the.context_blurb:
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick, working in Cambridge, showed how DNA, the molecule of heredity, is built: two strands twisted into a double helix, like a spiral ladder. They built it from other people's measurements, beat a famous rival who made a basic chemical slip, and ended their paper with one of the driest famous sentences in science.

They ran no experiment of their own. Their numbers came from others, above all the X-ray pictures of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins of King's College London, while Watson and Crick spent their days clamping metal parts from the Cambridge workshop into a model of the molecule.

Until about 1950 DNA seemed to most biologists too dull to carry genes, with its four bases supposedly present in equal amounts. Erwin Chargaff of Columbia measured each base separately and found that in every species the amount of adenine always equalled the amount of thymine, and guanine always equalled cytosine. That match makes sense only if A sits opposite T and G opposite C.

For weeks Watson shuffled cardboard cut-outs of the bases on his desk, and nothing would fit together at an even width. Jerry Donohue, a chemist in his office, told him the textbook shapes he had copied put hydrogen atoms on the wrong side of each base. With the corrected shapes, A paired with T and G with C, every pair the same width. A G-C pair is held by three hydrogen bonds and an A-T pair by two, links weak enough to release when the strands separate. Yet hydrogen bonds are not the main glue. Measurements by Frank-Kamenetskii's group in 2006 showed that about 70 percent of the helix's stability comes from neighbouring bases pressing their flat faces against each other, stacked like coins.

Their great rival was Linus Pauling, who had just solved the protein alpha-helix. In February 1953 he published a DNA model of three chains wound together with the phosphates packed at the core, exactly inside out. Three negatively charged backbones crammed together should fly apart, so Pauling kept an acidic hydrogen on each phosphate to cancel the charge. That meant his deoxyribonucleic acid was not an acid at all, and Watson and Crick said so in print.

On 25 April 1953 Nature published their note, barely over a page long, with no data and exactly one picture: a sketch of the twisted ribbons by Odile Crick, Francis's wife, a professional artist. Its last sentence is famously dry: the authors remarked that the pairing they proposed suggested a way the genetic material might copy itself, since each strand spells out the instructions for building the other. Watson later wrote that Crick walked into a nearby pub and told the room they had found the secret of life, though Crick remembered no such thing and nobody recorded it at the time.

Suggesting is not proving. Franklin Stahl and Matthew Meselson tested it in 1958 by growing bacteria on heavy nitrogen, switching them to ordinary nitrogen, and spinning their DNA in a tube where molecules settle by weight. After one generation the tube showed one band, exactly half-way between heavy and light, so every molecule was one old strand paired with one new.

One puzzle the helix could not touch is packing. A human nucleus is far narrower than a hundredth of a millimetre, yet it holds about two metres of DNA; the cell wraps it, a short stretch at a time, around millions of tiny protein spools.

the-double-slit-one-particle-interfering.context_blurb:
Send light, electrons or even large molecules at two openings and they land in stripes, as if each one went through both. Richard Feynman called this the only mystery of quantum mechanics. It has been tested with a card, a candle-dim lamp, spider silk and buckyballs, and you can begin at home with a laser pointer and a hair.

Tape a hair upright across the beam of a red laser pointer, never near anyone's eyes, and a wall several steps off shows a line of bright patches with dark gaps between them, the same pattern a slit as wide as the hair would make. Measure the spacing and you can work out how thick your hair is. In 1803 Thomas Young reported splitting a sunbeam with a slip of card turned edge-on; the overlapping halves made bright and dark bands, from whose spacing he worked out wavelengths near today's figures.

In 1909 a Cambridge research student, G. I. Taylor, dimmed a gas flame behind stacks of smoked glass until it was as faint as a candle a mile away. At the faintest setting he left his photographic plate exposed for three months. The stripes were just as crisp as in his brightest picture, though on average only about one photon at a time was in the apparatus. Physicists today will not rest the single-photon claim on Taylor, because light from a dimmed flame still arrives in random bunches, so two photons could sometimes be inside together. The airtight version came in 1986, when Philippe Grangier, Gérard Roger and Alain Aspect used photons announced one at a time.

Electrons came next. At Tübingen in the 1950s, Heinrich Düker and Gottfried Möllenstedt bent the two halves of an electron beam together with a gold-coated fibre, and Möllenstedt spun the fibre from spider silk; the story goes that he kept spiders in the lab. In 1961 his student Claus Jönsson, a physicist at Tübingen, did the real electron double slit, the same year Feynman began calling it a thought experiment never done in just that way.

In the early 1970s three Bologna physicists, Giulio Pozzi, Pier Giorgio Merli and GianFranco Missiroli, were the first to record single electrons arriving one by one on film, with an image intensifier borrowed from a Milan institute of anatomy. Akira Tonomura's Hitachi team filmed the build-up in 1989. At ten electrons the screen held a handful of dots sprinkled at random; by 140,000 the stripes were unmistakable, because the pattern lives in the statistics of many electrons. The beam was so sparse that two electrons were never inside at once, so the picture took over twenty minutes, and had the machine crept sideways by even part of one stripe's width, the stripes would have smeared into grey.

Molecules interfere too. In 1999 Anton Zeilinger and Markus Arndt's Vienna team sent C60 buckyballs, cages of sixty carbon atoms, through a grating, and the fringes appeared although the molecules were red-hot from an oven at roughly 900 kelvin. In 2019 the same group sent molecules of over 2,000 atoms through a two-metre interferometer, each with a wavelength roughly one-thousandth the width of a hydrogen atom.

Why does watching kill the stripes? The old answer was Heisenberg's: finding the path kicks the particle and smears the pattern. In 1998 Simon Dürr, Thomas Nonn and Gerhard Rempe measured that kick in an atom interferometer, and it proved much too weak to blur the stripes; they vanished because the path had become knowable. No mind is involved, and nothing runs backwards in time. In Yoon-Ho Kim's 2000 quantum eraser, erasing a partner photon's path information seemed to bring fringes back after the fact, but the screen's own raw record is a smooth blur, and fringes appear only when the hits are sorted afterwards by what happened to each partner.

the-earths-age-re-dated-by-better-clocks.context_blurb:
How old is the Earth? Over three centuries the answer grew from six thousand years to four and a half billion. Each estimate was honest for the evidence its author had, and each fell to a better instrument rather than to a better argument.

In 1650 the Irish archbishop James Ussher, a respected Trinity College scholar, dated creation to an October evening in 4004 BC. He measured nothing: he totted up the lifespans of the generations and the lengths of the kings' reigns recorded in the Bible, anchored to a date secular historians accepted.

In the 1770s the French naturalist Buffon wanted an experiment, not a text, to supply the figure. Picturing the Earth as a cooling molten ball, he had iron globes cast at his foundry, hauled them glowing from the furnace and timed how long each took to cool enough to hold in his bare hand. Scaled up to the Earth, that gave 74,832 years.

In 1862 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, ran the equations of heat backwards. His one measured starting fact was what miners knew: rock gets about one degree Fahrenheit warmer with every fifty feet of depth. From that gradient and a molten start, he allowed the Earth only tens of millions of years. That squeezed Charles Darwin, whose natural selection needed vast time. In 1859 Darwin had reckoned that wearing down the Weald of Kent alone took some 300 million years; under Kelvin's attack he halved the figure in later editions, then dropped it altogether, calling Thomson's views one of his sorest troubles.

John Joly, an Irish geologist, tried salt in 1899, dividing the ocean's sodium by what rivers deliver each year, and got 80 to 90 million years. But sodium leaves the sea again instead of simply piling up, so Joly had measured how long sodium stays in the ocean, not the ocean's age.

In 1895 the engineer John Perry, once Kelvin's assistant, showed in Nature that if the deep rock churns slowly as it cools, carrying heat upward like a simmering pot, the same maths permits an Earth of two or three billion years. Perry was polite, correct and ignored. A 2007 reassessment by England, Molnar and Richter argued that the neglect cost even more: for decades geologists argued over drifting continents without the moving interior that could explain them, though Perry had offered one.

In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fog a wrapped photographic plate. Radioactivity broke Kelvin's other assumption, that the planet merely spends its stored heat and never generates any; decaying atoms in the crust keep warming it. Science's favourite rescue story has Ernest Rutherford, lecturing in 1904 with Kelvin in the audience, saying that Kelvin had limited the Earth's age only if no new heat source turned up. Kelvin had indeed added a hedge like that in 1862, but it belonged to his reckoning of the Sun's lifespan, not to his Earth calculation, and the scene survives only in Rutherford's own retelling.

The numbers that worked came from atoms. In 1907 Bertram Boltwood compared the lead built up inside minerals with the uranium that remained, and got ages from 410 million to 2.2 billion years.

In 1948 Harrison Brown told his Chicago graduate student Clair Patterson that measuring the Earth's age would be duck soup. It took seven years, because lead from petrol was everywhere, in his beakers, his reagents and even his hair, and he had to build one of the world's first clean rooms. He dated meteorites, not Earth rock, because the restless interior has recycled Earth's original surface. A meteorite is debris left over from the birth of the planets and has stayed unaltered ever since. In 1956 five meteorites and a sample of ocean sediment fell on one line giving 4.55 billion years, and today's figure of 4.54 sits inside his error bars.

the-effects-that-dissolved-on-re-test.context_blurb:
Three of psychology's most famous findings, power posing, ego depletion and elderly priming, shared a pattern: a small first study, a lovely story, a huge audience, and then somebody ran the experiment again. None of the three scientists behind them was shown to have cheated. The effects simply dissolved under better tests.

In 2012 Amy Cuddy urged a TED audience to spend two minutes before a job interview with hands on hips, feet planted wide and chest thrust open, a stance she called the Wonder Woman pose, and the talk drew tens of millions of viewers. It rested on one 2010 study by Dana Carney, Cuddy and Andy Yap that tested just 42 undergraduates, a sample small enough for random noise to look like a real effect. The paper claimed more than a feeling: two minutes of posing supposedly sent testosterone up and cortisol, a stress hormone, down, and made people bolder gamblers.

In 2015 Eva Ranehill's team in Zurich repeated the experiment with a much larger sample. Only one thing survived: people still said they felt more powerful, while the hormone changes and the extra risk-taking vanished. The honest summary is not that power posing does nothing, but that it does not do what was claimed. In September 2016 Carney, the paper's first author, posted a statement saying she no longer believed power-pose effects were real, and listed the analysis choices that had produced the reported changes in hormone levels. Cuddy still defends a milder version.

Ego depletion began in 1998 with Roy Baumeister at Case Western Reserve University. Hungry students sat beside fresh-baked cookies, but half were allowed only radishes; given an unsolvable puzzle afterwards, the radish-eaters gave up sooner, and Baumeister concluded that willpower is a fuel tank that can run dry. By 2010 a meta-analysis of 198 tests seemed to make the effect certain. In 2014 Carter and McCullough corrected that analysis for publication bias, the habit of leaving failed studies in a drawer, and the effect shrank until it could not be told apart from zero. Then a preregistered replication run across 23 labs, with more than 2,000 participants, found essentially no effect at all.

Elderly priming came from John Bargh, working with two colleagues at New York University in 1996. Students unscrambled sentences sprinkled with old-age words such as wrinkle and Florida, and hidden stopwatches showed them taking longer to reach the elevator afterwards. Stéphane Doyen's team repeated the walk in 2012, timing it with infrared beams rather than a person with a stopwatch, and the primed students walked no slower than anyone else. In a second run they told half the experimenters that primed students would walk slowly and the other half that they would walk faster. Now a slow walk did appear, on the beams as well as the stopwatches, but only with experimenters who expected one, and the stopwatches of those expecting speed even clocked primed students as quicker. Doyen concluded that the testers' expectations mattered as well as the priming words. That is why good behavioural tests are blinded, so that neither subject nor tester knows the condition.

Investigators combing through the original labs' data found no fraud in any of the three; small samples, flexible analysis and an audience hungry for the story were enough. Sturdy effects, like the Stroop effect, survive retesting. In September 2012 Daniel Kahneman, who had praised priming in his own bestseller, sent leading researchers an open letter warning of a looming train wreck and urging them to set up a daisy chain of replications, in which each lab would repeat a priming result from the lab next to it.

the-ehrlich-simon-wager.context_blurb:
In 1968 the biologist Paul Ehrlich's bestseller The Population Bomb warned of coming mass starvation, and the economist Julian Simon argued that human ingenuity makes resources more plentiful, not scarcer. In 1980 the two men turned their quarrel into a test anyone could check: a bet on the price of metals.

Simon made the offer and insisted that Ehrlich himself pick which resources to bet on and for how long, so nobody could later claim the terms were rigged. The contract, signed in late September 1980, staked $1,000 across five metals, $200 apiece, chosen by Ehrlich and his colleagues: copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten. Ehrlich bet that scarcity would push their inflation-adjusted prices up within ten years.

When the decade ran out in September 1990, all five cost less in real, inflation-adjusted terms than they had at the signing, a clean sweep for Simon. Ehrlich paid up that October with a cheque for $576.07, matching how far the five metals' combined price had dropped, and so settled their public wager in full. The timing favoured Simon: a 2010 study that reran the bet over every ten-year span from 1900 to 2008 found Ehrlich would have won most of them, and ranked 1980 to 1990 among the worst spans for his side.

Simon had explained the result in advance in The Ultimate Resource of 1981. A rising price, he argued, is not a countdown to exhaustion but a signal that pays people to find substitutes, mine leaner ore, recycle and use less. That is why he called the human mind the ultimate resource.

Ehrlich paid but did not concede. To the New York Times he said the bet did not mean anything, and insisted to the BBC that it had been a fine bet which simply went against him. The same year he mailed the cheque, he won a MacArthur Fellowship. Prestige and accuracy are awarded separately.

the-electron-sea-why-metal-bends-where-s.context_blurb:
Bend a paperclip and it bends; strike a lump of rock salt and it shatters into flat-faced pieces. Both are orderly stacks of particles, and the difference is the glue that holds them together. A simple picture of that glue, a sea of electrons, explains why metals bend, carry heat and shine.

Metal atoms share their glue in every direction at once, while each bond in salt ties one particular positive ion to one particular negative neighbour. Paul Drude, a German physicist, pictured the inside of a metal in 1900: the atoms' outer electrons pool into one shared sea that wanders through the entire block, while the positively charged atom cores sit bathed in it.

Because the sea glues every core to all its neighbours, a layer of metal atoms can slip along and bond again in its new place, so the metal reshapes instead of cracking. Slide one layer of salt by a single atomic spacing, though, and positive meets positive and negative meets negative, so the repelling layers split apart along a flat plane.

The roaming electrons that carry an electric current carry heat as well, racing it through the whole metal. That is why a metal spoon in hot soup scalds your fingers within a minute while a wooden one barely warms; you can test it at supper.

Light is an electric wave, and a metal's free electrons respond to its push and re-radiate almost all of it straight back out, which is why polished silver makes a mirror while polished chalk stays dull. Smoothness alone does not make a mirror. Gold can be beaten into leaf under 100 nanometres thick, thin enough for light to pass through. Gold reflects the yellow and red end of the spectrum strongly, and the colours it does not reflect leak through, so light seen through the leaf looks bluish-green.

Ancient smiths found that a little tin makes copper into much harder bronze, and a little carbon turns iron into steel. The added atoms are the wrong size, so they warp the crystal and jam its slip planes, and the layers can no longer slide past one another freely.

Drude's picture is crude, and quantum band theory has replaced it underneath, yet it still gets all these everyday facts right. A model can be wrong at its foundations and still be the right picture to think with.

the-ether-dome-16-october-1846.context_blurb:
On 16 October 1846, in the domed operating theatre of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, the dentist William Morton held a glass globe of ether vapour to a young man's face while the surgeon John Collins Warren operated on his neck. The patient did not scream. Surgery without agony had arrived, though the true story is messier than the monument suggests.

Before then, speed was everything. Robert Liston could take off a leg in under half a minute while strong assistants pinned the wide-awake patient, because the shock of such pain could itself kill. The domed room, opened in 1821, has an odd ornament: since the 1820s it has housed the mummified body of Padihershef, an Egyptian stonemason from Thebes, accepted as a gift by the trustees.

The idea was old. In 1800 the young chemist Humphry Davy wrote that nitrous oxide, which had eased his own toothache, might be used in surgery. Instead, for over four decades, nitrous oxide and ether became the stuff of amusements: laughing-gas parties among the British upper classes and ether frolics among American medical students. In Georgia the country doctor Crawford Long etherised a young patient, James Venable, with a soaked towel and removed a growth from his neck in March 1842, years ahead of Boston. But Long waited seven years to publish, afraid critics would dismiss the painlessness as imagination or mesmerism.

Horace Wells, a Connecticut dentist and Morton's former partner, saw a showman's laughing-gas exhibition in December 1844 and the next evening let a colleague draw one of his own teeth under the gas. Weeks later he tried it before a Boston audience, and it failed: the gas ran out too soon, the patient groaned, and the onlookers hooted.

Morton turned to ether. One September night in 1846 a man named Eben Frost came to him with toothache, breathed ether and felt nothing as the tooth came out. A reporter happened to be present, and a short notice printed in the Boston Daily Journal the following morning is what got Morton invited to the hospital.

The patient on 16 October was Edward Gilbert Abbott, twenty-one. He did not cry out at the first cut, and the hospital record says it felt as though the area were being scraped with something dull; the famous line about a hoe is a later paraphrase. Morton's device was plain, a glass globe holding an ether-soaked sponge, with a tube and a mouthpiece. That night he improved it, because with the first design the patient kept re-breathing the air he had just breathed out; by morning it had one-way valves.

Warren is said to have told the sceptical crowd that this was no humbug, but that line survives only in later memories. His own journal that evening simply records an interesting operation performed at the hospital that morning. In 2022 surgeons re-read the hospital records. Abbott had a tangle of blood vessels under his jaw, Warren tied a ligature around it, Abbott stirred and cried out partway through, and when he went home in December the mass had not shrunk at all. The morning proved the anaesthetic, not the surgery.

Eleven days later Morton filed for a patent, disguising the drug under an invented name, Letheon, after the river of forgetfulness. The patent was soon worthless, because one sniff of the bottle gave away plain ether, known since 1540. Four men claimed the discovery: Long, who did it first and kept quiet; Wells, who tried in public and failed; the chemist Charles Jackson, who only suggested it; and Morton, who showed the world. When Boston raised a granite monument in 1868, the stone named the discovery and no discoverer at all.

Painless surgery had a grim sequel. It came about twenty years before germ theory, so surgeons cut longer and more often in unwashed coats on uncleaned tables, and deaths in the days after surgery kept climbing year after year. Joseph Lister's carbolic acid finally brought them down.

How anaesthesia works is still a mystery. It is used safely all over the world every day, yet a 2024 review still called the mechanism elusive. One pattern is solid: a drug's anaesthetic strength tracks how easily it dissolves in oil and fat, a link known as the Meyer-Overton rule.

the-file-drawer.context_blurb:
A shelf of published studies looks like a record of everything scientists tested. It is not: it is mostly a record of what worked. Studies that found nothing tend to disappear into drawers, and that quiet loss can mislead a whole profession without a single faked number.

The psychologist Robert Rosenthal gave it a name in 1979, the file drawer problem: studies that find nothing never get written up, and they drop out of sight. He also offered a check, his fail-safe number, which estimates how many hidden studies with null results it would take to erase a published effect. So when a report says that study after study shows something, the question that matters is not how many showed it, but how many were run.

In 2008 Erick Turner and colleagues found the drawer by comparing two records. The FDA had registered 74 trials of antidepressants, covering more than twelve thousand patients, before any results were in. In that registry 51 percent of the trials came out positive, but in the published journals 94 percent did. Of the 36 trials the FDA judged negative or doubtful, 22 were never published at all, and 11 more appeared in print dressed up as successes; only 3 were published the way the FDA had seen them. Doctors read the journals, not the FDA files, so a whole profession was sincerely misled by selective publication bias, the filtering of which results reach print.

Who does the hiding? In 2014 Annie Franco's team tracked 221 publicly funded studies from start to finish and found that most null results vanish because the authors themselves never write them up, expecting rejection, rather than because editors or reviewers kill them.

The bias can be national. In 1998 Andrew Vickers found that trials published from China and Russia never once reported a treatment as useless. A perfect success rate is a publishing policy, not a scientific finding.

The cost can be enormous. Governments spent billions stockpiling the flu drug Tamiflu trusting only brief published summaries. When Tom Jefferson's Cochrane team finally pried the full trial data from the maker, Roche, in 2014, the benefit had shrunk to roughly a day less of symptoms, with no drop in hospital admissions.

The repair that has worked came in September 2004, when the major medical journals announced that every clinical trial had to be entered in a public trial registry before it began, or they would not publish its results. A study that had to be announced cannot be quietly binned.

the-filter-that-caught-nothing-what-a-vi.context_blurb:
What is a virus? The question opened in the 1890s with a filter that should have caught every germ and caught nothing, and it is still being rewritten. A virus turned out to be a new kind of thing altogether: instructions wrapped in a protein coat, idle until it gets inside a living cell and borrows its machinery.

In 1892 at St Petersburg the young botanist Dmitri Ivanovsky studied a disease that mottles tobacco leaves. He forced juice from diseased leaves through unglazed porcelain whose pores no known bacterium could pass, painted the clear liquid onto healthy plants, and they caught the same mosaic disease. Ivanovsky made no leap. He guessed that either a chemical toxin had come through with the sap, or a bacterium tiny enough to squeeze through the pores had leaked past.

Martinus Beijerinck, a Dutch microbiologist, went further in 1898. He passed the filtered juice from one healthy plant to the next, again and again. A fixed dose of poison would have weakened with each passage, but this did not, so the agent had to be multiplying inside the living plant. He called it a contagious living fluid, contagium vivum fluidum, and that new category, not the filtering, was the real discovery.

Wendell Stanley, an American biochemist, purified tobacco mosaic virus from tons of sick plants in 1935 into dry needle-shaped crystals that kept in a jar like any chemical. Dissolved and brushed onto healthy leaves, the crystals infected them as strongly as the raw sap had. A thing that behaves like a chemical in a jar and like a living germ in a leaf broke the tidy line between chemistry and life.

The boxes are still being redrawn. In 1992 Timothy Rowbotham, tracking down where an outbreak of pneumonia came from, found something inside amoebae from a Bradford cooling tower that stained like a bacterium, and he froze it as Bradfordcoccus. In 2003 a Marseille lab examined it under an electron microscope: it was a virus, so huge that it had passed for a bacterium for eleven years, and it was named mimivirus.

Viruses are everywhere. In the surface ocean, the viruses that infect bacteria, called bacteriophages, burst open and kill somewhere between a tenth and two-fifths of the bacteria every day.

the-forgotten-organ-counting-the-hidden-.context_blurb:
Your body carries a hidden half: trillions of bacteria, living mostly in your gut, that some doctors call a forgotten organ. A Delft shopkeeper first saw them in the 1680s, a famous textbook number about them turned out to be a guess nobody rechecked, and germ-free mice show what they actually do.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek never went to university and knew no Latin. He ran a linen shop in Delft and took up lens-grinding to inspect the weave of the cloth he sold. His microscopes magnified about 275 times, against 40 or 50 for Robert Hooke's best. The working part was a tiny glass bead held between a pair of metal plates, pressed close to the eye, and he never revealed how he made them.

Though he scrubbed his teeth daily with salt, his mirror showed them dirtier than he expected. For his test of 1683 he skipped all cleaning for three days before scraping, and he compared samples from other people, including an old man who had never washed his mouth. Under his lens the scrapings swarmed with tiny creatures, and in his letter he wondered whether one mouth held more of them than the men in an entire kingdom. It is the first known description of bacteria.

In 2006 two doctors, Shanahan and O'Hara, made the case that the gut's bacteria form an organ of their own, up to a trillion in each gram of gut contents. Bacteria make up about 60 percent of the weight of faeces, which is mostly not leftover food.

For decades textbooks claimed ten bacterial cells in you for every human one. When three Weizmann Institute scientists, Ron Milo, Ron Sender and Shai Fuchs, traced the figure in 2016, every trail led to a single line of back-of-the-envelope maths in Thomas Luckey's 1972 paper, never rechecked. Luckey had imagined a kilogram of gut packed with bacteria, but the stomach and the first stretch of the small intestine hold almost none, kept nearly empty by acid and fast-moving food; nearly all live in the colon. Counting organ by organ for a 70-kilogram man, the team found about 1.3 bacterial cells for every human cell, give or take a quarter: roughly as many of them as of you.

Most of your own cells are red blood cells, about 84 percent of the count, and they have no nucleus or DNA. The old figure returns under one change of definition: compare the bacteria only with human cells that have a nucleus, leaving red blood cells out, and the ratio comes back to about ten to one. The authors called that a question of definition, not of measurement. Your own cells also hold several times more mitochondria, the power packs descended from bacteria swallowed long ago, than there are bacteria in your gut.

What do the microbes do? A germ-free mouse, raised in a sterile isolator, grows up wrong: in some mice the caecum, the gut pouch at the start of the large intestine, swells to a fifth of the body's weight. Give the mouse an ordinary gut community and the caecum returns to its normal size in a matter of weeks, which makes it a test of cause, not a correlation.

A 2011 study found germ-free mice livelier and bolder than ordinary mice, with changed gene activity in the brain. Giving them gut microbes early in life reset their behaviour, but colonising adults did not. Whether any of this applies to human mood, nobody yet knows.

the-francis-field-trial-what-a-good-test.context_blurb:
In 1954 nearly two million American schoolchildren lined up as Polio Pioneers to test Jonas Salk's killed-virus polio vaccine. The trial's judge, Thomas Francis Jr. of the University of Michigan, insisted on a design that still shows what a good test looks like, and the results showed exactly why the design mattered.

Before asking any other family, Salk tried the vaccine in 1953 on himself, his wife and their three sons. Francis, who had been Salk's teacher at Michigan, agreed to evaluate it only on his own terms. Besides a comparison group given a dummy shot, he required that the charity paying for the trial, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis with its March of Dimes money, stay completely out of judging the results.

Salk fought the design. A dummy shot in polio season meant that any of those children who were paralysed would, as he wrote, be paralysed at his own hands. He lost the argument. In the strictest districts a random draw split the children, and half received a dummy injection of the same tissue-culture brew as the vaccine with the poliovirus left out, so every syringe looked alike. No child, parent or doctor knew who got which; that is blinding.

Not every district agreed. 127 of the 211 study areas would not inject any child with a dummy; they offered the vaccine to second-graders only and kept watch on first- and third-graders as the comparison.

On 12 April 1955, ten years to the day after Franklin Roosevelt died, Francis faced more than 500 scientists and the cameras in Ann Arbor. The press release began by declaring flatly that the vaccine worked, and called it safe, effective and potent. His 113-page report refused the reporters a single headline percentage. It split the result by the three types of poliovirus, which the vaccine fought with very different success: roughly 60 to 70 percent protection against Type I, and over 90 percent against Types II and III.

The randomised districts show what the design bought. Paralytic polio struck vaccinated children at 16.4 per 100,000 and the dummy-shot group at 57.1, but the children kept out by their parents, with no more protection, came in at only 35.7 per 100,000, well below the dummy-shot rate. The volunteering families were better off and better educated, and their cleaner plumbing meant less exposure to the virus in infancy and so less natural immunity, leaving their children likelier to be paralysed later. Only a random draw makes two groups alike in everything but the injection.

That evening Edward R. Murrow asked Salk on television who owned the patent. Salk answered that the people did, that there was no patent, and asked whether you could patent the sun. The line is true but not the whole story: the Foundation's lawyers had already found that the vaccine could not be patented anyway, because inactivating virus with formaldehyde was long-established technique.

A field trial tests only the doses made for it. Thirteen days after Ann Arbor, children vaccinated in Idaho and California fell paralysed, struck by vaccine from Cutter Laboratories, where formaldehyde had left some poliovirus alive. The trial had answered its own question honestly; no trial can vouch for a different production line.

the-full-shell-and-the-evening-xenon-bro.context_blurb:
For sixty years chemists taught that a whole family of elements combined with nothing at all. Then, on a March evening in 1962, a chemist working alone in Vancouver broke that rule with two flasks, and the textbooks had to be rewritten.

Helium in party balloons, neon in old diner signs and argon in light bulbs belong to that column, once called the inert gases because they seemed to refuse every reaction. Their outer shells are full, with nothing to give away and no room to take more. Helium grips its electrons hardest of all: pulling one off takes more energy than for any other element, because its two electrons sit as close as electrons can to their nucleus.

Neil Bartlett, a chemist in Vancouver, had found that platinum hexafluoride, a fierce red gas, could pull an electron off molecular oxygen. He noticed that removing xenon's outer electron takes almost the same energy as removing oxygen's, about 1170 against 1175 kilojoules per mole. Late on 23 March 1962, alone in his lab, he let the red gas mix with colourless xenon, and at once an orange-yellow solid appeared, the first noble-gas compound in history.

He wrote the product as the neat salt Xe[PtF6], but later analysis showed the solid held two different salts mixed together rather than one pure compound. The discovery stood; the formula did not. The first noble-gas compounds all came from the heaviest members, xenon, krypton and radon, whose outer electrons sit farthest from the nucleus and are easiest to pull away, while light helium and neon still resist.

The sharpest twist concerns Linus Pauling. He had forecast fluorides of the heavy noble gases in 1933, yet in 1961, a year before Bartlett, he wrote that xenon was completely unreactive, arguing first one side and then the other. Within months other chemists had made simple xenon fluorides, and the column was renamed noble instead of inert.

the-furnace-we-can-never-open.context_blurb:
Nobody can open the Sun and look inside. Yet scientists have worked out what powers it, what it is made of and how stars forge the atoms in your body, using a weighed atom, a stubborn prediction and a tank of cleaning fluid nearly a mile underground.

Victorian physics' giant, Lord Kelvin, assumed in 1862 that the Sun kept hot by slowly shrinking under its own gravity, its contraction turning into heat. That allowed only some tens of millions of years of sunshine, too few for Darwin's slow evolution. Kelvin could not know that the atom hid a far bigger store of energy.

The clue came from weighing atoms. In 1920 Francis Aston, using his new mass spectrograph, found that four hydrogen nuclei weigh slightly more than one helium nucleus, by about 0.7 percent. If hydrogen fuses into helium, that missing mass turns into energy, and that energy is what makes the Sun shine. That August, at a British Association meeting in Cardiff, Arthur Eddington proposed that the Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium, years before anyone worked out the reactions. Critics said the core, at millions of degrees, was too cool for hydrogen nuclei to push past their electric repulsion. In his 1926 book Eddington replied that the critic should go and find a hotter place: the helium exists, so it was made somewhere. Quantum tunnelling later showed that nuclei slip through the barrier anyway.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne, a Harvard PhD student, read the Sun's spectrum and found it is mostly hydrogen and helium; Henry Norris Russell urged her to call the result almost certainly not real, and four years later he reached the same answer himself. To shine at about 3.85 × 10²⁶ watts, the Sun turns about four million tonnes of its own matter into energy every second, a small mountain's worth, and it has billions of years of fuel left.

Building carbon is harder. Two helium nuclei can stick together as beryllium-8, but it breaks apart in about 10⁻¹⁶ seconds, so a third helium nucleus almost never arrives in time. In 1953 Fred Hoyle insisted that carbon-12 must possess a still-undiscovered energy level, near 7.68 million electron-volts, that lets three heliums combine, for one reason: carbon is abundant, so the stars must somehow be able to forge it. Within months Ward Whaling, in William Fowler's lab at Caltech, found the level near 7.65, almost exactly where Hoyle said it would be, and it is called the Hoyle state.

To test the theory, Raymond Davis Jr caught neutrinos from the Sun's core deep in a South Dakota gold mine, Homestake, using a tank of a hundred thousand gallons of the fluid dry cleaners use. Now and then a neutrino turned a chlorine atom into argon, and he counted the argon atoms one by one. For decades the tank caught only about a third of the neutrinos John Bahcall's model of the Sun predicted. In 2001 Canada's Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, which could see all three types, showed that neutrinos switch identities in flight, so the missing two-thirds had simply turned into kinds Davis's tank could not see.

Fusion in stars builds elements only up to iron. On 17 August 2017 gravitational-wave detectors caught GW170817, two neutron stars spiralling together and colliding, and telescopes watched heavy elements, gold and platinum among them, being forged in the blast.

the-great-barrington-takedown.context_blurb:
In October 2020 three epidemiologists put their names to a short open letter in the Massachusetts town of Great Barrington, proposing a different strategy for COVID-19. How officials answered it, in public and in private, shows the difference between a scientific argument and a campaign against the people making it.

Sunetra Gupta of Oxford, Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford and Martin Kulldorff of Harvard called their idea focused protection: shield the old and the sick harder than lockdowns did, and let lower-risk people resume ordinary life. Within about two weeks more than ten thousand medical and public-health scientists had signed it too.

Days after it appeared, Francis Collins, then the NIH director, privately emailed Anthony Fauci and Clifford Lane, calling the authors fringe epidemiologists and asking for a quick and devastating published takedown of the letter's premises. The emails surfaced later through a Freedom of Information request.

A real scientific reply came too. The John Snow Memorandum in The Lancet argued that the vulnerable could not in practice be shielded and that unchecked infection would swamp the hospitals. The declaration's authors answered that lockdowns had not protected the vulnerable either. The hospital worry was genuine, and calling people fringe did nothing to answer it.

Of all the closures, the authors condemned school closures most sharply, as the case with the flimsiest risk argument and the deepest measured cost; Sweden, which kept its schools open, was their counterexample. In 2024 Collins said he had never seen the evidence behind the CDC's six-foot social distancing rule, enforced for two years.

On 25 March 2025 the Senate confirmed Bhattacharya to lead the National Institutes of Health, the very job Collins held when he dismissed them as fringe. That does not prove the declaration right in every respect, but it closed the circle.

the-great-dying.context_blurb:
Some 252 million years ago, as the Permian period closed, life on Earth came closer to a full reset than at any other time, in the worst mass extinction in the rock record. Geologists can still read the crime scene: the weapon, the timing and the survivors, though they still argue over how the killing was done.

Textbooks long said 96 percent of ocean species died, a figure from an earlier method that counted genera. Direct species counts now put the loss at about 81 percent, still the worst ever: the method improved, not the crisis.

The prime suspect is the Siberian Traps, one of the largest volcanic outpourings in Earth's history, which buried a continent-sized stretch of Siberia under lava at exactly this time. The lava itself was not the main killer. Magma rising through the Tunguska basin cooked buried Permian coal beds, releasing a pulse of carbon dioxide that warmed the planet by about 8 degrees and starved the seas of oxygen. Warm water holds less oxygen, and no coal formed anywhere on Earth for millions of years afterwards.

The timing comes from uranium-lead dating of zircons, tiny crystals in volcanic ash beds at Meishan in China, which squeezes the main extinction pulse into a span of about sixty thousand years.

Survivors inherited an emptied world. In South Africa's earliest Triassic bone beds one stubby, tusked plant-eater, Lystrosaurus, accounts for up to nine in ten land-animal fossils, and a lone survivor that suddenly dominates after a mass extinction like this is called a disaster taxon.

The trigger is agreed; the details are not. The top open dispute is ranking the kill mechanisms, extreme warming, oxygen-starved seas, acidifying oceans and ozone damage from volcanic gases, by how much harm each did.

the-green-flash-at-sunset.context_blurb:
In the last second before the Sun's top edge slips below a clean sea horizon, its final sliver can flare vivid green. Air acts as a weak prism, bending green light slightly more than red, so the Sun's green picture lags the red one as it sinks, and for an instant only the green edge is left.

A serious competing idea said the green lived inside the observer's eye: an afterimage in the opposite colour, left on the retina after gazing at the red Sun. But cameras have no tired retinas, and in 1925 Lucien Rudaux photographed the flash.

The bending happens at every clear sunset, yet the flash is rare, because the pure green rim is far too thin to see. It almost always needs an inversion over the horizon, a layer of air whose temperature runs the wrong way, the layering that makes mirages, stretching the last of the Sun like a lens until the green is thick enough to notice. Look only at the very last instant, never at the Sun itself.

the-greening-nobody-forecast.context_blurb:
Since 1981 satellites have measured how much leaf covers each patch of Earth's land. They were not looking for good news; they were counting leaves. What they found was a greener planet, and the honest account of why includes both the chemistry of the air and the work of farmers and foresters.

Zaichun Zhu's team totalled 35 years of those readings, from a NOAA weather satellite and a NASA satellite, in 2016. Between a quarter and half of Earth's vegetated land had grown significantly greener, something the models had not forecast. Running the data through ten ecosystem models, they credited about 70 percent of the trend to the extra carbon dioxide in the air feeding plant growth; richer air lets a leaf take in what it needs while losing less water. Those shares are model output, not a direct measurement.

A 2019 study led by Chi Chen, using finer satellite images, found that China and India were responsible for roughly one third of the added leaves, mainly by planting trees and farming intensively. Much of the greening is land management, not chemistry.

The direct test grows real plants in open air, ringed with pipes that release extra carbon dioxide all season. In a sweetgum forest at Oak Ridge, after eleven years, the early burst of growth dwindled once the soil's nitrogen ran low.

There is a cost as well. In 2014 Samuel Myers's team grew wheat, rice, peas and soybeans with open-air enrichment: the crops grew bigger, but the grain carried less zinc, less iron and less protein per mouthful. Greening is real and already counted in carbon budgets, but it does not cancel warming.

the-hard-problem-why-anything-feels-like.context_blurb:
Why does anything feel like anything? Scientists can trace how the brain sees, hears and decides, but not why any of that comes with an inner experience. The philosopher David Chalmers named this the hard problem in the mid-1990s, and it remains one of the great open questions: nobody yet knows the answer.

Every day an anaesthetist switches a patient's inner experience off before surgery and back on afterwards, yet nobody can say what physical thing is being turned off. Back in the 1600s René Descartes named the pineal gland, a small structure on the brain's midline that does not come as a left-right pair, as the place where mind and body meet. Thomas Nagel, a philosopher, asked in 1974 what it is like to be a bat: you could know every detail of how echolocation works and still have no idea how it feels to the bat. That leftover is what a science of consciousness has to explain.

In 1998 the neuroscientist Christof Koch wagered a case of wine with Chalmers that within 25 years researchers would identify the brain activity that marks consciousness. When time ran out in 2023, Koch paid Chalmers, handing over the wine on stage, and then proposed a new bet.

Two rival theories make testable predictions. Integrated Information Theory, Giulio Tononi's idea, measures how tightly a system binds its information together, and it points to a hot zone at the rear of the cortex. Its rival, Global Neuronal Workspace Theory, places the action at the front. In the early 2020s the COGITATE project staged a tournament between them. Each camp sealed its predictions before any scans, and the team studied more than 250 people with three methods at once: intracranial EEG, recorded from epilepsy patients who already had electrodes in their brains, along with MEG and fMRI. When the results appeared in the spring of 2025, they crowned neither side cleanly: IIT passed two of its three sealed predictions and the workspace theory none of its three.

The fight is fierce. In September 2023, three months after the tournament's first results were announced, a letter signed by 124 researchers demanded that IIT be labelled pseudoscience until it offers firmer predictions that could fail, and its defenders, Koch among them, answered in print. Other contenders include higher-order thought theories and predictive processing. Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff place consciousness in quantum-scale events inside microtubules, tiny tubes within neurons; most researchers reject the idea, but it is a serious, published rival.
