the-herrick-twins-kidney-23-december-195.context_blurb:
On 23 December 1954, in a Boston hospital, the surgeon Joseph Murray moved a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his dying identical twin, Richard: the first organ transplant that lasted. Every earlier attempt had failed within days, because the patient's body attacked another person's tissue.

Murray had seen that attack while treating burned soldiers on an army ward during the war. Skin from a donor stitched onto a burned soldier would take and look healthy for weeks before the patient's body turned on it and destroyed it, while grafts between identical twins lasted. The barrier was the immune system telling whose tissue was whose.

The operation raised a new moral problem: removing a healthy organ from a healthy man who needed no surgery himself. The team met Ronald again and again and laid out every risk, but would not say whether he ought to agree; the choice had to be his alone.

In the operating room the new kidney turned pink and started producing urine while the patient was still open, the first sign that it worked. Richard gained roughly eight more years, during which he wed a nurse from the hospital and raised two children. He died in 1963 of heart failure, and the transplanted kidney was still working. Making transplants work for people who are not twins took drugs that hold back the immune system, at the price of a lifelong higher risk of infection.

the-higgs-a-forty-eight-year-wait-for-on.context_blurb:
In 1964 several physicists proposed that particles gain mass from an unseen field that pervades the universe. Peter Higgs's version made a prediction that took forty-eight years, and the largest machine ever built, to test.

That year the journal Physics Letters turned down Higgs's short paper. He added a paragraph pointing out that his mechanism predicted a new, heavy particle no one had seen, and Physical Review Letters printed it; that paragraph is why the particle bears his name. He was not alone. Three groups found the same mechanism within months, and the first, in August, was François Englert and Robert Brout in Brussels. A London trio followed in November, so it is properly the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism.

The popular line that the Higgs gives things their mass holds for basic particles such as the electron and quarks, but only about one percent of a proton's mass comes from it. The other 99 percent is the energy of the churning quarks and gluons bound inside, turned into mass by E = mc².

On 4 July 2012 CERN announced the discovery: two detectors kept deliberately apart, ATLAS and CMS, each saw the same bump near 125 GeV. Higgs, 83, was in the room. Wiping his eyes, he said it was really an incredible thing that it had happened in his lifetime. He disliked the nickname the God particle, which came from Leon Lederman's 1993 book of that title; Lederman said he had wanted to call it the goddamn particle because it was so hard to find.

The discovery opened a question. Simple quantum arithmetic says the Higgs mass should be dragged up a trillion trillion times higher than it is. The favourite fix, supersymmetry, predicted a family of heavier partner particles, and the Large Hadron Collider has not found them. Nobody yet knows the answer.

the-hiss-the-pigeons-could-not-explain.context_blurb:
In 1964 at Bell Labs in Holmdel, New Jersey, two radio astronomers, Robert Wilson and Arno Penzias, were plagued by a faint, steady hiss in their giant horn antenna. It came from every direction, day and night. By refusing to explain it away, they found the oldest light in the universe, the afterglow of the Big Bang.

Cosmic origins were the last thing on their minds. The 20-foot horn had been built in 1959 for NASA's Project Echo satellite, and they were calibrating it, measuring its own noise, so it could serve as a quiet instrument for radio astronomy. One by one they eliminated the radio clamour of New York, military radar and the lingering glow of a 1962 nuclear blast high in the atmosphere. Fearing the horn's own aluminium joints leaked noise, they covered the riveted seams with tape.

A pair of nesting pigeons had coated the inside with droppings. Penzias and Wilson chased the birds out and cleaned the horn, and the hiss was not one bit quieter: it was arriving from the sky itself. What remained was an extra warmth of about 3.5 degrees above absolute zero, the same wherever they pointed.

Forty miles away, at Princeton, a group led by Robert Dicke was preparing its own receiver to search for the cooled-down glow of a hot young universe. When Penzias phoned to describe the noise, Dicke hung up and told his colleagues, "Boys, we've been scooped."

The prediction was older still. Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman, building on George Gamow's idea of a hot beginning, calculated in 1948 that a faint leftover warmth of roughly five degrees above absolute zero should fill space, and nobody built an instrument to look. Even earlier, in 1940, Andrew McKellar, studying absorption lines another astronomer had recorded, noticed that interstellar cyanogen molecules were gently excited, as if warmed to about 2.3 degrees above absolute zero. Nobody linked it to the birth of the universe.

The hiss is light released about 380,000 years after the beginning, when the young universe grew cool enough for atoms to form and the glowing fog turned clear. Then it was a glare at some 3,000 degrees; expansion has stretched it into microwaves less than three degrees above absolute zero. In 1989 NASA launched the COBE satellite, which found the glow's spectrum to be the purest blackbody curve ever measured. It also found tiny warm and cool patches, differing by about one part in a hundred thousand: slightly denser regions that gravity later gathered into galaxies, stars and, eventually, people.

the-hoax-papers-sokal-1996-and-the-griev.context_blurb:
Can a journal be fooled into printing nonsense? Two famous hoaxes tested the gatekeepers of academic publishing, a physicist's in 1996 and a trio's in 2017 and 2018. A third episode shows the same trick works on technical journals too, which narrows what any hoax can prove.

Alan Sokal, a physicist at New York University, placed an article in Social Text, a cultural-studies journal, in May 1996, arguing that the physical world is nothing but a construct of society and language, salted with physics terms used wrongly. Three weeks later he revealed in Lingua Franca that it was a deliberate test. The fair detail is that Social Text did not then use peer review and never sent the paper to a physicist; the editors took it on Sokal's credentials and its political fit. So it exposed editorial judgement, not peer review, which was Sokal's own narrower claim.

In 2017 and 2018 Helen Pluckrose, James Lindsay and Peter Boghossian answered that objection by sending twenty fake papers to journals that did use peer review, in fields they called grievance studies. By the time the project was exposed, four had been published and three more accepted, while six were rejected.

One, printed in Gender, Place & Culture under the invented name Helen Wilson, claimed to observe rape culture and queer performativity among dogs and their owners at parks in Portland, Oregon, and a reviewer praised it as incredibly innovative. Another, which Affilia, a journal of social work, accepted as original feminist theory, was really a passage from Hitler's Mein Kampf reworded in the vocabulary of feminist theory. The project ended in October 2018, not because a reviewer spotted the content, but because staff at Gender, Place & Culture checked whether Helen Wilson was a documented real person. She was not.

A fair critic adds one more case. In 2014 the publishers Springer and IEEE withdrew more than 120 conference papers produced by SCIgen, a random paper-writing program built at MIT, after Cyril Labbé of Grenoble catalogued them. A hoax measures what a review system catches; by itself it cannot show whether a field's ideas are true or false.

the-hockey-stick-fight.context_blurb:
In 1998 and 1999 Michael Mann, Raymond Bradley and Malcolm Hughes published a graph of Northern Hemisphere temperatures over centuries: a long, gentle decline ending in a sharp modern rise, nicknamed the hockey stick. It became a political emblem, then the target of an outside audit. The fight that followed shows why published science should come with data and code that a stranger can rerun.

Mann was a junior researcher at UMass Amherst, holding a postdoctoral fellowship paid for by the US Department of Energy, when he built it, and it appeared in Nature in the spring of 1998. Nobody had thermometers in AD 1400, so the curve was built from 112 stand-ins for temperature, such as tree rings, ice cores, corals and old records of glaciers. The network thins with age, and only about 22 of the series reach all the way back to AD 1400, so the oldest stretch rests on the fewest records.

In January 2001 the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change put the curve in its Summary for Policymakers, claiming the 1990s were probably the hottest ten years in a millennium in the Northern Hemisphere, and launched the report with a giant print of it as the backdrop.

The audit came from outside climate science. In April 2003 Stephen McIntyre, a minerals-exploration consultant, asked Mann for the data, could not reproduce the result from the published description, and worked through the statistics with Ross McKitrick, an economics professor. Their 2005 paper named the disputed step. Before combining North American tree-ring records, MBH98 condensed them into a few summary patterns by principal-component analysis, and it centred that step on the years 1902 to 1980, when thermometer readings exist. That choice, they argued, favours series that behave oddly in the twentieth century.

In June 2006 a twelve-member National Research Council panel chaired by Gerald North agreed that the method was biased, but found that curves built without it looked qualitatively similar. It also said strip-bark bristlecone pines, ancient trees kept alive by a single ribbon of bark, should be avoided, since man-made nitrogen falling from the air could be fertilising their recent rings. Its confidence was high for the last four centuries and fell away before that. Auditing cuts both ways: a 2006 congressional report by Edward Wegman, a statistician, backed the critics, but its study of co-author networks was retracted in 2011 for plagiarism, including text lifted straight from textbooks and Wikipedia.

In a 1999 email that leaked a decade later, Phil Jones of the Climatic Research Unit wrote of using Mike's Nature trick to hide the decline. The cover graphic he described replaced the tree-ring values after 1960 with thermometer readings, because those tree rings had begun to fall while thermometers rose, and its caption never mentioned the swap. In 2010 the Muir Russell review found no fraud and did not doubt the scientists' honesty, but judged that the figure misled readers, though splicing records together is acceptable in itself.

The lasting result was a habit. Mann's 2008 reconstruction in PNAS, built from 1,209 series, gave a public web address where anyone could download all the data and the Matlab code, something the 1998 paper had not offered.

the-human-genome-project-and-the-20-000-.context_blurb:
In 1990 scientists set out to spell out a person's entire DNA, all three billion letters, one by one. The Human Genome Project became a race between a public consortium and a private company, and its biggest surprise was how few genes we turned out to have.

Two American agencies, the NIH and the Department of Energy, launched it in October 1990 on a fifteen-year, three-billion-dollar plan, and it finished in thirteen years, two ahead of plan, for roughly $2.7 billion. Its reference DNA came from twenty volunteers recruited in 1997 through a newspaper advertisement in Buffalo, New York, each promised that no more than a tenth of the sequence would be theirs. In fact one anonymous man supplied roughly three-quarters of the 2001 draft, known only as RP11.

In May 1998 Craig Venter launched a private rival, Celera Genomics, and promised to finish in three years for about $300 million: the same job in a fifth of the time, for a tenth of the money. Celera packed about 300 sequencing machines into one building, smashed the entire genome into random pieces, sequenced them all at once and let computers reassemble the overlaps. The public side mapped each chromosome first and read ordered pieces one at a time. Celera's genome blended DNA from five anonymous donors, and after leaving the company in 2002 Venter revealed that he was one of them.

A truce came at the White House in June 2000, when Bill Clinton, with Tony Blair joining by satellite, announced a joint working draft. The finished sequence was declared on 14 April 2003, timed to fall fifty years after Watson and Crick described the double helix.

Then came the surprise. Biologists had expected 100,000 or more protein-coding genes, one for each protein a complex animal seemed to need, but the count settled at about 20,000, roughly what a millimetre-long soil worm carries. Ewan Birney had started a sweepstake on the number in 2000 at Cold Spring Harbor, and more than 460 researchers bet. Lee Rowen won in 2003 with 25,947; no one had bet lower, and even her guess overshot the true count.

How can so few genes do so much? Most human genes break the old rule of one gene, one protein: a gene's working copy, its messenger RNA, is cut apart and the pieces are rejoined in different combinations, so one gene yields many proteins. Size does not track complexity either. The biologist Ryan Gregory's onion test points out that a common onion carries roughly 16 billion letters of DNA, about five times as many as a human.

The genome declared finished in 2003 was not. About 8 percent of it, the long runs of repeats at the chromosome centres, called centromeres, and tips, called telomeres, had defeated every machine, because identical repeats cannot be placed by their overlaps. The Telomere-to-Telomere consortium closed the last gaps in 2022.

How much of the genome does anything? In 2012 the ENCODE consortium declared at least 80 percent of it functional, and newspapers buried junk DNA. Dan Graur and colleagues objected that ENCODE had measured chemical busyness, not work that natural selection keeps in place. A cleaner measure lines the human genome up with other mammals' and finds stretches that have stayed almost unaltered across many tens of millions of years. A 2014 study and a 2023 analysis of 240 mammal species put that share at roughly 8 to 11 percent; how much of the rest does any job, nobody yet knows.

Tony Blair promised a medical revolution. Sequencing a genome now costs about $600, yet fewer than one percent of the diseases caused by a single faulty gene have a gene-therapy cure.

the-immortal-chicken-heart-that-wasnt.context_blurb:
For decades a scrap of chicken heart kept alive in a flask in New York was hailed as proof that cells never age. Nobody ever reproduced it. The experiments that overturned it found a counter inside every cell, and then the enzyme that can reset it.

Alexis Carrel, a French-born surgeon and Nobel laureate, began the culture in 1912 at the Rockefeller Institute, feeding a fragment of chick-embryo heart every day. Newspapers marked its birthday each January, and the lab kept it going for about thirty-four years, until 1946. Carrel said it proved that well-fed cells never grow old, so that aging was only a failure of food and cleanliness.

Working at Philadelphia's Wistar Institute in 1961, Paul Moorhead and Leonard Hayflick found the opposite: normal human cells split some forty to sixty times and then simply stopped, still alive but no longer copying themselves. Senior biologists blamed sloppy technique. So the pair combined old male cells, forty doublings along, with young female cells, fifteen along, in one flask of the same medium. After twenty more doublings the old male cells had all stopped while the young female cells carried on, so the clock had to sit within each cell rather than in the food they shared.

Then how did Carrel's culture last? Hayflick suspected the food, a mash of whole chick embryos: each feeding probably smuggled in new live cells that restocked the flask. The honest verdict is never replicated and most likely contaminated, not proven fraud.

Alexei Olovnikov, a Russian biologist, reasoned in 1971 from how DNA is copied that the counter must sit at the very ends of each chromosome, because the copying machinery cannot reach the tip of a linear strand, so a little is lost at every division. Those ends are now called telomeres. He also predicted an enzyme that adds DNA back. In 1984, in Elizabeth Blackburn's Berkeley lab, the graduate student Carol Greider found it in a pond ciliate: telomerase, which rebuilds the tip of each chromosome.

Cancer cells break the limit. Henrietta Lacks's cancer cells, taken in 1951 and known as HeLa, still multiply in labs worldwide because, like most cancers, they have switched telomerase back on, so their chromosome tips are constantly rebuilt.

the-immunity-that-was-already-there.context_blurb:
Natural immunity is the trained defence the body keeps after surviving an infection, the same machinery a vaccine is designed to imitate. During COVID-19, measurements of how well it held up were published by The Lancet and by the CDC itself, yet most mandates gave it no credit.

A child who recovers from measles almost never catches it again, because her body keeps memory B cells, which pour out antibody, and memory T cells, which kill infected cells, ready to crush the virus within hours of a second attack. Vaccination teaches both kinds of cell without the illness.

For COVID-19, a 2023 Lancet meta-analysis of 65 studies from 19 countries found that a past infection still protected about 88.9 percent against severe disease 40 weeks later, even against Omicron BA.1. Protection against catching the virus again was another matter. Against Omicron BA.1 it fell to about 36 percent at 40 weeks, because the variant could slip past earlier immunity, an ability called immune escape. Both results were true at once.

The CDC's own report of January 2022, covering two states, California and New York, in the second half of 2021, found that in the Delta wave, unvaccinated people who had already had COVID caught it less often than vaccinated people who never had; those with both did best of all. Yet most American mandates of those years gave a documented past infection no credit at all: it counted as zero.

Consent has its own history. In August 1947 the court at Nuremberg that tried Nazi doctors opened its verdict with ten principles for research on people, and the first demands, as an absolute, that the person experimented on freely agree.

the-knee-jerk-a-decision-your-brain-neve.context_blurb:
Perch on the edge of a table, let one leg hang, and tap the tendon just under your kneecap: the foot flies up before you have chosen anything. The kick is a reflex, a decision your brain never makes. Its real trigger is a stretch sensor inside the thigh muscle, and the circuit exists so your knees do not buckle every time your weight shifts.

The round trip lasts roughly 18 milliseconds, far too quick for the brain to take part. A sensory fibre carries the signal into the spinal cord, and the spinal cord sends it straight back out to the muscle. It is among the body's shortest circuits: the incoming fibre enters the cord low in the back and connects to the outgoing motor neuron across just one synapse. Snatching a hand away from a flame, by contrast, runs through several in-between neurons and takes longer.

Muscles can only pull, never push. Charles Sherrington, a physiologist at Cambridge, noticed that at the same instant the cord fires the thigh muscle, it silences the hamstring, the muscle behind the thigh, so the two do not fight. He called this reciprocal innervation.

The brain still has a say. When a knee-jerk is faint, a doctor asks the patient to lock his hands together and tug, a trick found by Ernő Jendrassik, and the kick returns briskly. The brain cannot fire the kick itself, yet it can turn the reflex up like a volume knob.

the-law-of-small-numbers.context_blurb:
Small samples do not just carry more error than large ones; they manufacture extreme results, at both ends. Even trained scientists forget it. The law of small numbers explains strange cancer maps, a costly school reform and why so many published findings shrink when they are retested.

Toss a coin ten times and eight or more heads turns up about once in every eighteen tries; toss it a thousand times and eight hundred or more heads essentially never does.

In 1971 Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, two Israeli psychologists, quizzed experts at a psychology meeting and found them putting a gambler's faith in a sample of just twenty people, expecting a tiny sample to mirror the whole world. They titled their paper Belief in the Law of Small Numbers. One question asked which of two hospitals, a big one with about 45 births a day or a small one with about 15, would log more days when boys made up over 60 percent of the births. Most answered about the same, but it is the smaller hospital, because with only 15 births a day the share of boys wanders much further from half.

When the statisticians Harris Zwerling and Howard Wainer charted kidney cancer county by county across the United States, the lowest rates and the highest rates both turned up in rural counties of the Midwest, South and West. Those counties hold so few people that their rates leap around by chance in both directions. Among 1,662 Pennsylvania schools, small schools crowded the best fifty, and among the bottom fifty too, six times more often than expected. Small schools are not better, only more variable. That instability was read as merit: the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation spent heavily on small schools, sometimes breaking large schools into smaller ones, trusting such rankings.

Scientists keep falling for it. In 1962 Jacob Cohen found that psychology studies had only about a 46 percent chance of detecting a medium-sized effect, and when Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer repeated the survey for 1960 to 1987, it had fallen further, to about 37 percent. In 2013 Katherine Button, John Ioannidis and colleagues found that typical brain-science studies had only 8 to 31 percent power. In such a field the only results to reach significance are those that chance pushed too far, so the published effects come out inflated, a trap called the winner's curse.

the-laws-that-outlived-the-science.context_blurb:
Forced sterilization is usually pictured as a Nazi crime. In fact the first law came from an American state, tens of thousands of Americans were sterilized, and the programmes ran on for decades after the science behind them had collapsed and after the Nazi record was exposed.

In April 1907 Indiana became the first place on Earth with a compulsory sterilization law, voted through in an ordinary legislative session, letting prison and asylum superintendents sterilize inmates they judged unfit. About thirty states followed, and over the decades about 60,000 to 70,000 Americans were sterilized under such laws, around two-thirds of them women.

The biggest programme ran in California, one of the most modern and science-minded states, which sterilized about 20,000 people between 1909 and 1979, about one in three of all American cases. The Nazi revelations did not end it. North Carolina's Eugenics Board, which ordered about 7,600 sterilizations between 1929 and 1974, carried out most of its work after the war, still judging people by IQ scores and social histories. Oregon's board held on the longest, issuing a final sterilization order in 1981 and disappearing only in 1983.

The programmes ended on legal and civil-rights grounds, not scientific ones. The first state apology came from Virginia in 2002, about 25 years after the big programmes like California's had stopped. In 2013 North Carolina became the first state to pay living victims.

the-lockdown-meta-analysis-that-correcte.context_blurb:
Did the spring-2020 lockdowns save many lives? Three economists set out to measure it. The most instructive part of their work is that they changed their own headline number when better data came in, and published the correction under their own names.

Steve Hanke of Johns Hopkins, with Lars Jonung of Sweden and Jonas Herby of Denmark, asked one narrow, checkable question: by how much did the mandated lockdowns reduce COVID-19 deaths? They said plainly that this measures the benefit side only; the costs, from lost schooling to deferred cancer diagnoses, they left for others to count.

They began with 19,646 papers, screened them in three rounds and kept a final shortlist of 32. Their rule threw out every computer simulation of how the virus might have spread, including Imperial College's famous Report 9, and kept only studies using difference-in-differences, which compare the change in places under a policy with the change in places without it, so shared trends cancel out.

Their January 2022 working paper had reported an average death reduction of just 0.2 percent. In their November 2024 paper in the journal Public Choice, built on studies using the Oxford stringency index, the figure came out at 3.2 percent. Their own number rose sixteenfold, more than ten times over, toward more benefit from policies they had criticised, and they published it themselves. To give it scale, they set their estimate of roughly 6,000 deaths avoided in Europe and 4,000 in the United States by the end of June 2020 beside seasonal influenza, which kills about 72,000 Europeans and 38,000 Americans in an ordinary year.

The most famous opposing figure came from Seth Flaxman's Imperial College team in Nature in June 2020: a model of 11 European countries credited the lockdown measures with preventing about 3.1 million deaths by early May. Herby, Jonung and Hanke do not claim nothing worked. They argue that voluntary behaviour change did most of the mitigation, as people avoided crowds and the sick once the danger was visible, whether or not an order told them to. Their finding is that the mandates added less than promised, not that the virus was mild.

the-loudest-sound-ever-recorded.context_blurb:
Early on 27 August 1883 the volcanic island of Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, blew apart. Its roar was heard across about a fifth of the planet, and it is still the loudest sound in recorded history.

The British ship Norham Castle was about 40 miles away, and its captain, Sampson, wrote in his log that the explosions were so violent that the eardrums of over half his crew had been shattered.

No microphone of the time could have measured it. The famous figure of about 172 decibels comes from a pressure gauge at the Batavia gasworks, in what is now Jakarta, about 160 kilometres off: the barometer jumped by more than 2.5 inches of mercury, and scientists converted that pressure spike into a loudness.

A viral claim of 310 decibels is impossible. A sound wave swings above and below normal air pressure, and at about 194 decibels its low-pressure half has already dropped to a perfect vacuum, which cannot go any lower. Anything stronger is a blast wave, not a sound.

Far from the volcano the wave sank below the pitches human ears can hear, but barographs around the world recorded it sweeping past seven times in about five days, circling the globe again and again. Today a worldwide network listens for such infrasound to catch secret nuclear tests.

the-machinery-the-trusted-news-initiativ.context_blurb:
Two institutions show how the fight over online disinformation was organised. One is private and still operating; the other was federal and lasted less than four months.

In 2019 the BBC launched the Trusted News Initiative. Its founding partners included Reuters, the Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and the Washington Post, and also the tech companies that carried that news to readers: Google, YouTube, Facebook, Microsoft and Twitter. In plain terms it is a private club where news organisations and the platforms that spread their work sit down together to agree on what they will treat as disinformation. It began with election disinformation, and on 27 March 2020 its members widened its remit to COVID-19 information; a later extension anticipated the 2020 American election.

Children's Health Defense and Robert Kennedy Jr took four of its members, including the BBC and the AP, to court in January 2023, invoking not the law of free speech but antitrust law, Section 1 of the Sherman Act, claiming that competitors had agreed together to suppress rival publishers. That is a claim, not a finding, though in 2025 the Justice Department filed a statement supporting the plaintiffs' legal theory.

The federal effort came from the Department of Homeland Security. In April 2022 Alejandro Mayorkas, the Homeland Security secretary, announced to Congress a new Disinformation Governance Board, an internal working group with no enforcement power, meant to help judge which claims circulating online were true and which false. Critics across the political spectrum called it a Ministry of Truth, its director quit, and the department's own advisory council recommended ending it: within about four months it was shut down.

the-magic-bullet-hunt-from-a-dye-that-st.context_blurb:
In late-1800s Berlin, the physician and chemist Paul Ehrlich noticed that certain dyes stained one type of cell and left the cells beside it clean. If a dye could single out one cell on a slide, he reasoned, a chemical might single out an invader inside the body. He named the imagined drug a Zauberkugel: a magic bullet.

His method was slow and systematic: make a family of arsenic compounds, number them one by one, and test each on infected rabbits. Ehrlich coined a word for that hunt, chemotherapy, which only later came to mean cancer drugs. Compound 606 was made in 1907 and shelved as a failure. Two years later, at Ehrlich's insistence, his Japanese colleague Sahachiro Hata retested it with more care, and it proved the first real chemical cure for syphilis, sold as Salvarsan. A negative result can be a badly run test.

A generation later, at Bayer, Gerhard Domagk screened industrial dyes the same patient way. In late December 1932 he gave a red dye, Prontosil, to one group of mice, then infected them and an untreated group with a lethal dose of streptococcus; on Christmas Eve every treated mouse was alive and every untreated mouse was dead.

The twist came from the Pasteur Institute in Paris in 1935 and 1936: in a glass test tube Prontosil did nothing, killing no bacteria at all. The body splits the dye and releases a smaller, colourless molecule, sulfanilamide, which is the real drug, so a cheaper glassware screen would have thrown the winner away.

Domagk was named a Nobel laureate in 1939 but could not accept: Hitler had banned Germans from taking Nobel Prizes, and the Gestapo detained him and made him put his name to a letter turning it down. He finally received his medal in 1947.

the-measurement-problem-the-part-no-one-.context_blurb:
Quantum mechanics is the most precisely tested theory in science, yet in its ordinary form it does not say what actually happens when a particle meets a measuring device. It describes a smooth spread of possibilities right up to the moment of measurement, and then one definite result is simply there. Several very different interpretations reproduce every laboratory result anyone has obtained, and no experiment has yet told them apart. How measurement works remains a live argument, not a solved one.

Two proposals are bolder: the theory published in 1986 by Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber, and Diósi and Penrose's idea that gravity triggers the change. They add a real, spontaneous breakdown of superposition that grows stronger for heavier objects, so, unlike the interpretations, they forecast effects that could be measured. That makes them testable, and experiments have already excluded some of the values their adjustable numbers could take. Underground searches for the faint radiation such collapses should give off have ruled out the simplest version of the Diósi-Penrose model, and interference experiments with ever heavier molecules keep squeezing the rest.

the-mesmer-commission-of-1784.context_blurb:
In the 1780s the Vienna-born doctor Franz Mesmer ran one of the most fashionable practices in Paris. He taught that an unseen fluid, which he named animal magnetism, flowed between all bodies, and that illness came when it dammed up. Patients clutched iron rods sticking out of a wooden tub, the baquet, to the sound of music, until they collapsed in convulsions that counted as the cure working.

In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed a royal commission to test the doctrine. Its most famous member was Benjamin Franklin, the 78-year-old American ambassador, and because he was too ill to travel, many trials were held at his house and garden at Passy. The eerie music at Mesmer's sessions came from the glass armonica, and Franklin knew it well, because he had invented that very instrument himself in 1761.

Mesmer refused to cooperate, so the commissioners worked with Charles d'Eslon, a royal physician and Mesmer's best-known follower, testing d'Eslon's own patients. That made the test stronger: the patients already believed in the fluid, so if the tests failed, no one could claim the subjects had been chosen to fail.

In Franklin's garden d'Eslon secretly magnetised one tree, and a blindfolded boy was led from tree to tree. He collapsed at the fourth tree he hugged, and none of the trees he had reached had been treated. The belief did the work, not the fluid.

Its report, published that August in about twenty thousand copies, found no fluid at all but agreed that the fits were real, brought on by the patients' own imagination. It is often called the first scientific description of what we now call the placebo effect.

the-metal-that-melts-in-your-hand.context_blurb:
Set a small silvery ingot of gallium on a warm palm, and within about a minute it slumps into a shining puddle. Gallium is a metal with a strange set of habits, and its discovery gave the periodic table one of its most famous victories.

Gallium turns liquid at 29.76 degrees Celsius, a little cooler than your body, so a warm hand is enough. Caesium melts even lower, at 28.5 degrees, yet no chemist would hold it, because the dampness of human skin makes it react violently, enough to burn the hand. Drop a frozen chunk of gallium into a beaker of the liquid metal and the chunk floats on the surface. Like water, gallium expands as it freezes, so the solid is lighter than the liquid, which is rare among metals. The other end of its range is just as odd: gallium boils above 2,200 degrees Celsius, so it stays liquid across about two thousand degrees, and gallium-filled quartz thermometers can read furnaces where mercury would boil away.

Liquid gallium is also a menace to aluminium. A droplet left overnight on an aluminium bench seeps along the boundaries between the metal's crystal grains and destroys their grip on one another, so the bench crumbles while looking almost unchanged, an attack called liquid metal embrittlement.

In 1871 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for a missing element he called eka-aluminium and described its properties in advance. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, a French chemist studying zinc ore from the Pyrenees, found it in August 1875: his spectroscope showed a pair of violet lines belonging to no known element, and he was certain almost at once. His first sample of the new metal weighed in at a density near 4.7, well short of Mendeleev's predicted 5.9. Mendeleev wrote back insisting that the metal must still be impure and should be cleaned and weighed again; Lecoq did, and got 5.904.

the-missing-mass-zwicky-rubin-and-an-hon.context_blurb:
Most of the matter in the universe seems to be invisible. Astronomers can weigh it by its pull, yet nobody has caught a single particle of it, and nobody yet knows what it is. The story runs from a cluster of galaxies in 1933 to the spinning edges of Andromeda and to tanks of liquid xenon buried underground.

In 1933 Fritz Zwicky clocked the speeds of galaxies within the Coma Cluster and applied the virial theorem, a rule linking a cluster's motions to its mass. The cluster needed far more mass than its stars supplied to hold together, and he called the missing stuff dark matter. His factor of about 400 leaned on the era's badly overestimated Hubble constant, the expansion rate of the universe, so the real shortfall is smaller, but it is real. Then the idea sat largely ignored for some forty years.

Vera Rubin brought it back. In 1965 she became the first woman given observing time at Palomar Observatory, and finding only a men's room, she taped a paper skirt she had cut out onto the figure painted on the door. Her partner Kent Ford built an image-tube spectrograph, which amplified faint light so that a galaxy's outer gas clouds could be measured in about a tenth of the old time. In our solar system the outer planets move slower, because gravity weakens with distance. But around 1970 Rubin and Ford found that the stars near Andromeda's edge circled as quickly as those near its centre, as if unseen mass were pulling them along. These flat rotation curves, seen in spiral after spiral by Rubin, Ford and others in the 1970s, finally made the missing mass impossible to ignore.

Zwicky had also predicted that a massive galaxy could bend the light of a more distant one like a lens. The first confirmed case came in 1979 from Weymann, Walsh and Carswell: one quasar showing up twice, its light split around a galaxy in front. Lensing weighs whatever is there, shining or not. In the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy clusters caught mid-collision, X-rays show the hot gas stripped away and left in the middle, while lensing shows that the bulk of the mass passed right through the crash along with the galaxies.

The main rival, Mordehai Milgrom's 1983 Modified Newtonian Dynamics, tweaks gravity at tiny accelerations and fits single spiral galaxies well, but it struggles most with galaxy clusters, above all the Bullet Cluster, where the visible mass and the gravitating mass sit apart. Ordinary neutrinos were ruled out as most of the dark matter because they move too close to the speed of light; such hot particles would have streamed out of small clumps and smeared away the structure from which galaxies grew. The favourite candidate, weakly interacting massive particles, has been hunted with ever larger vats of liquid xenon deep underground, from LUX in 2013 to LZ in 2023, and there is still no confirmed detection. No one yet knows what dark matter is.

the-molecule-nobody-believed-in-nuclein-.context_blurb:
In 1869 a young Swiss doctor, Friedrich Miescher, discovered the substance we now call DNA. For some seventy years afterwards most biologists thought it far too dull to carry heredity, and the man who found it kept his boldest guess to himself.

Working in a makeshift lab in an old kitchen at Tübingen Castle, Miescher needed fresh human white blood cells every morning, and he scraped them from pus-soaked bandages sent over from the local hospital. From the cells' nuclei he pulled a strange substance he called nuclein. It was rich in phosphorus and shrugged off the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin, and it had not a trace of sulfur, which ruled out a protein, since proteins carry sulfur in two of their amino acids.

His supervisor, Felix Hoppe-Seyler, who edited the journal, doubted the finding. He kept the paper out of print for two years while he had his own students run the whole extraction again, and it appeared in 1871 alongside their confirmation. For decades most biologists took nuclein to be a mere store of phosphorus, kept for the cell to draw on: interesting chemistry, but no carrier of heredity.

Miescher himself suspected more. In 1892 he wrote to his uncle, Wilhelm His, that heredity might be spelled out by chemical variety, the way an alphabet of 24 to 30 letters spells every word in every language. But he confided the idea only to his uncle and never argued it in public, so the wider world never heard it from him.

Only in the 1940s and 1950s did the field look again. Erwin Chargaff measured DNA's bases, and after meeting James Watson and Francis Crick in Cambridge in May 1952, he later wrote that he had never encountered a pair so short of knowledge and so long on ambition.

the-molecules-that-wouldnt-stop-stauding.context_blurb:
Rubber, starch, nylon and the plastic of a grocery bag are all made of giant molecules, chains thousands of units long. In the 1920s that idea was heresy. Hermann Staudinger fought the leaders of German chemistry for a decade to establish it, and he won by experiment, not argument.

Living things built chains first. Cellulose, a chain of glucose units, makes up about a third of all plant matter, which makes it the most abundant organic polymer on Earth. Chemists were already making chains without knowing it. Around 1900 American wire makers needed shellac, a varnish secreted by an Indian insect, faster than it could be gathered, so Leo Baekeland set out to copy it in his New York lab. In 1907 he made Bakelite instead, called the first true plastic because it was built up from two small factory-made chemicals, phenol and formaldehyde, while earlier materials such as celluloid were natural polymers chemically treated.

Measurements of rubber, starch and cellulose gave molecular weights in the tens of thousands, and almost nobody believed them. The ruling view said rubber was small molecules stuck together in clusters by weak forces, so the huge weights were an illusion. In 1920 Staudinger, a professor in Zurich, published a paper on polymerisation arguing that each rubber molecule is one immense chain of thousands of links held by the same bonds as any small molecule. In 1922 he coined the word macromolecule. Heinrich Wieland, a fresh Nobel laureate, wrote to him in 1927 urging him to drop it: no organic molecule could top a weight of roughly 5,000, and anything bigger would be as unstable as the Tower of Babel.

Staudinger answered at the bench. Working with Jakob Fritschi in 1922, he hydrogenated rubber, filling in all of its double bonds, which the clump theory relied on, yet the product still behaved like rubber and weighed over 100,000. The fight ended with an instrument from outside it. At Uppsala, Theodor Svedberg's ultracentrifuge whirled solutions so fast that molecules sank at rates set by their mass, and in 1926 it weighed haemoglobin at about 67,000, more than thirteen times Wieland's ceiling. In 1927 X-rays showed Staudinger and Johannes Hengstenberg that the repeating box of a polyoxymethylene crystal held only four to six units, though the chains ran to more than a hundred units. The only reading was that each chain must thread through many of those boxes in a row. He won the Nobel Prize in 1953.

You can see chains at home. Pull a strip of grocery bag slowly and a cloudy white neck forms; keep pulling steadily and, instead of tearing, the neck creeps along, eating up the unstretched plastic. The thin neck is stronger, not weaker, because the tangled chains in it swing round and line up side by side to share the load. In 1965 at DuPont, Stephanie Kwolek made a solution of a new polymer that came out cloudy and watery, which looked wrong; Charles Smullen spun it anyway, and the fibre, Kevlar, was pound for pound some five times stronger than steel. Its chains were stiff rods that had stacked into parallel ranks while still in solution.

At DuPont, Wallace Carothers's chemists learned that building a long chain is mostly arithmetic: one stray molecule caps a chain, so nylon's two ingredients, adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, had to match one for one, exactly. They made the pair form crystals of nylon salt, a compound holding exactly one molecule of each, so chemistry, not a balance, fixed the ratio.

the-mpemba-effect-a-schoolboys-question-.context_blurb:
Erasto Mpemba was a 13-year-old cookery student in Tanzania in 1963 when he noticed something odd. The freezer was crowded, so he slid his ice-cream mixture in without letting it cool, and it froze before his classmates' cooled mix. His teacher told him he must have confused himself, and his classmates laughed.

He kept asking anyway. When the British physicist Denis Osborne came to give a talk at his school, Mpemba put the question to him. Osborne was openly sceptical, but instead of brushing the boy off he returned to his university lab and ran the experiment himself. In 1969 the two published together, with Mpemba named as first author, and Osborne wrote that no question should be ridiculed. Writers as far back as Aristotle had reported something similar, and been forgotten.

Sixty years on, the question is still open. Two Cambridge researchers, Paul Linden and Henry Burridge, made the most carefully controlled attempt yet in 2016 and found nothing that could be reliably repeated, while other laboratories still report an effect. Evaporation, dissolved gases and currents in the water are all suspects, and no one yet knows the answer. Try it yourself with two ice-cube trays; if you see nothing, that is a real result too.

the-muons-that-should-never-have-reached.context_blurb:
Cosmic rays striking the top of the atmosphere spray particles downward, and the commonest one to reach the ground is the muon, a heavy cousin of the electron: about one passes through each square centimetre of your hand every minute. Its journey is the classic proof of Einstein's special relativity.

Each muon starts life some 15 kilometres overhead and races down at nearly the speed of light, but its short lifetime means it ought to decay after roughly 660 metres. Yet vast numbers of muons reach the ground.

The first test came in 1940, when Bruno Rossi and his colleague Hall compared muon counts high on a mountain in Colorado and down in Denver, and found that faster muons lived longer than slower ones. In 1963 Frisch and Smith counted about 563 muons an hour at the summit of Mount Washington in New Hampshire, then carried their counter down to Cambridge, Massachusetts. Physics without relativity predicted that just 27 or so per hour would survive the trip down, but they counted about 412.

Seen from the ground, the muons' internal clocks were running about nine times slow. From the muon's own point of view its clock runs normally; instead, the atmosphere's 15 kilometres shrink to a few hundred metres. Time dilation and length contraction are one fact seen from two seats.

the-nuremberg-code-ten-rules-written-in-.context_blurb:
The founding document of modern research ethics was written not by a medical society but by three American judges, in their verdict at Nuremberg in August 1947, after trying Nazi doctors for deadly experiments on prisoners in the camps. Its ten rules are called the Nuremberg Code.

Its first point declares, in one plain sentence, that a human subject's voluntary consent is absolutely essential, and every research-ethics document since has echoed it. Two American doctors served as expert witnesses, and a memo by one of them, Alexander, reappears nearly verbatim in parts of the Code, whose central demand before any experiment is informed, voluntary agreement from the person. That agreement must be free of force, fraud, deceit or duress, or any other hidden pressure.

The fifth point bans experiments expected to kill or cripple, with one deliberate exception: perhaps when the experimenting doctors are themselves among the subjects. Another rule gave subjects a power nobody had written down before: the right to stop the experiment at any moment.

The Code had a glaring weakness: no law anywhere made it binding. It gained teeth only through later documents: the Declaration of Helsinki in 1964, the American law of 1974 that created ethics review boards, and the Belmont Report of 1979. American medicine shrugged it off. The Yale scholar Jay Katz summed up the attitude: doctors saw it as a fine code for barbarians but needless for ordinary physicians like themselves. How little it changed shows starkly in two cases: the Tuskegee syphilis study ran on for another 25 years, and the Guatemala experiments, in which American doctors deliberately exposed about 1,300 Guatemalans to disease, were under way during the trial itself.

the-patent-clerks-miracle-year.context_blurb:
In 1905 Albert Einstein, twenty-six, with no laboratory, no university post and not yet a doctorate, sent four papers to Germany's leading physics journal in about six months, any one of which could have made a career. Physicists call it his miracle year.

His day job, at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, was judging applications for patents on new inventions, at the rank of technical expert, third class. He split his day, he joked, into eight hours of office work, eight of science and eight of sleep. Home was a small flat at Kramgasse 49, shared with Mileva Marić, his wife, and their infant son Hans Albert. Years before, in December 1901, Einstein had advertised private physics lessons at three francs an hour. A Romanian student of philosophy, Maurice Solovine, replied, but no money changed hands: the first lesson turned into an argument, and the arguments into a reading club with Conrad Habicht that they called the Olympia Academy. His closest sounding-board was the engineer Michele Besso, whom Einstein recommended to the patent office; it hired him in 1904 one grade higher than the man who had recommended him. Besso is the only person thanked in the relativity paper.

The May paper solved an eighty-year-old puzzle. In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown had watched specks from pollen grains jitter endlessly in still water. Einstein showed the specks are knocked about by water molecules striking them unevenly from all sides. His formula linked a speck's wandering to temperature, the fluid's thickness and the speck's size, so anyone with a microscope could measure Avogadro's number, how many molecules make up a mole. That mattered, because two leading scientists, Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, still refused to call atoms real: Mach admitted nothing unobservable, and Ostwald wanted a physics of energy alone. Jean Perrin's measurements in 1908 and 1909 settled it. The same year Einstein sent a fifth piece to the University of Zurich, the thesis that earned his doctorate, a new way to work out how big molecules are.

The June paper, on special relativity, rewrote space and time. The journal had no formal peer review: its editor Max Planck read the paper and passed it for printing. The fourth paper, just three pages, carries a title that asks a question: Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content? There is no E, m or c on the page; he used the letter L for energy and V for light's speed. It ends by handing the idea to experimenters, suggesting that salts of radium, whose energy content changes greatly, might put the theory to the test.

In May 1905 he wrote to Habicht, greeting him as a frozen whale, and promised four papers, calling only one of them very revolutionary: the paper about radiation and the energy carried by light, which treated light as coming in packets. He was right that it was the dangerous one: for years other physicists dismissed it, because it clashed with the wave theory of light. His Nobel Prize, the held-over prize for 1921, never mentions relativity; the committee member Carl Wilhelm Oseen chose wording that honoured his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect instead.

the-peppered-moth-re-tested.context_blurb:
The peppered moth is the textbook case of natural selection caught in the act. Its story runs from a sooty Victorian city to a field test in two woods, a fraud accusation, a seven-year re-test and finally the stretch of DNA that turned it black.

In 1848, near smoky Manchester, a collector caught the first known jet-black peppered moth, normally a speckled grey species, and by the 1890s nearly every one in the district was black. Coal smoke did two things: soot blackened the tree bark, and sulphur dioxide killed the pale lichens that had made the bark speckled, so pale moths lost their camouflage against hunting birds.

In 1924 the geneticist Haldane calculated that the jump from a few dark moths in 1848 to nearly all dark by 1895 could not be random chance: the dark form must have enjoyed about 50 percent greater fitness. In the 1950s Bernard Kettlewell released marked moths into two woods with opposite bark, sooty Birmingham and clean Dorset, so that whichever form was hidden in one wood would stand out in the other. Birds took most of the light moths in Birmingham and most of the dark ones in Dorset. Then the experiment ran backwards. After the Clean Air Act of 1956, cleaner air and lighter bark returned, and at surveyed sites black moths dropped from more than nine in ten to fewer than one in twenty.

In 2002 the journalist Judith Hooper's book Of Moths and Men turned real questions about Kettlewell's methods into a charge of fraud. Biologists including Michael Majerus and Bruce Grant checked and judged the fraud charge to be without merit, while agreeing that the method criticisms deserved better experiments. Majerus answered with one. From 2001 to 2007 he set almost 5,000 moths out where they would naturally rest in his garden and spent the summers watching with his own eyes as birds picked moths off the trees. He died in 2009, and his colleagues published the result in 2012: birds took more of the conspicuous form.

In 2016 Ilik Saccheri's team found the cause in DNA, a stretch of about 22,000 letters inserted into the gene cortex, which shapes wing scales. It dates to around 1819, so the black variant was already present, though rare, when the soot arrived.

the-periodic-table-in-your-pocket.context_blurb:
A smartphone is a slab you can hold in one hand, yet it contains roughly two-thirds of all the stable elements, about sixty of the eighty, each doing a job that no cheaper element does as well.

The touchscreen senses your finger through an invisible film of indium tin oxide, one of very few materials that conduct electricity while staying clear; a copper coating would turn the screen into a mirror. The tiny speaker and vibration motor need very strong magnets for their size, so they use neodymium-iron-boron magnets, the strongest permanent magnets known. Those magnets weaken when warm, so makers add a little dysprosium, which lets the magnet hold its strength at high temperatures. Dysprosium is among the costliest and scarcest elements in the phone.

Pure on-screen reds come from a phosphor made with europium, which gives the light back as a sharp, clean red at about 611 nanometres instead of the muddy smear of ordinary dyes. Terbium does the matching job for green, near 545 nanometres. Hundreds of tiny capacitors store and release charge on the circuit board. The most compact are tantalum capacitors, in which a film of tantalum pentoxide as thin as 20 nanometres, grown on tantalum powder, packs a large charge into a tiny space. Even the glass is chemistry: it is soaked in molten salt so that larger ions swap into places held by smaller ones, jamming the surface into permanent compression that resists cracks.

Phones also rely on gallium, in the arsenide chips that handle radio signals and the nitride chips that make blue LEDs. In 1871 Dmitri Mendeleev predicted this element as eka-aluminium, describing how dense it would be and where it would melt years before anyone held it, proof that his table could forecast the traits of elements still unknown.

the-phases-of-venus.context_blurb:
Venus is the dazzling "star" that hangs near the Sun at dawn or dusk. Late in 1610 Galileo Galilei aimed his new telescope at it and saw that the planet changes shape, just as the Moon does. That small observation helped topple a picture of the heavens that had stood for fourteen centuries.

Anyone with a small telescope can repeat his watch. Over the months Venus grows from a thin sliver to a half, a fat gibbous shape and nearly a full disc, then back again. One full round, as seen from Earth, takes about 584 days, far longer than Venus's own 225-day year, because Venus must gain a whole lap on the moving Earth before the lineup repeats.

Its size changes too. Nearly full, Venus lies on the far side of the Sun, a small, distant dot. Swung round to our side, it shows us mostly its dark night side, lit along one edge, yet it looms about six times wider. Nearness wins, so Venus shines brightest as a crescent.

Why did the shapes matter? In Roman Alexandria, Claudius Ptolemy had put Earth at the centre of everything. His Venus rode a small circle, an epicycle, pinned to the line joining Earth to the Sun, so it was forever on the near side of the Sun. A lit face always points at the Sun, so a Ptolemaic Venus could show only crescent phases, never a half or anything fuller. A fat gibbous Venus finished Ptolemy's geometry.

Fearing a rival, Galileo hid his claim in a puzzle. He mailed Johannes Kepler a scrambled Latin line which, unscrambled, said that the Mother of Love imitates the figures of Cynthia. Poets called Venus the Mother of Love, and Cynthia was a name for Diana, goddess of the Moon, so the boast meant that Venus copies the phases of the Moon. The jumble timestamped the find without giving it away.

He also wrote about the phases to Christoph Clavius, an aging Jesuit in Rome and an architect of the Gregorian calendar. The choice was shrewd: as chief mathematician of the Collegio Romano, Clavius carried more weight than any other astronomer in the Catholic world, and his backing could shield a claim inside the Church or sink it.

Many books say the phases proved that Earth moves. They did not. Tycho Brahe had offered a compromise in which Earth sits still, the Sun goes around Earth, and every other planet goes around the Sun. Tycho's Venus still orbits the Sun, so it would run through exactly the same cycle of phases as Copernicus's. The phases killed Ptolemy and left Tycho standing for another century, until Newton's gravity and James Bradley's stellar aberration settled the case.

You can check the geometry with bare eyes. Venus appears only near dawn or dusk, as the morning or evening star, never high at midnight. Its orbit lies inside Earth's, so it can never stray far from the Sun: its greatest elongation is about 47 degrees. Mercury, closer in, is held to some twenty-eight degrees, and that cap is itself the measurement that pins each orbit inside ours.

the-piccards-a-balloon-turned-upside-dow.context_blurb:
Auguste Piccard was a Swiss physicist who wanted to go where no human had been: the stratosphere, the calm, thin air above the weather. To get there alive he had to invent something new. Later he flipped his own design on its head, and his son rode the result to the deepest known spot in the ocean.

On 27 May 1931 Piccard and his young assistant Paul Kipfer rose from Augsburg, Germany, beneath an enormous hydrogen balloon. Climbing to 15,781 metres, Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer became the first humans ever to enter the stratosphere.

At that height an unprotected person blacks out and dies within minutes. Piccard rode inside a sealed aluminium ball that held sea-level pressure inside while the pressure outside fell away, the direct ancestor of every airliner cabin.

Then he flipped the design. A balloon, he reasoned, is a heavy cabin hanging under a light fluid that floats up through a heavier one. Invert it, and a steel cabin hangs under a float filled with gasoline, a liquid lighter than water that the deep barely squeezes, sinking through the sea. He named it a bathyscaphe, from the Greek for "deep" and "ship", and it began a new family of ocean craft.

In 1960 Auguste's son Jacques Piccard and the American naval officer Don Walsh took the bathyscaphe Trieste down into Challenger Deep, nearly eleven kilometres down in the Pacific near Guam. About nine kilometres down, a bang shook the craft. The men talked it over and kept going. An outer window of Plexiglas on the entry tunnel had cracked, the flooded shaft they had climbed through, so their steel crew sphere was untouched.

On the bottom they reported a flatfish, a claim biologists still doubt. In 2014 Paul Yancey's team argued that bony fish hit a limit near 8,200 metres. A small molecule called TMAO holds their proteins in shape against the pressure, and the deeper a fish lives, the more its cells must carry, until they are as concentrated as seawater and can pack in no more.

Then the deepest place on Earth sat empty for 52 years, until James Cameron dove alone in Deepsea Challenger in 2012. In 2019 Victor Vescovo's Limiting Factor became the first craft built to make the trip again and again: a record is not a capability.

Every crewed deep craft, Trieste, Alvin and the rest, carries its crew inside a ball. When water presses equally from every side, any other shape bends, and bending is how steel and titanium fail first. A sphere answers that even squeeze with pure compression in its wall, the stress those metals bear best.

the-placebo-and-why-blinding-exists.context_blurb:
A placebo is a dummy treatment: a sugar pill, a shot of salt water, a capsule with nothing inside. Doctors give one to a comparison group in a trial so they can tell whether a real drug does anything at all. Its story shows how hope and plain time can fool patients and doctors alike.

Imagine eighty out of a hundred patients with aching knees say a new drug helped. That proves nothing yet, because most people improve anyway: aches come and go, and bad days give way to better ones. The real test is how many would have improved without any drug at all, so every honest trial compares its patients with a group given a fake.

The fake itself has a strange dose-response. A pair of sugar pills eases pain more than a single one, and capsules outdo tablets. The more impressive the ritual, the stronger the effect, and the champion of all is a salt-water injection.

Fake surgery has fooled doctors too. In 1959 Leonard Cobb, a cardiologist in Seattle, put a popular operation for angina, the crushing chest pain of a starved heart, to the test: surgeons tied shut an artery running behind the breastbone. Some of his patients got only a cut in the skin, and that pretend operation eased their angina about as well as the real one.

It happened again in 2002, when the Houston surgeon Bruce Moseley tested knee surgery for arthritis. One group was put under anaesthetic and given cuts in the skin, with nothing done inside the knee. Those patients fared about the same as the ones who had the real operation, and neither real-surgery group ever reported less pain or better movement.

How strong is the placebo, really? Asbjorn Hrobjartsson and Peter Gotzsche, two Danish researchers, pooled trials in 2001 that had pitted a placebo against no treatment at all. Placebos reliably shifted what patients reported feeling, above all pain, but barely touched anything a doctor could measure in the disease itself. A placebo mostly changes how you feel, not what the illness is doing.

That fits an older correction. In 1955 Henry Beecher's paper "The Powerful Placebo" told doctors that about one patient in three responds to a fake, a figure still quoted today. In 1997 Kienle and Kiene went back through his fifteen trials and found that most of that response was really patients getting better on their own, the natural course of illness counted as a placebo effect.

The strangest result came in 2010. Ted Kaptchuk's team at Harvard handed people with irritable bowel syndrome a bottle plainly labelled "placebo" and told them the pills inside were inert. After three weeks that group had improved significantly more than patients who got no treatment. The trial was small, short and measured only what patients reported. Still, expectation leaks into every measurement, which is why the best trials keep both patients and doctors blind to who got the real thing.

the-playbook-they-had-already-written-wh.context_blurb:
Long before anyone needed it, the World Health Organization had a plan. In September 2019, well before COVID-19 appeared, it published a guide telling governments what to do in the next great pandemic before any vaccine existed. The PDF is still free online, so anyone can open it and compare its advice with what governments actually did in 2020.

The guide covered non-drug public-health measures against pandemic flu: masks, hand-washing, school closures, travel rules, everything a country can try before vaccines or medicines arrive. Flu is a different virus from the one behind COVID-19, but this was the WHO's standing advice for a deadly respiratory pandemic.

Its summary table graded each measure against four levels of severity. Beside that grid ran one more column, whose heading said flatly that the measures beneath it were never to be recommended, in any circumstances at all.

Quarantine of exposed people who feel well sat in that column. The guide gave two written reasons: it saw no obvious rationale for confining healthy people, and it foresaw considerable difficulty in carrying the measure out. It did not argue from freedom; it argued from evidence and feasibility.

Border screening sat there too. Fever checks at airports cannot see the travellers who matter most, people already infected who have not yet shown a single symptom. A tool that cannot see what it hunts will not catch it.

Schools were treated differently. Planned school closures were not in the never column: the guide suggested them for a severe epidemic or pandemic, but only after weighing their harms, and only for a limited time. The closures of 2020 in the United States ran far longer than that caveat imagined.

Workplaces got the sternest warning. The guide called closing them a last resort, to be considered only in extraordinarily severe epidemics and pandemics, the top of its four-level scale. Broad closures in 2020 did not wait for that threshold.

The guide was also honest about itself. It scored its evidence with a system called GRADE, which runs from very low through low and moderate to high, and nearly every recommendation rested on evidence rated very low. A document that modest cannot be summed up as "following the science", and in 2020 its standing advice was reversed without the reversal ever being argued out in public.

the-price-tag-and-the-private-jet.context_blurb:
The physics of carbon dioxide trapping heat does not change from year to year. What changes is the fight over what to do about it: who pays, who decides, and how the danger is sold. A few real episodes show that fight in plain numbers.

France's government planned to raise the carbon share of its fuel tax, a burden that landed hardest on rural diesel drivers. From 17 November 2018 protesters filled roundabouts across France in yellow safety vests, and the movement took the vests' French name, gilets jaunes. The vest made an instant uniform because French law has required every driver to keep one in the car since 2008, so anyone could join by pulling it out of the glovebox.

On 4 December Prime Minister Edouard Philippe suspended the increase for six months, and the next day he told parliament it was dropped from the 2019 budget altogether. On 10 December President Emmanuel Macron went on television and promised minimum-wage workers 100 euros more a month. Nothing about the physics changed that month; only the politics did.

In 2016 voters in Washington State weighed Initiative 732, a carbon tax beginning at $15 a tonne paired with a cut in the state sales tax, a revenue-neutral swap that many economists admired. It lost by 59 to 41 percent, and some of its fiercest opponents were not oil companies. The state Democratic Party, the state labour council and environmental-justice groups fought it, and the Sierra Club refused to back it, largely because they wanted the money spent on programs rather than handed back to taxpayers.

Most years in January the World Economic Forum gathers presidents and billionaires in Davos, a Swiss mountain resort; in 2022 the meeting fell in May. CE Delft, a Dutch consultancy hired by Greenpeace, tallied the planes coming and going near the resort during the 2022 gathering and counted roughly 1,040 private-jet flights. The researchers tied about half of them to the meeting itself.

The message reaches children too. In 2021 the psychotherapist Caroline Hickman led a poll of ten thousand young people, all between 16 and 25, in ten nations, published in The Lancet Planetary Health. Three in four agreed that the future is frightening, and the paper's title called that feeling climate anxiety. The poll proves neither that the danger is real nor that it is fake; it measures what the way adults talk about it does to the young.

Economists fight too, and not over the physics. William Nordhaus and Nicholas Stern, two mainstream economists of the same school, set prices on a tonne of carbon dioxide far apart: Stern's about 85 dollars, Nordhaus's a small fraction of that. The gap comes from one choice, the discount rate: how much less a harm counts when it falls on people generations from now. Stern, in 2006, used a rate near 0.1 percent a year, so far-future damage counts almost in full and his price runs high; Nordhaus used about 1.5 percent, and his price runs far lower. That is a question of ethics, not of physics.

Words are part of the fight. In 2007 the Boston Globe columnist Ellen Goodman wrote that people who denied global warming stood level with Holocaust deniers, and "denier" spread through the press, flung even at critics who agree that carbon dioxide traps heat but question the policies. The Associated Press later told its writers to drop that label and to avoid "skeptic" as well, since skepticism belongs to honest inquiry, and suggested "doubter" instead.

the-prophecys-price-sterilisation-quotas.context_blurb:
In 1968 the American biologist Paul Ehrlich warned in The Population Bomb that the 1970s would bring mass starvation unless governments cut births in poor countries. The famines he forecast never arrived. But in India and China, governments did cut births by force, and millions of ordinary people paid for the prophecy.

For India, the book went beyond advice. Ehrlich called for compulsory sterilisation of Indian men who had three or more children, and proposed that the United States supply helicopters and surgical instruments to speed the work. A recommendation in a book is not proof that it caused anything, but the idea was in print.

In June 1975 India's prime minister, Indira Gandhi, suspended citizens' rights and governed by decree after a court condemned her election as corrupt. That period, the Emergency, lasted until March 1977. In September 1976 her younger son, Sanjay Gandhi, took charge of the population campaign and ran it as an unofficial parallel government.

Under Indira Gandhi's Emergency, sterilisations leapt from 2.7 million in one year to 8.3 million in the next, from July 1976 to June 1977, most performed without consent. Doctors did not act alone. Officials passed quotas down the civil service until teachers and clerks had to deliver people for the operation or lose their pay or their jobs. Tie a career to a number, and the number is what you get.

Villages fought back. On 18 October 1976 in Muzaffarnagar, in northern India, police held seventeen villagers for the operation, and a crowd gathered at the police station to demand their release. Police fired on the crowd, killing about thirty people.

The Emergency ended at the ballot box, not by decree. Voters threw Congress out in March 1977, and Indira Gandhi was beaten even in her own seat of Rae Bareli. The winners' slogans hammered one Hindi word again and again: nasbandi, which means sterilisation. It is still the name Indians give that year.

China went further. In 1980, at a meeting in Chengdu, the engineer Song Jian, trained in the mathematics that guides missiles, fed China's population into the same family of equations. His group set China's ideal long-term population at about 650 to 700 million, some two-thirds of the billion people then alive there, a target only a one-child rule held for decades could reach. Song had met the Club of Rome's population models at a control-engineering conference in Helsinki in 1978.

The tidy story says the equations proved the case and the Party obeyed. Scholars such as Wang Feng and Daniel Goodkind dispute it: Party leaders had already settled on one-child limits before 1980. Goodkind likened Song's team to expert witnesses called by a prosecutor who had already made up his mind, so the mathematics lent scientific prestige to a decision already taken.

From 1980 most Chinese families were held to one child, backed by fines and sometimes by forced abortions. Many families wanted a son to carry the name, and ultrasound let parents learn a baby's sex before birth. In 1981 about 108 boys were born for every 100 girls; by 2000 the figure was near 117, leaving some 32 to 36 million more men than women in those generations. The planners had modelled births as a number, and never modelled a family's wish for a son.

the-quantum-tech-already-in-your-pocket.context_blurb:
Quantum mechanics sounds like the physics of strange thought experiments, but it is also the physics in your pocket. Writing in Scientific American in 2001, Max Tegmark and John Wheeler reckoned that roughly 30 percent of America's economy rests on inventions made possible by quantum mechanics, and their examples began with semiconductors in computer chips and lasers in CD players before reaching hospital scanners.

The semiconductor age began in late 1947 in New Jersey, at Bell Labs. John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed fine gold contacts onto a crystal of high-purity germanium, and on 23 December they played speech through their little device, loud enough for everyone to hear. Silicon took over the industry within a decade, but the first working transistor was germanium.

Their device worked, but it was fragile and fussy. Their colleague William Shockley soon designed a rugged version from three treated layers of crystal, the junction transistor, and it became the workhorse of early transistor radios and computers, until a later design, the MOSFET, took over the chips of today. All three men shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Bardeen was not done. In 1972 he shared a second physics Nobel with Robert Schrieffer and Leon Cooper for the theory of superconductivity, which explains why electrons in certain chilled metals pair up and glide through the crystal with zero resistance. No one else has won the physics prize twice.

Why do crystals behave this way? In a solid, electrons may hold only certain bands of energy, with forbidden gaps between them, a purely quantum rule with no version in classical physics. In a light-emitting diode, an LED, current drives an electron to drop from a higher band to a lower one, and it gives off a single photon whose energy matches the gap. The width of the gap fixes the colour, so a wider gap makes a bluer photon, and an LED's colour comes from its material, not its voltage.

Nick Holonyak of General Electric made the first LED a human eye could see in October 1962 by blending two compounds of gallium, the arsenide and the phosphide, and its band gap made it glow red. Green followed within a few years. Blue took three more decades, because no one could make a blue diode efficiently. The trick fell to Shuji Nakamura, Isamu Akasaki and Hiroshi Amano, who grew crystals of gallium nitride and shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. Their blue LED was the missing piece for white light: every white LED bulb is a blue LED coated with a yellow phosphor, and your eye blends the two into white.

The laser half of the story began in Malibu, California, on 16 May 1960. With his assistant Irnee D'Haenens beside him, Theodore Maiman of Hughes Research Labs fired a spiral flash lamp into a small cylinder of synthetic ruby, aluminium oxide laced with chromium, and the rod threw out the first laser beam. Others had expected a gas to come first.

You can test laser physics on a kitchen table. Shine a cheap red laser pointer at a low angle onto a CD or DVD: its tracks lie in tiny, even rows, 1.6 micrometres apart on a CD, close enough to the wavelength of red light that the disc works as a diffraction grating. Bright dots line up across the wall, and from their angles you can work out the wavelength yourself instead of trusting the packet.

Those three inventions are settled technology. The much-hyped quantum computer is not, yet. Narrow demonstrations on contrived tasks exist, but no general-purpose quantum computer has beaten an ordinary machine on a problem anyone actually wants solved, and the open obstacle is error correction: the fragile qubits lose their quantum state too fast, and fixing their errors costs an enormous overhead.
