the-radium-craze.context_blurb:
Marie and Pierre Curie discovered radium in 1898, and for about thirty years afterwards Americans bought the glowing element as a health product. It went into watch dials, toothpaste, face cream and drinking water. Its story is a lesson in how a real and powerful force can be sold as a cure before anyone tests what it does inside the body.

One popular gadget, the Revigator, patented in 1912, was a crock lined with radium ore. Buyers filled it with water at night and drank the "charged" water in the morning, expecting the radioactivity to give them a boost of health every day. The adverts promised that it would prevent arthritis and senility and restore what they called the lost element of freshness.

The most famous tonic was Radithor, little bottles of radium-laced water sold by William Bailey, who called himself a doctor but never was one. Bailey dared the public, for a $1,000 prize, to prove that a bottle held less radium than its label said, and he knew he was safe: every bottle really did carry its promised dose.

That honesty was the poison. Radium sits in calcium's column of the periodic table, three rows further down, so the body treats it like calcium and files it away in bone. Radium-226 lasts about 1,600 years, so whatever lands in the skeleton keeps firing alpha particles for the rest of a life.

Eben Byers, a Pittsburgh industrialist and amateur golf champion, injured his arm in 1927, took Radithor on a doctor's advice, and felt wonderful. He drank about 1,400 bottles in three years. By the end surgeons had removed most of his jaw and holes were forming in his skull, and he died in March 1932. Decades later a Wall Street Journal headline said the radium water had worked just fine, right up until his jaw came off.

Workers paid first. From 1917 a New Jersey company, US Radium, employed young women to letter watch faces with glowing numerals in a paint called Undark. They were taught to point their brushes with a three-step drill, "lip, dip, paint", swallowing a little paint every time, while the male chemists downstairs worked with lead aprons and tongs.

When the dial painters started to lose teeth and break jaws, the company's doctors blamed syphilis and phosphorus poisoning, labels that also wrecked the women's reputations. In 1924 the dentist Theodor Blum first described the true disease, radium jaw, and from 1925 the pathologist Harrison Martland proved that radium was to blame.

In 1927 the dial painter Grace Fryer and four workmates sued the company. Newspapers called them the five women doomed to die, and the company settled in 1928. Their fight helped force the country to accept that radiation at work is a real danger to the people exposed to it.

The same killing power can heal. Radium-223 follows calcium into bone just as the old radium did, but it lasts only about eleven days, so it strikes nearby tumours and then fades. American regulators at the FDA approved it in 2013, as monthly shots sold as Xofigo, for prostate cancer that has spread into the bones.

the-radium-girls-and-the-element-that-fi.context_blurb:
In the late 1910s and 1920s, young women in two factory towns, Orange in New Jersey and Ottawa in Illinois, earned good wages painting glowing numbers on watch dials. The paint held radium, a radioactive element, and nobody told them what it would do. Their slow poisoning, and their fight in court, changed how the world treats danger at work.

To keep a fine tip on the brush, supervisors taught the painters a three-word drill: lip, dip, paint. Each stroke put a little paint in the mouth.

The glow came from a mixture. Radium alone does not shine much, so the paint, sold as Undark, blended it with crystals of zinc sulfide; each alpha particle from the radium struck the crystals and made them flash a faint blue-green.

The painters, mostly teenagers, loved the stuff. At the end of a shift some of them daubed leftover paint on their nails and their teeth so they would glow in the dark on a night out. Years later their jaws began to crumble, because the body handles radium like calcium and stores it in bone, where it keeps firing radiation for life.

Rich customers were not safe either. The Pittsburgh industrialist Eben Byers drank the radium tonic Radithor for years on a doctor's tip, until surgeons removed his jaw. When he died in 1932 he was buried in a lead-lined coffin, because his body was still radioactive enough to be a danger in its own right.

To prove the radium was still inside the painters long after they had quit the factory, the medical examiner Harrison Martland turned the women themselves into his instruments. He measured the gamma rays streaming from their living bodies and the radon gas in the air they breathed out. He also laid bones from victims on unused dental film in the dark, and the bones fogged the film by themselves.

Out in Illinois, the Radium Dial Company let its painters go on pointing brushes with their lips for years after the New Jersey cases. On 10 February 1938 the dial painter Catherine Wolfe Donohue, so weak she could not sit up at the hearing, set a small box on the table as evidence. Inside lay pieces of her own jawbone that had broken loose in her mouth. An arbitrator ruled for her that April, and she died in July.

the-rainbow-you-can-build-with-a-garden-.context_blurb:
A rainbow looks like a thing hanging in the sky, but it is really a direction: light that countless falling drops send back toward one pair of eyes. You can build one with a garden hose.

Stand with a low Sun at your back and spray a fine mist. The bow is part of a full circle, and its centre is the antisolar point, exactly opposite the Sun, marked by the shadow of your own head on the grass. Every drop that sends you red light lies about 42 degrees from that point, so each drop returns its light along a cone of one fixed width, and violet comes from about 40 degrees. Drop size plays no part, so every rainbow is the same size.

Try the hose at a July noon and you get nothing. As the Sun climbs, the ring's centre sinks, and once the Sun stands more than 42 degrees high the whole ring lies below the ground, under your feet.

Because a rainbow is a direction, nobody ever reaches one. Walk through the mist and your arc is rebuilt from a different set of drops at every step, and two friends side by side see two separate bows made of different water.

Moonlight makes bows too. On nights around the full Moon, Kentucky's Cumberland Falls throws a moonbow, grey-white to the eye, yet a long camera exposure shows its reds and greens. In light that dim, the cone cells of your eye that sense colour never switch on.

Each drop spreads sunlight into every colour, like a prism, but sends your eye only one colour and flings the rest past your head. The band of colour is therefore a map of how high each drop sits: drops high in the arc send you red, and lower ones send violet.

Why a sharp band and not a glow? Rays enter a drop at every height, bend, bounce off its back and bend again leaving, fanning out over a broad spread of angles. But the total bend has a minimum near 138 degrees for red, and at that one angle rays from many entry heights pile up together. Subtract 138 from 180 and you get the familiar 42.

On a dewy lawn the cone meets the ground and makes a dewbow in the beads on the blades. Flat ground slices the cone open, so the bow on the grass traces a hyperbola that opens wider the farther out it runs.

After a heavy shower a fainter second bow may appear near 51 degrees, about nine degrees outside the first, with its colours flipped so red faces inward. Its light reflected twice off the back of each drop before escaping, and the extra bounce costs it over half its brightness and spreads it nearly twice as wide. Alexander of Aphrodisias, who ran Aristotle's old school at Athens about AD 200, first wrote down that the strip between a double bow is darker than the sky on either side. The main bow throws its light inward and the second throws it outward, so nothing is aimed into the gap, still called Alexander's band.

On the ground, the earth cuts every rainbow in half. From an airliner at ten thousand metres the drops below you come into play, and once the Sun sinks under about three degrees, almost touching the horizon, the bow closes into a complete ring.

For centuries scholars reasoned about rainbows by reasoning about clouds. Between 1304 and 1311 the Dominican friar Theodoric of Freiberg tried something new in a darkened room: he sent a single sunbeam into a water-filled glass globe, treating it as one raindrop blown up big enough to follow the rays.

In 1637 Descartes calculated the angle. Textbooks long said he traced some ten thousand rays, but in 1983 Frank Barmore showed that the number had been copied from book to book. Descartes stepped across the drop in tenths, saw where the angle stopped changing, then refined the strip between eight and nine tenths near the edge, a few dozen careful sums.

Just inside the violet edge you may spot faint pink, purple and green fringes, supernumerary bows that no ray-tracing predicts. In 1804 Thomas Young explained them as interference: light that took two slightly different paths through one drop recombines a little out of step, reinforcing in some directions and cancelling in others. George Airy fixed their spacing in 1838, and that spacing reveals the size of the drops.

the-repairs-that-actually-work.context_blurb:
Science has a replication crisis: too many published findings fail when someone else repeats the study. The cure is not cynicism but more checking, done in the open. One simple tool is preregistration, in which researchers post their hypothesis, sample size and analysis plan with a timestamp before they collect any data.

A stronger version is the registered report: a journal reviews the question and the method first and promises to publish the paper whatever the result. In 2021 the psychologists Scheel, Schijen and Lakens set ordinary psychology papers beside registered reports. Among the ordinary papers, 146 of 152, about 96 percent, confirmed the authors' first guess, but only 31 of 71 registered reports, about 44 percent, did. The authors warn that this is a comparison of two different literatures, not a controlled experiment, yet the gap makes anyone look twice at a positive result.

The movement's motto comes from Richard Feynman's 1974 commencement speech at Caltech, later printed as "Cargo Cult Science". He told the graduates that the first rule is never to fool yourself, because you are the easiest person of all to fool.

the-river-in-the-sky-nobody-would-read.context_blurb:
High over Japan in the 1920s, a meteorologist named Wasaburo Oishi found one of the great winds of the planet, and almost nobody heard him. The rest of the world learned about it again only in war, when American bomber crews flew straight into it.

At the Tateno observatory, in what is now Tsukuba, Oishi launched balloons and followed them by telescope. In winter they raced off on a narrow band of furious westerly wind close to the ceiling of the weather, the river of air we now call the jet stream.

Oishi wrote up his findings in nineteen reports, 1,246 pages, from 1926 to 1944. He chose Esperanto, an invented international language: he was president of the Japanese Esperanto Institute and hoped it would carry his work abroad. It did the opposite, and almost no one outside Japan read them.

When American B-29 bombers reached Japan late in 1944, their crews meant to bomb from 30,000 feet and found themselves inside winds of 200 to 300 miles an hour. At full throttle some planes barely crept over the ground, and bombs fell miles off target. General Curtis LeMay's fix was to bring the bombers down to about 25,000 feet, under the core of the jet. Later he sent them in low to firebomb.

Japan tried to turn the wind into a weapon. From 3 November 1944 its army released some nine thousand paper balloons carrying bombs into the jet, aiming them at North America. The planners had assumed the wrong wind speed, and the real crossing took three to four days. Only a few hundred balloons arrived, but six civilians died near Bly, Oregon, on 5 May 1945, the only deaths from enemy action in the contiguous United States during the war.

What drives the river? The jet forms where air temperature changes steeply from one region to the next, high up at the ceiling of the weather. The steepest such contrast is between warm equatorial air and cold polar air, and it is sharpest in winter, so the jet howls through the winter months and eases off in the summer. Check any departures board: an eastbound flight from New York to London routinely beats the westbound return by about an hour.

the-same-machine-run-backwards-motor-and.context_blurb:
An electric motor turns current into spin; a generator turns spin into current. They look like opposite inventions, but they are one piece of physics read in two directions. Michael Faraday found it in London in 1831, and it still runs every power station, every electric car and every bicycle dynamo.

At the Royal Institution, Faraday mounted a copper disc on an axle so its rim spun through the gap of a horseshoe magnet. Cranked by hand, it turned the steady work of his arm into a steady electric current, and it is the ancestor of every dynamo since.

That same year he pushed a bar magnet into a coil of wire and watched a meter needle jump. Many expected a magnet simply resting beside a coil to give a steady current, but Faraday found that the coil gives current only while the magnetic field is changing; a magnet lying still, however strong, gives nothing.

Feed current back into Faraday's disc and it spins by itself. Industry learned this by accident at Vienna's world fair of 1873. Hippolyte Fontaine, partner of the Belgian inventor Zenobe Gramme, wired one Gramme dynamo to another some 500 metres off, meaning to show power sent across a distance. To everyone's surprise, the second machine's shaft began turning by itself: a dynamo run backwards is a motor.

The machine keeps honest books. Switch on a bicycle's hub-dynamo headlamp and the pedals suddenly push back harder, because, by Lenz's rule, an induced current always flows so as to fight the change that made it. The lamp's energy has to come from somewhere, and it comes from your legs.

Drop a strong neodymium magnet down a thick copper pipe and you can watch the rule work. Copper is not magnetic, yet the magnet drifts down in slow motion, as though through honey, because its motion stirs swirling eddy currents in the copper whose own magnetism pushes back.

Electric cars sell the same physics as a feature. On a long downhill, regenerative braking lets the car's own momentum spin the drive motor, so it works as a generator and sends current back into the battery instead of wasting the energy as brake heat.

Faraday's other 1831 device, an iron ring carrying two separate coils, became the transformer that steps high-voltage power down for your house. Induction needs a changing field, so a transformer cannot transform direct current, whose steady flow makes a steady field; that is why the grid runs on alternating current.

So are motor and generator really one machine reversed? As physics, yes. As hardware, an engineer adds a caveat: each real machine is wound, geared and cooled for one job, so perfect reversibility is a schoolbook ideal.

the-schedule-vaers-and-the-study-nobody-.context_blurb:
Two loud claims surround the American childhood vaccine schedule: that it is proven safe, and that it is proven dangerous. The honest question is narrower. How would anyone actually know whether the whole schedule, every dose in its order, is as safe as an alternative? Answering it means counting carefully and knowing what each count can show.

Alexander Glenny, a British scientist at London's Wellcome Laboratory, was only trying in 1926 to purify diphtheria toxoid, so he clumped it with potassium alum into a solid he could wash. Guinea pigs injected with that solid made a far stronger antibody response than animals given the plain toxoid. Glenny had found the adjuvant effect, and aluminium salts have been in vaccines ever since.

The schedule has grown, and by how much depends on the counting rule. In 1986 it held eleven doses, seven shots and four by mouth, against seven diseases. Count every dose from birth to eighteen, yearly flu shots included, and the 2025 schedule came to about 50 to 54 doses against 16 to 18 diseases. Other rules give other headlines; nobody disputes the growth, only what it means.

Count the load instead. Antigens are the particular molecules that the body's defences learn to spot. In the 1980s a single whole-cell shot against whooping cough held thousands, because the whole killed bacterium went into the vial, while the entire 2025 schedule carried only some 150 to 200 antigens in all. Or count aluminium. Over the first six months a baby got about 1.5 mg from vaccines in 1986 and about 4.4 mg under the 2025 schedule, while a formula-fed baby swallows about 38 mg in the same months. That compares amounts, not routes into the body, so researchers went and measured.

The biggest such study followed 1,224,176 Danish children born from 1997 to 2018 and found no extra autoimmune, allergic or neurodevelopmental illness with more vaccine aluminium. Nobody assigned the doses: Denmark kept switching vaccine brands, so a child's total depended mostly on the year of birth. Barely one child in a hundred got no aluminium at all, so the study compares more against less, not vaccinated against unvaccinated.

The early-warning net is VAERS, which opened in November 1990. Anyone at all may file, a patient or parent as easily as a doctor, though only doctors and manufacturers must report certain events. So a report is an account, not a verified injury. In an ordinary pre-pandemic year VAERS logged between thirty and fifty thousand reports; by the close of 2021 it held more than 717,000 linked to COVID-19 vaccines. Both sides quoted such totals as risks, but the CDC warns that VAERS cannot give a rate, because it never learns how many people got the shot to begin with.

The net can still work. RotaShield, the first vaccine against rotavirus, won its licence in August 1998; by July 1999 VAERS held fifteen reports of intussusception, a bowel folding in on itself. The CDC urged suspension within days, and the maker withdrew the vaccine that October. Its replacement, RotaTeq, passed a trial of 68,038 babies with no extra risk, yet when Yih's team later searched the FDA's Mini-Sentinel records they found roughly 1.1 extra cases for every 100,000 first doses. A trial that size could never see a risk that rare. RotaTeq stayed in use, because one in 100,000 is a different decision from RotaShield's one in 10,000.

Critics often quote a 2011 Harvard Pilgrim report saying that under 1 percent of adverse events after vaccination get reported. Check its source: Ross Lazarus and Michael Klompas took that line from studies published earlier, cited as background for their project, not from anything they measured. Their planned test against VAERS never ran, because, the report says, CDC contacts stopped responding.

In 2013 the Institute of Medicine reviewed the schedule. It found nothing to show the schedule unsafe, but no study had ever examined the number of doses, their timing, their order and the ages they are given, all together. The decisive trial, leaving some children unvaccinated at random, the committee would not endorse, calling it unethical. Comparing children on the standard schedule with those on alternatives fails too, the committee wrote, because the two groups may differ in more ways than the schedule. No randomised trial of the whole schedule exists; that is not the same as finding danger, and treating either statement as the other is an error.

the-shipyards-flaw-detector-in-the-mater.context_blurb:
Ultrasound lets a doctor watch an unborn baby move without a single X-ray. Its first scans of the body's insides came off a machine built to hunt cracks in steel boilers, borrowed in Glasgow by the obstetrician Ian Donald, who had picked up a little radar in the Royal Air Force during the war.

On 21 July 1955 Donald drove two carloads to a boiler works at Renfrew run by Babcock & Wilcox, where an ultrasonic tester searched steel for hidden flaws. The boots were full of fibroids and ovarian cysts recently removed from his patients, because he wanted to know whether different lumps threw back different echoes. He also needed something normal to compare them with, a control, and the story goes that the company kindly supplied a big lump of steak. Legend or not, the rule is sound: test something known before you trust an odd reading.

Late in 1956 a 23-year-old engineer named Tom Brown, at a Glasgow instrument firm, heard a strange tale of a professor who was hunting for flaws in women with a machine meant to find flaws in metal. Brown phoned Donald, and by late 1957 they had the first contact scanner in clinical use.

Every probe runs on physics found in Paris in 1880. The brothers Jacques and Pierre Curie squeezed crystals of quartz and other substances in a small vise, and a voltage appeared across the crystal's faces. A year later Gabriel Lippmann worked out the reverse, which the brothers confirmed: feed in a voltage and the crystal changes shape. One crystal can therefore speak, by pinging, and listen, by turning echoes into voltage.

The gel a technician smears on the skin is not for comfort. Air reflects nearly all ultrasound, so even a thin film of it between probe and skin bounces the whole beam back; the gel shuts the air out.

Sound-ranging was a sea technology first. In 1914 Reginald Fessenden took his underwater oscillator aboard the Revenue Cutter Miami to the iceberg lanes of the Grand Banks, where the Titanic had sunk two years before. He measured how deep the water ran, picked up an echo off an iceberg some two miles distant, and sent Morse code through the sea itself.

The scanner measures depth with a clock, not a ruler. Sound moves through soft tissue at about 1,540 metres a second, so an echo that returns 100 microseconds after the ping has travelled about 15.4 centimetres; that is the trip down and back, so the reflector lies about 7.7 cm deep.

The first great proof was a woman sent to Donald's ward with what X-rays and examinations called inoperable stomach cancer. His echoes disagreed, and surgery found a vast ovarian cyst that filled her entire abdomen, large but removable, and she was cured.

Donald did not invent medical ultrasound. In 1940s Vienna, Karl Dussik and his physicist brother Friedrich seated patients with the tops of their heads in a water bath and sent sound right through the skull to a receiver on the far side. Dussik took the patterns for the brain's fluid-filled ventricles. Then in 1952 Guettner's group at Siemens in Erlangen showed that the pattern came from the skull bone itself, whose thickness varies from place to place, and not from the brain. A promising method can give beautiful, consistent, false results for years until someone tests its assumptions.

The road that won was reflection. John Wild, an English surgeon in Minnesota, aimed a borrowed US Navy radar trainer at tissue and, with the engineer John Reid, found that cancerous tissue throws back stronger echoes than healthy tissue. By 1956 they had tested the method on 117 breast cases, right more than nine times in ten.

The echoes are faint. A boundary returns sound according to how much the tissues on either side differ in acoustic impedance, density multiplied by sound speed. Fat and muscle differ only a little, so a fat-muscle boundary sends back only about 1.4 percent of the sound, and whole pictures are built from returns that small.

Operators also pick a frequency, between roughly 1 and 18 MHz. Higher frequencies show finer detail, but tissue soaks up sound faster the higher its frequency, so a 7 MHz beam would be swallowed long before it reached a liver, and deep organs are scanned at 3 to 5 MHz instead.

the-sky-does-fall-tunguska-chelyabinsk-a.context_blurb:
Rocks from space do not have to hit the ground to do damage. Two great blasts over Russia, Tunguska in 1908 and Chelyabinsk in 2013, show how a falling asteroid can explode in the air, and how scientists measure one when no instrument was waiting.

On the morning of 15 February 2013 a stony rock about 18 metres wide tore apart some 30 kilometres above Chelyabinsk, releasing about as much energy as thirty Hiroshima bombs. No one was killed, yet 1,491 people sought medical help, almost all of them cut by window glass that the shock wave blew inward.

Barely four to six tonnes of the rock's original nine thousand ever reached the ground. The biggest piece smashed through the frozen surface of Lake Chebarkul, and when divers raised it that October it read 654 kilograms, then the scale gave way and the stone cracked into three pieces.

Why were so many people at their windows? The flash reached everyone instantly, in silence, while the bang took more than two minutes to arrive, so people walked to the glass to look and were standing there when the shock wave hit. Count the seconds between lightning and thunder and you can time the same gap yourself.

No telescope saw it coming. Surveys swept the sky nightly, but the rock came in from the direction of the Sun, hidden in the daytime glare where no telescope on the ground can look.

Siberia had seen a bigger one. Something burst over the Podkamennaya Tunguska river on 30 June 1908 and flattened the forest. For several nights afterwards the sky over Europe glowed so brightly that people in Britain could read outdoors at midnight, because about a million tonnes of fine dust had been flung high above the clouds, into the calm layers above the weather.

With no tracking data for Chelyabinsk, two scientists in Colombia, Jorge Zuluaga and Ignacio Ferrin, worked out its speed, path and orbit in under a week. Their raw material was dashboard-camera video, which many Russian drivers keep running in case of insurance disputes.

A worldwide web of stations that listen for sound too low for human ears also caught the blast. The network had been built to detect secret nuclear tests, and twenty of its stations picked it up, one of them in Antarctica. Its infrasound alone gave about 460 kilotons, close to the 500 from every other method combined: two different instruments, one answer.

Dashcam clips are shaky and uncalibrated, so researchers went to the exact spots where clips were filmed, photographed the night sky from each one and laid the stars over the daytime footage. The stars became a ruler, fixing the fireball's true direction frame by frame.

Why did the rock burst so high? At 19 kilometres a second, the air piling up in front of it pushed harder than its cracked body could withstand. It began to break at 45 kilometres, with almost all the air still below, then shattered about eleven more times before 30 kilometres, dumping nearly all its energy into the air in a fraction of a second.

In 1947 the Sikhote-Alin fall in eastern Russia left more than 200 craters, and Barringer Crater in Arizona was dug by a body of similar modest size. Both were solid iron rather than stone: small iron bodies survive the plunge and dig real holes, while small stony ones burst before they land.

Leonid Kulik reached the centre in April 1927 after travelling by boat, on foot and with reindeer across the swampy forest, expecting an iron meteorite in a crater. He found neither. In a central patch roughly eight kilometres wide, trees still stood upright, scorched and stripped of every branch, because a blast directly overhead pushes straight down; farther out the trunks lay flat, pointing away from the centre.

In 1965 Willard Libby, inventor of radiocarbon dating, and two colleagues proposed that Tunguska was a lump of antimatter. Annihilation would have raised the carbon-14 in the air by about seven percent, so they searched the yearly growth rings of trees for the spike, and found almost nothing.

More than a century on, the blast's energy is still unsettled. Seismographs, barometers and maps of some 2,150 square kilometres of fallen forest have all been studied, yet published estimates still run from about 3 to 50 megatons. No fragment has ever been confirmed, and whether it was a stony asteroid or a comet is still argued.

the-superconductor-nobody-can-explain.context_blurb:
A superconductor is a material that, cooled enough, carries electric current with no resistance at all. Physicists have known about it for more than a century and can explain it in ordinary metals, yet the best superconductors ever found, brittle ceramics, still have no accepted explanation. The field has also produced some of science's most spectacular false alarms.

A teacher can show it on a desk. Chill a small black ceramic tile with liquid nitrogen and set a strong magnet above it, and the magnet hangs in mid-air, locked in place, because the cold tile has become a superconductor, which drives magnetic fields out of itself. Start a current circling a loop inside such a tile and it runs on and on, with no heat and no fade, because its electrical resistance is exactly zero ohms. That is a cliff, not a slope.

The discovery came in Leiden in 1911. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes had become the first person to liquefy helium, which happens near 4.2 kelvin, just above absolute zero. He dipped a solid mercury wire into it and its resistance vanished outright; his notebook says, in Dutch, mercury practically zero. He had discovered superconductivity, and it won him the 1913 Nobel Prize. In 1957 John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer explained it in ordinary metals, and their theory seemed to set a ceiling on how warm a superconductor could be.

Then in 1986, at IBM's laboratory in Zurich, Georg Bednorz and Alex Muller tested a brittle ceramic that metal specialists had largely ignored, an oxide of lanthanum, barium and copper. It superconducted at 35 kelvin, and the pair won the Nobel Prize the very next year. Months later Maw-Kuen Wu in Alabama and Paul Chu in Houston changed one ingredient and pushed the temperature to about 93 kelvin. That crossed a practical line, because the coolant could now be liquid nitrogen, which boils at 77 kelvin and costs less than milk, instead of scarce liquid helium.

Nearly forty years and dozens of rival pairing models later, physicists still have no accepted explanation of how these copper-oxide ceramics superconduct. The materials sit inside working MRI magnets and power cables while the theory stays unsolved.

The great prize, superconductivity in a warm room at everyday pressure, draws bold claims. In July 2023 a pair of Korean chemists claimed exactly that online for a copper-doped lead apatite, and a video of a flake tilting over a magnet went round the world. Within three weeks researchers at the Max Planck institute in Stuttgart grew pure single crystals of it, and they turned out to be transparent purple insulators. A copper sulfide impurity had faked the drop in resistance. Science did not just argue about the claim; it made the stuff and measured it.

Real progress comes with fine print. In 2019 Mikhail Eremets's group in Mainz saw lanthanum hydride superconduct at 250 kelvin, only 23 degrees short of the temperature at which water freezes, and reporters called it room temperature. But it only worked squeezed to about 170 gigapascals in a diamond anvil cell, more than a million times the pressure of the air around us.

Worse came from Rochester. Ranga Dias, a physicist there, put two claims of room-temperature superconductivity into Nature, in 2020 and 2023, and both were retracted, the second after eight of his eleven co-authors asked for it. The theorist Jorge Hirsch was the first to question the published data, and argued that some of it had never been measured in any laboratory. In 2024 a university inquiry found that Dias had fabricated data, which means he invented numbers he had never measured.

the-tell-what-actually-gives-a-faked-res.context_blurb:
Faked science is rarely exposed by an authority announcing the truth. Again and again it falls to someone who checks a physical thing: a stain, a swab, a column of numbers, a raw data file, a name on a register. Four famous cases show the habit at work, and it is a habit anyone can learn.

Paul Kammerer, a biologist in 1920s Vienna, claimed proof of a serious idea in a live debate, that traits an animal acquires in life can be inherited. He made midwife toads breed in water instead of on land and reported that the males grew dark, rough mating pads on their front feet, the grip patches other frogs use, and passed them to their young. In 1926 the American herpetologist Noble examined the last surviving specimen under a microscope and reported in Nature that the dark pads were India ink that someone had injected beneath the skin. Kammerer blamed a lab assistant and took his own life six weeks later.

In March 1974 the dermatologist William Summerlin, at Memorial Sloan-Kettering in New York, showed off white mice that, he said, had accepted patches of dark skin from unrelated mice with no drugs to stop rejection. A lab assistant wiped one dark patch with alcohol, and the colour came off: Summerlin had drawn it with a felt-tip pen.

Sir Cyril Burt, the most celebrated educational psychologist in Britain, built his fame on identical twins raised apart, and his figures shaped school policy for a generation. Early in the 1970s Leon Kamin, an American psychologist, read Burt's twin papers one after another and saw that the correlation figures stayed identical to three decimal places even as new twins were added, which real data almost never does.

Burt had died in 1971. In 1976 the Sunday Times journalist Oliver Gillie went looking for two research assistants named on Burt's papers, Margaret Howard and J. Conway. He found no trace of either at University College London, where Burt had worked for decades, or anywhere else.

Burt's family chose Leslie Hearnshaw, a well-regarded historian of psychology who had known Burt kindly, to write the official life, and everyone expected a defence. Instead Hearnshaw, reading Burt's own papers and diaries, concluded in 1979 that the twin data were unreliable or invented. Later writers, Robert Joynson and Ronald Fletcher, argued the case was overstated, and other twin studies have found similar results, so whether Burt faked his figures is still disputed.

Starting in 2007, two biostatisticians at MD Anderson in Texas, Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes, tried to repeat Duke University's celebrated genomic tests for choosing a cancer patient's chemotherapy. Rebuilding the analysis from the raw files, they found gene lists shifted by a row and patient samples given the wrong labels. They had found errors, not proof of a lie, yet Duke had already put real patients into trials that used the tests.

For three years their warnings went nowhere. Then in July 2010 the editor of a little newsletter called The Cancer Letter, Paul Goldberg, discovered that Duke's oncologist Anil Potti had claimed on grant applications a Rhodes Scholarship he had never held; the Rhodes Trust had no record of him. Duke suspended Potti within days, the trials stopped, and eleven papers were eventually retracted.

the-terrella-a-model-earth-on-the-bench.context_blurb:
Can a model on a workbench tell you about a whole planet? Twice, scientists made a little Earth, watched what it did, and reasoned that the real Earth must do the same. The first time, in 1600, the idea took hold; the second time, three centuries later, it was mocked for decades before a satellite proved it right.

William Gilbert, personal physician to Queen Elizabeth I, wondered why ships' compasses swing north, and suspected that the planet itself is a huge magnet. To test the guess, he carved a lump of lodestone, a naturally magnetic stone, into a sphere and called it a terrella, Latin for little Earth. When he moved a small compass over the ball, the needle behaved just as a ship's compass does at sea.

Gilbert built on a finding by the London compass-maker Robert Norman, who in 1581 mounted a magnetised needle so it could tilt as well as turn. A ship's compass is made to swing only flat, which hides the effect, but in Norman's workshop the free needle's north end tipped down toward the floor. Gilbert reproduced the dip on his terrella and showed it grows steeper nearer the poles: a bench model predicting a measurement at sea.

Gilbert also untangled two forces everyone had lumped together. Rubbed amber grabs bits of straw briefly; lodestone attracts nothing but iron, yet holds on for good and points north. For the amber kind he coined a new Latin word, electricus, from the Greek elektron, amber. Not until 1820, when Oersted saw a compass needle jump beside a current, were the two forces joined again.

He tested sailors' lore too. An old claim held that rubbing garlic on a compass kills its power, so Gilbert smeared garlic on his own compass needle, and it pointed as well as ever.

Three centuries later Kristian Birkeland, a Norwegian physicist, made a new little Earth: a magnetised sphere coated with glowing paint inside a vacuum chamber. He fired a beam of electrons at it, and glowing rings formed about its poles, just like the aurora.

Birkeland argued that the real aurora is made by particles from the Sun carrying electric charge, steered down Earth's magnetic field lines onto the polar sky. Sydney Chapman, Britain's foremost geophysicist, led the objection that buried the idea for fifty years: electric currents, he held, cannot cross the vacuum of space. Birkeland died in Tokyo in 1917 with his theory still called crank science.

A US Navy satellite crossing the auroral zone in 1967 found electric currents running along Earth's magnetic field, exactly as Birkeland had predicted. They are now called Birkeland currents.

Earth's field keeps its own records. Cooling lava locks in a copy of the field, so layer upon layer of old flows forms a record, and it shows that north and south have swapped many times. The most recent full flip came about 780,000 years ago, and no one can yet predict the next. You can watch the field change yourself: the magnetic north pole has been drifting toward Siberia, for years at about 50 kilometres a year, and lately at about 35.

the-three-millimetre-shield.context_blurb:
High above the weather, a thin layer of ozone blocks the harshest ultraviolet light from the Sun, the wavelengths that would sterilise the ground. Two French physicists found it without looking for it, simply by measuring sunlight with great care.

In 1913 Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson recorded the Sun's spectrum and found that a band of ultraviolet light, below about 310 nanometres, never reached the ground. The shape of the gap matched the fingerprint of one chemical, ozone, so they had detected an invisible gas, high up in the atmosphere, purely by the light it removed.

You might expect such a shield to be a thick blanket. It is not. Collect all the ozone over your head and press it to sea-level pressure, and it makes a film only about three millimetres thick, close to what Fabry and Buisson measured in 1920. Scientists now measure ozone in Dobson units, where the global average of 300 units equals three millimetres.

The units honour the Oxford scientist Gordon Dobson, who built a ground instrument that gauges the total ozone above it by setting two ultraviolet wavelengths side by side. His real achievement, between 1928 and 1958, was a lasting network of identical stations around the world, from Arosa to Egypt, India, California and New Zealand. One of them, at Halley Bay in Antarctica, was set up for the International Geophysical Year of 1957.

the-tides-the-moons-grip-on-the-ocean.context_blurb:
Twice a day the sea climbs the shore and slides back again, so reliably that tide tables are printed weeks ahead. Working out why took some of the greatest minds in science, and one of them, Galileo, got it famously wrong.

In Canada's Bay of Fundy the sea climbs and drops about sixteen metres, the height of a five-storey building. What keeps that clock so exact is the Moon's gravity as it passes overhead; the bay's funnel shape only makes the swing bigger.

Stay for a lunar day, which lasts about 24 hours 50 minutes because the Moon moves on in its orbit, and you count two high tides, about twelve hours apart. But why two?

Galileo thought he knew. In his 1632 Dialogue he called the tides his best proof that Earth moves, and he scorned Kepler's suggestion that the Moon draws the oceans as a kind of occult magic. Galileo said that the tides were water sloshing in the ocean basins, the way water slops in a barge, as the Earth spins and orbits at once. Kepler, the man he mocked, was right: even the greatest names are checked by the test.

The real puzzle is the second bulge on Earth's far side. A popular textbook account blamed centrifugal force, and it is wrong. The Moon's pull weakens with distance, so it tugs the near water hardest, the solid Earth less, and the far water least; the Earth is pulled away from the far water, which is left behind as a second bulge.

Every month the largest tides arrive at new and full moon, when Sun and Moon line up. Sailors call them spring tides, and the name has nothing to do with the season: it is the old verb, to spring up or leap, and they come twice a month all year.

Tides are slowly changing the Moon itself. Earth's spin carries the bulge a little in front of the Moon, and the bulge tugs the Moon forward along its orbit, so it drifts about 3.8 centimetres farther away each year while Earth's day lengthens. We know the number because laser pulses fired from Earth bounce off retroreflectors that Apollo astronauts left on the Moon, timed to the millimetre. The mirrors are still there and still answering, a running test anyone can point to.

the-transplant-that-beat-squeamishness.context_blurb:
Clostridioides difficile, C. diff for short, is a gut infection that can kill, and its commonest cause is the treatment for some other illness. The cure that works best was reported in 1958 and then left almost untouched for fifty years, because people could not stomach it.

Take a strong antibiotic for a chest infection and the drug sweeps the colon nearly clean. C. diff was living there all along in tiny numbers, kept down by the crowd of bacteria around it, and the antibiotic cleared away those neighbours, the very crowd that had held it down. The disease comes from a vacancy, not an arrival, which is why more antibiotics so often fail to end it.

If the problem is a vacancy, the fix is to refill it. In 1958 Ben Eiseman, a surgeon in Denver, had four patients dying as the lining of the colon sloughed away, and nothing standard helped. He and his colleagues treated the four with enemas prepared from the stool of a healthy donor, and all four recovered quickly. The obstacle afterwards was never the evidence; it was disgust.

Proof came from Amsterdam, where Els van Nood's team set the best antibiotic, vancomycin, against one dose of donor stool delivered through a tube passed down the nose and past the stomach. The tip of that tube reached the duodenum, where the small intestine makes its first bend, so the new community could seed the whole gut from upstream. About four patients in five were cured by a single treatment, and the results were so lopsided that the trial stopped early.

Regulators followed. In December 2022 the FDA licensed Rebyota, the first stool-derived product approved as a drug in the United States, given rectally. In April 2023 a second approval came in a form far easier to accept: purified bacterial spores in a capsule a patient simply swallows.

Success against C. diff sent researchers rushing to try the transplant for obesity, autism, bowel disease and depression, with much murkier results. The deeper gap is that nobody yet knows which particular microbes in a donor's stool do the healing. The purified-spore capsules are partly an attempt to find out, by stripping the mixture down and seeing what is enough.

the-twelve-letters-that-shouldnt-be-ther.context_blurb: The spike protein of the virus that causes COVID-19 must be cut by a specific human enzyme at a specific site before the virus can enter a human cell. The site is called a furin cleavage site. The closest known natural relative of the virus, a bat coronavirus matching it over about ninety-six percent of its genome, is missing exactly that short stretch of twelve letters. So are the two hundred-plus other closely related natural coronaviruses that have been sequenced. The site is not alien to coronaviruses in general. Some other coronaviruses have one. But its absence in this virus's own nearest wild cousins is unexplained. The proposal was rejected. The honest status is that no one has shown where those twelve letters came from.

the-twitching-frog-galvani-versus-volta.context_blurb:
In Bologna in the 1780s, the anatomist Luigi Galvani found that the legs of dead frogs kicked when metal touched them, and decided that living tissue stores the electric fluid of life. Alessandro Volta said the frog was beside the point, and to prove it he built the first battery. Both were right, about different things. 

A skinned frog's leg hung on a brass hook on Galvani's bench. A spark machine crackled nearby but touched nothing; when an assistant's steel blade brushed the hook, the dead muscle twitched. Soon he needed no machine at all: legs hung on brass hooks from an iron railing kicked the moment hook met rail.

Galvani published in 1791 and placed the current inside the creature itself, stored in its own flesh and nerves. He called it animal electricity and likened a frog to a Leyden jar.

Volta praised the book privately and attacked it in public. Then he altered the experiment in a single respect, using one metal for both contacts instead of two, and the leg lay still. The twitch, he argued, came from two different metals joined through something wet, the frog being only a sensitive detector.

He wanted a demonstration with no animal in it, so he held a zinc strip and a silver strip together and set the pair against his tongue. The taste was sharp and sour, like acid. Sulzer had felt that tingle in 1752 and blamed vibration; Volta read it as a current, his own wet tongue completing the circuit.

Galvani answered in 1794 with no metal anywhere. He laid the cut end of one frog's nerve against another frog's muscle, and that muscle contracted too. He published the result without his name on it.

Volta's reply was to build the alternative. In March 1800 he described to Sir Joseph Banks a column of zinc and silver discs, each pair parted by brine-soaked cardboard, which gave sparks and a shock. Pile and battery were other people's words: Volta, who denied that electricity was animal, asked that his invention be named an artificial electric organ, after the layered tissue of the electric eel.

The new instrument opened chemistry within weeks. Nicholson and Carlisle had a pile running in London by that May and used its current to pull water apart into two gases, hydrogen and oxygen. In 1807 Humphry Davy drove Britain's biggest battery into molten potash, and shining beads of potassium, a metal nobody had ever seen, caught fire in the air; his cousin Edmund recorded that Davy bounded about the room in delight.

Politics ended Galvani's part. Napoleon's new republic demanded a loyalty oath from every professor in Bologna in 1797, and Galvani would not swear. It took everything at once: his professorship, his pay, the pension that would have followed and the roof over his head. He died at his brother's home in 1798, while Volta collected a medal from Napoleon and, in time, the unit of voltage named for him.

Galvani's nephew Giovanni Aldini turned the work into spectacle. In London in January 1803, before a crowd, he ran current from a pile into the face of the hanged murderer George Forster: the jaw quivered and one eye opened. The Newgate Calendar says one witness, Mr Pass, a beadle of the Surgeons' Company, was killed by fright shortly after he got home. That one sentence is the only source, so a detail everybody repeats is just the kind worth chasing to its origin. Frankenstein is remembered as carelessly: lightning, bolts at the neck, the creature rising. Mary Shelley's novel has none of it; those images came from James Whale, who filmed the book in 1931.

The quarrel was settled by measurement. Emil du Bois-Reymond built his own instruments: a galvanometer of some twenty-four thousand coils, and electrodes that cancelled the metal-contact effect. In 1847, with his fingers dipped in wired bowls of brine, he clenched the muscles of his own arm, and the needle swung. Volta had been right about the frog-leg experiment, and Galvani right about the bigger thing: animals do make electricity.

A century later Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley showed how. A resting nerve cell sits about seventy thousandths of a volt negative inside, and firing swings it briefly positive. Working on a squid's giant nerve fibre, they found that sodium rushes in while potassium rushes out, and they won the 1963 Nobel Prize. Charged atoms crossing a membrane, not electrons in a wire: your nerves are doing it now.

the-unseen-graveyard-right-to-try-and-th.context_blurb:
Every rule about medicines has two columns. A cautious regulator can save a generation of children from a dangerous drug, and the same caution can keep a dying person from a medicine that might have helped. Honest accounting means counting both columns, including the deaths nobody can interview.

The 2018 Right to Try Act is unusual because its popular name honours no legislator. Instead it carries four names: Jordan McLinn, Matthew Bellina, Frank Mongiello and Trickett Wendler, who were patients with fatal illnesses, or the family of such a patient. Three had ALS; McLinn was a boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who lobbied Congress himself.

The law came from the bottom up. For four years campaigners passed near-copies of it in one state after another, Alaska making forty-one, in order to build political pressure for a federal law. Washington caught up rather than led.

The door the Act opens is narrow. A drug qualifies only once it has passed Phase I safety testing, the first stage in people, without waiting for the full proof of effectiveness. The Act is also a permission, not an order. Three parties along the chain may each still say no: the company that makes the drug, the insurer that would pay, and the doctor who would write the prescription. Supporters answer that permission is exactly what such a patient needs, since the older pathway required the agency's leave.

The other column opens in the late 1950s, when a German morning-sickness drug called thalidomide left thousands of European babies born with badly deformed limbs, at least four thousand of them. American families were largely spared because Frances Kelsey, a Canadian-born pharmacologist reviewing the drug for the FDA, kept sending the application back for thin safety evidence; thalidomide turned out to cause severe birth defects in babies whose mothers took it. Her demand was never to ban it, only to see the data. Congress responded in 1962, in a law President Kennedy signed, by adding a second hurdle to the old safety standard: a maker now had to prove that its drug actually works, generally through two randomised trials.

Then comes the cost. In 1973 the economist Sam Peltzman used the years before 1962 to estimate what would have happened without the new rules and compared that with the years after. He found the rules had roughly halved the rate at which new medicines reached patients, with no matching gain in their quality. Medicines never developed leave no patients to interview, which is why that graveyard stays unseen.

Patients have said so loudly. During the AIDS crisis, promising drugs sat in testing for years while people died, and on 11 October 1988 about 1,500 activists lay down for nine hours at the headquarters of the FDA in Rockville, Maryland. It was ACT UP's first national action, and 176 people were arrested.

the-volunteer-detectives-elisabeth-bik-a.context_blurb:
Peer review is supposed to catch bad science before it is printed, and often it does not. Much of the catching now happens afterwards, by volunteers who read published papers closely and compare the pictures in them. The best known of these readers is a Dutch microbiologist, Elisabeth Bik.

Bik started in 2013 for a personal reason: she found that somebody had plagiarised one of her own papers. Looking for other cases like it, she found a far larger pattern, and eventually left a full-time science post at Stanford to work on research integrity instead.

What she hunts is a copied picture. A photograph of cells, or of a western blot with its dark bands of protein on a gel, carries a random spatter of specks that belongs to that image alone, a kind of visual fingerprint. Rotate it, mirror it or stretch it, and the specks still line up with the original, so a faked result that would hide perfectly in a table of numbers shows itself in a picture to a patient reader.

How common is it? By 2016 Bik and two colleagues had examined 20,621 papers by eye and published the tally in the journal mBio. Roughly one paper in twenty-five carried a wrongly duplicated image. Four percent of the biomedical literature shocked editors who had assumed review was catching such things, and several journals would not touch the study, so it appeared first as a preprint.

Two websites now carry much of this after-the-fact checking. PubPeer, opened in 2012, invites readers to post remarks on any published study, which they find by its reference code, and Retraction Watch, a blog begun in 2010, follows papers that get pulled. Neither is a journal, a university or a government; both run largely on volunteers.

The stakes can be enormous. Matthew Schrag, a neuroscientist at Vanderbilt, was paid in 2021 to examine a struggling Alzheimer's drug, and the work led him to a celebrated 2006 paper by Sylvain Lesne, cited some 2,300 times, which claimed that one particular form of amyloid, called Ab*56, directly caused memory loss in mice. Schrag found signs of spliced and duplicated images; the journalist Charles Piller published the evidence in 2022, and Nature retracted the paper in June 2024.

Sometimes two checks converge at once. Early in 2014 the Japanese biologist Haruko Obokata announced that a quick dip in acid could reset an ordinary cell into a stem cell able to grow into any tissue. Laboratories around the world could not make it work, while readers on PubPeer spotted reused images, and both lines pointed the same way. The papers were withdrawn that July, and genetic testing showed the cells had been ordinary embryonic stem cells all along.

the-wall-that-wasnt-there-the-sound-barr.context_blurb:
People once spoke of the sound barrier as though a wall hung in the sky. There was no wall, but the danger was real, and beating it took a stubborn pilot, a sawn-off broom handle and one brilliant piece of engineering.

The name came from a misreading. In 1935 the British scientist W. F. Hilton showed a reporter a graph of how sharply a wing's resistance rises as a plane nears the speed of sound, and called that steep climb a barrier. The papers printed two words, and the public pictured something solid overhead.

The danger was real enough. Diving fast late in the Second World War, pilots were killed by their own aeroplanes. A diving Spitfire answered a sideways push on the stick by rolling the wrong way, because its soft wings twisted under the aileron's load and the twist won. Engineers call it control reversal.

Bell's engineers had no data from supersonic flight, so they copied a shape that had been flying faster than sound for two hundred years: the X-1's fuselage was shaped after a heavy half-inch Browning machine gun bullet, giving, as they said, a bullet with wings.

That rocket emptied its tanks within a few minutes, nothing like enough to climb from the desert floor as well, so the X-1 was carried aloft in the bomb bay of a B-29 bomber and dropped at 20,000 feet. Chuck Yeager lit the rocket and climbed past Mach 1 in the plane he had named Glamorous Glennis for his wife.

Two nights before the flight a horse threw him, and the fall broke two ribs beneath his right arm. He kept it from the Air Force, which would have grounded him. The trouble was the hatch, which he had to lock by forcing a stiff lever across with that same injured arm. Only the project engineer, Jack Ridley, knew, and he quietly sawed the handle off a broom in the hangar for Yeager to use as a lever.

Ridley solved the deeper problem too. At Mach 0.94 on the eighth powered flight the stick did nothing: a shock wave stood on the tailplane's hinge, so moving the elevator behind it changed nothing. Ridley stopped using the elevator for pitch and had the whole horizontal tail pivot as one piece. That all-moving tail, the stabilator, is nearly universal on combat aircraft today.

Ernst Mach had photographed the physics sixty years early. In Prague in 1887, he and Peter Salcher caught a bullet in flight by lighting it with an electric spark too brief to blur the image. Their plates showed a cone of piled-up air with the bullet at its point, the cone a supersonic jet drags today.

The cone's angle measures speed. A protractor can read it off any such print, and the faster the object flies beyond Mach 1, the narrower that angle grows and the further back it sweeps. At Mach 3 the half-angle measures about 19 degrees.

A boom is not one bang at the moment of crossing. Suppose a fighter crosses the coast supersonic and keeps that speed far inland. A boy 120 miles from the sea under the path hears his crack as the cone sweeps across him, so the sound was made almost overhead, a little short of where he stands. The cone drags a boom carpet along the ground, roughly a mile wide for every 1,000 feet of altitude.

Under a supersonic airliner you hear two cracks in quick succession, less than half a second apart. A ground gauge draws the shape: pressure leaps, falls smoothly below normal, then leaps back, because one shock comes off the nose and the other off the tail.

In 1964 the American government tested whether a city could live with booms, by booming one. Military jets cracked over Oklahoma City roughly eight times daily from February to July, 1,253 booms in all. Residents filed more than nine thousand complaints and over four thousand formal claims, of which the government paid 229, about $13,000 in total. A quarter of those surveyed could not accept it, and in 1973 civil supersonic flight over American land was banned.

The oldest boom is in your back garden, because a cracking bullwhip really does drive a tip of leather past the speed of sound. Goriely and McMillen worked out the physics in 2002: since a whip tapers, a loop running down it must speed up as it reaches the thin end, the same energy carried by ever less leather.

the-war-of-the-currents-told-honestly.context_blurb:
In the 1880s two ways of delivering electricity fought for the future. Thomas Edison's direct current lit lower Manhattan from a station on Pearl Street, but at household voltages it fades over distance, so a city would have needed a power house every mile. Alternating current won, for reasons of physics rather than personality.

Think about what happens inside a wire. Power equals voltage times current, so for a given amount of power a higher voltage means a smaller current, and heating loss rises with the square of the current, so halving the current quarters the waste. Sending power far down a thin copper line therefore calls for the voltage raised as high as possible, which keeps the current in the wire small.

Only alternating current can do that, thanks to one piece of hardware Faraday had already invented. In 1886 the engineer William Stanley lit Great Barrington, a modest Massachusetts town, using a transformer, an iron ring with two coils, which stepped the voltage up for the wires and down again for the lamps. Direct current had no answer to it.

Alternating current still lacked a good motor, and in 1888 Nikola Tesla patented one. He fed several alternating currents, each out of step with the others, into coils set in a ring about an iron rotor, and together they made a magnetic field that walked around the inside of the ring, dragging the rotor after it. Nothing slid against the rotor, so there was nothing to wear out and no sparking. George Westinghouse licensed the patents that July.

The contest ended not in a courtroom but in a bid. Westinghouse and Tesla came in under Edison's camp for the contract to light the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, and on opening day President Cleveland pressed a golden key that set the fair's machinery running, before a sea of electric lamps lit the grounds by night. Some twenty-seven million visitors saw that White City glow, and the contract carried Westinghouse on to Niagara Falls, which from November 1896 sent power twenty miles to Buffalo.

the-whales-that-walked.context_blurb:
Whales are mammals that breathe air, nurse their young and once walked on land. Proving it took two centuries, a famous misnaming, an accident with a hammer, and two rival methods that came to agree.

Richard Harlan, an American naturalist, examined one huge vertebra from Louisiana in 1834, compared it with fossil sea reptiles and named the creature Basilosaurus, king lizard. It was really a whale. Since zoological naming favours the earliest published name, the largest whale of its age keeps a reptile's name forever.

Richard Owen, Britain's leading anatomist, caught it: he pointed at cheek teeth carried on two roots each, and wrote that such teeth are unknown in fishes and reptiles. A reptile's teeth are single-rooted pegs, shed and replaced for life. Owen's own proposed name lost, so the anatomy won and the name did not.

The public had other ideas. In 1845 a showman, Albert Koch, sold New York tickets to a sea serpent he called Hydrarchos. One visit satisfied the anatomist Jeffries Wyman: Koch had wired together bones from five or six separate Basilosaurus animals and padded the backbone out with fossil shells.

The oldest known whale is far smaller. Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell found a skull in fifty-million-year-old rock in Pakistan in 1981 and named the animal Pakicetus. It stood no bigger than a wolf. Nothing in the skull's shape looked like a whale, and one feature carried the whole claim: a dense thickened lip of bone wrapped round the capsule that houses the ear, which isolates vibration so sound can be placed underwater, where a land ear fails.

That skull was all anyone had for twenty years, and a journal cover carried the artist's guess from it: a half-submerged river hunter shaped like a crocodile. In 2001 Hans Thewissen's team found the rest of the skeleton: a long-legged runner on land, four working legs, no more amphibious than a tapir. The guess had been honest and wrong. The bones did carry one aquatic clue, abnormally dense limbs, which act as ballast so an animal can sink and walk a riverbed.

Then come legs that swam. Ambulocetus natans, three metres long, turned up in Punjab in 1992. Nobody has watched one hunt, yet Thewissen read its method from the skull, because its eyes sat high on the head and looked upward, as a crocodile's do when it lies just under the surface watching the world above.

Later whales kept the legs as miniatures. A sixteen-metre Basilosaurus from the Egyptian desert, reported in 1990, still had both hind limbs in place, each a mere thirty-five centimetres long, and each held a whole leg in little: a knee joint, fused ankle bones and three small toes.

Biologists call such a limb vestigial. The word means only that its old job, walking, is gone, and the same 1990 paper gave the little leg a duty it still did: steering two animals into position while mating.

Molecular biologists came at it another way. In 1999 Nikaido, Rooney and Okada read jumping genes: a scrap of DNA lands at one spot in a genome and, in practice, never leaves, so a shared landing site is hard to explain except by common ancestry. Their answer put hippos closest to whales. It backed a 1994 case by Graur and Higgins, who had placed whales within the even-toed hoofed mammals, the group of deer, pigs, camels and cattle. Fossil hunters did not believe it.

The fossil camp, following Leigh Van Valen, favoured extinct hoofed meat-eaters with similar triangular teeth. In 2001 both camps published early whale ankles from Pakistan in one month, and each held the weight-bearing foot bone grooved like a pulley at both ends. That double groove belongs to the even-toed hoofed mammals alone, so the molecular reading was right. Gingerich's own 1990 paper had read such feet the other way; he published the bones that refuted him.

Their nearest known cousin surfaced by accident. A. Ranga Rao, an Indian geologist, had collected fossils of a small deer-like plant-eater, Indohyus, in Kashmir, and his widow passed the rocks to Thewissen after his death. In the laboratory a worker's hammer slipped and split one skull open. The break bared the middle ear, and there sat the same dense thickened margin that had once marked whales alone. Indohyus matches whales in four ways at once: that ear, its premolar shape, dense limb bones, and the oxygen in its teeth, a record of a life spent largely in water.

the-wrong-strength-glue.context_blurb:
Two handy products began as failures. One chemical stuck to everything and was thrown out twice; another would not stick properly. Both became useful only when somebody changed the question he asked of it.

Harry Coover's team at Eastman Kodak wanted, in 1942, to mould clear plastic cheaply rather than grind each piece from glass. What they needed in quantity were the sights a fighter pilot aims his guns through. Their mixture welded itself to the moulds and glassware, so Kodak dropped it.

Nine years later, at Kodak's Tennessee plant, the chemist Fred Joyner tested the same compound while studying heat-proof plastics. To measure how much it bends light he spread a thin layer between the glass prisms of a refractometer, and the prisms welded shut, ruining that instrument for good. The accident matched 1942; what had changed was the specification in Coover's head. He read the wreck as a result: glue needing no heat, no clamp and no drying time.

Kodak sold it from 1958 as Eastman 910. On a television panel show in January 1959 Coover glued a steel cable to a bar with a single drop, and the host, Garry Moore, was hoisted clear off the studio floor dangling from the joint.

Why so fast? Nothing evaporates as superglue sets. The trigger is the film of water lying on practically every surface, even a dry-looking benchtop. Hydroxide ions from that moisture attack the molecule and start a chain reaction that zips its small molecules into long solid chains within seconds.

The molecule is built to be attacked. Two greedy groups, a cyano and an ester, crowd the carbon next door to its double bond and haul electrons off it, so that bond is left stripped and defenceless. The same pair spreads the charge on the growing chain, so once started it keeps going. Skin, offering moisture and amino acids at once, is the worst thing to touch.

Then why does a tube not harden on the shelf, with water vapour all around? Because the maker adds an acid, which holds the reaction back until the liquid reaches a surface. Test the consequence: a thin smear bonds better than a fat blob, because the reaction starts at the surfaces and a thick bead never sets through.

Crime labs made the chemistry a tool. Seal a stolen laptop in a chamber, warm a few drops of superglue until they fume, and invisible fingerprints appear, because the vapour feeds on sweat residue and grows hard white polymer along every ridge of the mark.

The opposite accident happened at 3M in 1968. Spencer Silver poured in too much of one reactant by mistake while chasing the strongest sticky glue on 3M's shelf, a glue meant for bonding the panels of an aircraft together. Out came its mirror image, and it sat unused while Silver pitched it at seminar after seminar, calling it a solution that was still waiting for its problem.

His stuff is not weak glue thinned down. A Post-it carries tough acrylate spheres on its sticky side, spread so thinly that the sheet meets the paper only at scattered points, like resting on a heap of marbles. They will not dissolve, melt or flow, and they spring back to round when squashed, so the note peels away cleanly and grips again dozens of times.

The use came from a choir stall. Art Fry, a 3M engineer who sang in a St. Paul church, marked his hymnal in advance, and at every service the little markers slipped from between the pages, leaving him singing from the wrong one. He had sat through one of Silver's seminars, and he saw that how thickly those spheres are spread sets how hard the sheet grips.

Even then it nearly died. In 1977 the pads went on sale in four test cities as Press 'n Peel, on ordinary stationery shelves, and almost nobody bought one: a shopper in the aisle could not tell what a pad was for. Joe Ramey and Geoff Nicholson, who worked for him, refused to give up. They picked Boise, Idaho, and gave pads away free, pressing samples into the hands of secretaries and office managers. Nine in ten said they would buy the pads, double any rate 3M had ever seen.

The pads reached shops nationwide in April 1980, canary yellow, and that colour has never changed, for the least glamorous of reasons: the laboratory next door happened to keep a stack of canary yellow scrap paper.

theranos-show-me-the-machine-working.context_blurb:
Theranos promised to change medicine: hundreds of blood tests from one prick of a finger, run on a box of its own design called the Edison. At its peak the company was valued near nine billion dollars. The claim broke chemistry long before it broke the law, and the people who exposed it were junior staff, not the famous board or the regulators.

The box did little of the work. When investigators looked, the Edison ran only about a dozen of the advertised tests, and the rest went through commercial analysers, bought from Siemens and quietly modified.

Start with the volume. A pricked fingertip yields somewhere between fifty and a hundred microlitres, and one routine glucose test uses roughly fifteen of them. Split a single drop across hundreds of tests and each portion falls below the smallest quantity the chemistry can detect.

Theranos made up the difference with salt water, because an analyser designed for blood drawn from a vein wants more liquid than a fingertip gives. Diluting a sample drags whatever is being measured down toward the instrument's noise and multiplies every small error, which is ruinous for a test like blood potassium, where the healthy range is narrow. A diluted sample can push a well patient into an alarm or hide a real crisis.

The internal numbers were already dreadful. In October 2014 some 29 percent of the Edison's own quality-control checks fell outside the company's acceptable range, and federal inspectors later found its hormone test missing the company's accuracy mark on most days of February 2015, so patients were handed wrong readings. The founder and chief executive who had promised otherwise was Elizabeth Holmes.

Forbes had made her famous. In 2014 the magazine valued Theranos near nine billion dollars and reckoned Holmes, at least on paper, the world's youngest female billionaire to have built her own fortune, some 4.5 billion of it. Once reporters had shown what the machines could not do, Forbes recalculated in 2016 and put her worth at zero dollars.

Regulators delivered their verdict in January 2016. After inspecting the laboratory in Newark, California, where tests included the prothrombin time used to set doses of the blood thinner warfarin, the federal lab regulator wrote that the practices there posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety. That is the gravest finding it can make, and Walgreens stopped sending blood from its stores to the lab.

In May 2016 the company took a step medical laboratories almost never take: it voided or corrected tens of thousands of results, about two years' worth, including tests for calcium, estrogen and testosterone. At least one doctor in Phoenix had already sent a patient to an emergency room on the strength of a bad number.

The criminal trial ended in San Jose in January 2022, and a sentence of eleven years and three months followed that November. The jury found that Holmes had defrauded investors, who had wired more than 140 million dollars, but acquitted her of defrauding the patients tested at Walgreens. The lesson for anyone handing over money or blood is simple: ask to watch the test run start to finish, on that machine, now.

thomsons-corpuscle-and-the-model-built-t.context_blurb:
At the end of the nineteenth century J.J. Thomson found something smaller than an atom, then built a picture of the atom around it, precise enough that one experiment could kill it. To be refuted by its own prediction is a compliment to a model.

Cathode rays were the mystery: a glow from a metal electrode in an evacuated tube. Thomson measured the bend a magnet gave the beam, then measured again with another metal electrode, then with another gas in the tube; the figure never budged. A ray belonging to its metal should have changed with the metal.

Charge would show in an electric field, and nobody had got that bend, a point critics pressed. Thomson managed it in 1897 at no higher voltage, by realising that gas still inside the tube conducted and screened the field away.

From the two bends he got the mass carried per unit of charge, and set it against hydrogen's, the lightest thing known. His particle proved a thousandfold lighter than any hydrogen atom. He called it a corpuscle, and claimed more than two measurements could guarantee: that all matter is of one and the same kind, the substance out of which every element is built. Lecturing at the Royal Institution in April 1897 he met disbelief, and years later he recorded a physicist present confessing that he thought Thomson was pulling their legs.

The name came before the thing. From the laws of electrolysis, by weighing metal that a current deposits, George Johnstone Stoney reasoned that charge comes in one smallest lump, sized it in 1874 and in 1891 called it the electron.

His 1904 atom was arithmetic, not decoration. He calculated where corpuscles would sit and circle inside a ball of positive electricity: one in the middle, a pair facing, a trio in a triangle, rings beyond. His target was the old riddle of why an element's properties come round again at regular intervals. Rings fill and close, he proposed, the outermost fixing how an element combines. He never wrote the words plum pudding, and his corpuscles moved, not set in dough.

The rings came from a water dish. Around 1878 Alfred Marshall Mayer floated corks pierced by magnetised needles under a magnet. Six or fewer spread into one ring, equally spaced; the seventh was driven inside that ring, near the middle of the water.

Thomson corrected himself too. He had guessed about a thousand corpuscles to an atom, then counted them in 1906 by three unrelated routes: light spreading through a gas, X-rays scattering, beta rays being soaked up. All three landed near one corpuscle for hydrogen and twenty-five for a molecule of air. He had been wrong a thousandfold, and proved it.

Then came the kill, and Thomson published its arithmetic. His 1910 paper asked what his atom required of a fast, heavy alpha particle crossing gold foil hundreds of atoms thick. Smeared positive charge cannot shove hard, so thousands of feeble nudges would heap into a bell curve, and the most his paper allowed was a bend of roughly two degrees. The experiment found one alpha in twenty thousand turning back past a right angle, off the bottom of that curve altogether.

His own student ran it. Ernest Rutherford reached the Cavendish in 1895, worked under Thomson, performed the test that wrecked his atom, and in 1919 took over his chair.

About 1913 Thomson steered a positive neon beam through crossed fields onto a photographic plate, puzzled that pure neon weighed an awkward 20.2. The plate showed two distinct patches, one at mass twenty and one at twenty-two. An element arriving in two weights means isotopes, so that figure was a mixture's average.

The family had the last joke. In the 1920s his son George Paget Thomson fired electrons through a thin crystal onto a plate, as Clinton Davisson was doing in America, and the electrons spread and interfered just as light waves do. The two shared the 1937 Nobel Prize, thirty years after J.J. took his for showing the electron behaves as a particle, and neither prize was a mistake. That is wave-particle duality.

Even the dead model left a live question: where N equal charges settle over a sphere to make repulsion cost the least energy. It is called the Thomson problem, and a cousin of it is on Steven Smale's 1998 list for the new century. Proofs exist for a handful of small values of N and for twelve; everything else rests on computer search.
